pages.tldr: A 1 minute typing test is the standard 60-second check of typing speed: type the passage for exactly one minute, then get instant WPM, accuracy, and error counts. WPM is scored as correct characters divided by 5 divided by 1 minute, so 300 correct characters equals 60 WPM, with both raw and net (errors subtracted) scores shown. pages.heroP: Test your typing speed in exactly 60 seconds. This one minute typing test measures your words per minute (WPM) and accuracy — the standard quick check most typing sites use.

seo.h2: 1 minute typing test
p: A 1 minute typing test is the standard way to measure typing speed: you type a passage for exactly sixty seconds, then read your score in words per minute (WPM) and accuracy. One minute is long enough to smooth out a lucky or unlucky burst, and short enough that you can retake it every day without thinking about it. Most schools, employers and online benchmarks quote speed from a sixty-second run, which makes this the most comparable single measurement in typing.

seo.h2: How the one minute test works
p: Select the 1 min duration, click the text area and start typing — the timer starts on your first keystroke, not before, so you can settle your hands first. While you type you see the live countdown, your current WPM and your accuracy. When the clock reaches zero the test locks and shows the full result: net WPM, raw WPM, accuracy, characters per minute, errors and a consistency score.

Net WPM is the number that matters: it is your gross speed with errors deducted, so a fast but sloppy run scores lower than a slightly slower clean one. Raw WPM ignores errors and shows your pure finger speed. The gap between the two tells you whether to push speed or tighten accuracy. After the result you also get a per-key report — the letters you miss most and the letters that slow you down — which turns one sixty-second run into a practice plan.

seo.h2: One minute vs other test lengths
p: Every duration answers a different question. Short sprints measure peak speed, the classic sixty seconds measures your working speed, and the long formats expose what fatigue does to your accuracy. The table below shows what each length on this site actually tells you and when to use it.

DurationWhat it measuresBest for
15 secondsPeak burst speed before fatigueWarm-up, quick daily check
30 secondsBurst speed with a little settlingTracking sprint progress
1 minuteWorking speed — the standard benchmarkRésumés, school, daily measurement
2 minutesSpeed sustained past the first adrenalineChecking if your 60s score holds up
3 minutesEarly fatigue effects on accuracyExam-style practice
5 minutesReal stamina and concentrationData-entry and transcription work
10 minutesFull endurance typingLong-form writers, professionals

A useful rule: if your two-minute score is much lower than your sixty-second score, your speed is real but your consistency is not — practise accuracy, not sprints. If the two scores are close, your technique is stable and you can safely push for more speed.

seo.h2: What your 1 minute score means
p: Typing speed falls into rough bands. Around 40 WPM is the average adult — fine for everyday email and documents. Between 60 and 80 WPM beats most office workers and is the usual 'fast typist' claim on a résumé. Above 80 WPM is professional territory, and anything past 100 WPM puts you in roughly the top one percent of typists.

Accuracy matters as much as the headline number. A 55 WPM run at 98% accuracy is worth more to an employer than 70 WPM at 90%, because error correction is the hidden tax on every document you produce. Aim for 97% accuracy or better first; speed follows on its own.

seo.h2: Reading your 1 minute result in detail
p: The headline number is net WPM: correct characters typed, divided by five, divided by the time — the industry-standard formula, with errors already deducted. Next to it sits raw WPM, your gross speed before any penalty. When the gap between the two is small, your technique is clean and speed work will pay off. When the gap is wide, every extra word of speed is being bought with mistakes you then pay back in corrections.

The consistency percentage measures the evenness of your keystroke timing. Two typists can finish with the same net score while one typed in smooth rhythm and the other in bursts and stalls; the smooth typist gets the higher consistency, and in real work the smooth typist tires less and errors less. Below the scores, the per-key report lists your most-missed letters and your slowest letters — they are rarely the same key. Missed keys need accuracy drills; slow keys need repetition until the reach becomes automatic.

Every result is saved privately in your browser, so the one-minute run doubles as a progress log. Comparing today's score with last week's tells you more than any single run, because daily scores wander by a few points in both directions — the trend line is the real measurement.

seo.h2: How to get a higher 1 minute score
p: Warm up with a 15-second sprint, then take the full minute seriously — your second run of the day is usually your best. Keep your eyes on the screen and your fingers on the home row; every glance at the keyboard costs you several words over sixty seconds. Type slightly below your panic speed: the single biggest score killer is the error-and-backspace cycle.

Train the text types that slow you down. If numbers and punctuation break your rhythm, run a few rounds in numbers or quotes mode until they feel automatic — symbols are the most common slowdown in any timed run. Use the weak-key report after each test and drill those letters specifically instead of re-typing whole passages you already handle well. Ten focused minutes a day beats an occasional hour.

seo.h2: Five mistakes that cap your 1 minute score
p:
• Typing at panic speed. Pushing past the point where your accuracy holds, then donating the gains back through corrections. The fix feels backwards but works: slow down five percent and the net score climbs.
  • Looking at the keyboard. Every glance breaks rhythm and costs several words over sixty seconds. If you still need to look, spend a week on home-row drills before chasing speed.
  • Ignoring symbols. Digits and punctuation are where otherwise-fast typists lose the most time, because practice usually means plain prose. A few rounds a week in numbers or quotes mode closes that gap quickly.
  • Retaking immediately without reading the weak-key report. You rehearse the same errors and they set deeper. Read the report, drill the two worst keys, then retest.
  • Practising in rare long sessions. Typing skill is motor memory, and motor memory consolidates with daily repetition. Ten focused minutes every day moves the score more than an occasional hour.

seo.h2: A simple 7-day plan for a higher 1 minute score
p: Day one: take the test once, note your net WPM and accuracy, and read the weak-key report carefully — that is your baseline. Day two: accuracy day. Type slower than feels natural and finish above 98%; the number does not matter today. Day three: symbols day, in numbers and quotes modes, because symbols are the most common rhythm-breaker.

Day four: weak-key day. Take the two keys the report flagged and drill them with short 15-second rounds until the reach is automatic. Day five: speed day — warm up with two 15-second sprints, then give the full minute everything you have; sprint-warmed fingers reliably score higher. Day six: stamina day, one two-minute run. If it lands far below your sixty-second score, consistency — not speed — is what to train next.

Day seven: rest your hands, then retake the baseline under the same conditions as day one — same time of day, same keyboard, same warm-up. Compare net WPM, accuracy and consistency side by side. Most people see a real gain in the first week, almost all of it coming from accuracy rather than raw speed. Repeat the cycle and let the trend line compound.

seo.h2: Setting up a fair 1 minute test
p: Scores are only comparable when conditions are stable. Test at the same time of day — most people type noticeably faster mid-morning than late at night — and on the same keyboard, because key travel and layout differences change your numbers more than a week of practice does. Sit with both feet on the floor, wrists slightly raised, and close anything that might interrupt you mid-run.

Warm up with a single 15-second sprint before the measured run; cold fingers underperform by several points and make your history noisy. Then settle, breathe, and start typing — the timer waits for your first keystroke, so there is no reason to rush the start.

seo.h2: The 1 minute test for jobs, exams and daily use
p: Employers asking for a typing speed almost always mean a sixty-second net WPM figure, so this page is the number to quote. Many government, bank and court clerk exams also use short timed passages; practising the exact one-minute format removes the pacing anxiety on test day. For everyday improvement, a daily sixty-second run with your score history saved in the browser is the simplest possible progress tracker.

Want the raw keystroke view as well? The CPM typing test shows your characters per minute next to WPM, the words per minute test explains the scoring in detail, and the typing speed calculator converts your score into the other units employers use.

seo.h2: Why sixty seconds became the standard
p: The one-minute format won out because it sits at a sweet spot between stability and effort. Anything shorter — ten or fifteen seconds — measures your burst speed, which flattered by adrenaline and a lucky first word; anything longer starts measuring fatigue as much as skill. Sixty seconds is long enough for the lucky and unlucky moments to average out, so two runs on different days produce genuinely comparable numbers, yet short enough that retaking it daily costs nothing.

That comparability is why schools, employers and typing benchmarks settled on the minute as the default unit of account. When a job posting says 'types 60 WPM', it almost always means sixty WPM measured over a one-minute passage at high accuracy. Practising in exactly that format means the number you quote and the number they test are the same number.

There is a practical benefit for training too. Because a run costs only a minute, it survives as a habit: before work, after lunch, between tasks. Skill in typing compounds through exactly that kind of frequent, measurable repetition, and no other duration makes measurement this cheap.

seo.h2: What to do after a one minute test
p: A single number is not progress. Log the score, then use the typing practice plan for a week and retake the same length under the same conditions. If the score moves, keep the routine; if it stalls, the how to get better at typing guide explains which drill matches which bottleneck.

If you are still looking at the keyboard while you type, the ceiling on this score is technique rather than finger speed: the home-row method behind touch typing is what lets a sixty-second round be read from the screen instead of copied from the keys.

seo.h2: Sources for the numbers on this page
p: Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.

The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.

Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.

p: Last updated 2026-10-20. Written and maintained by the Typing.Rerivo team; scoring formulas, sources and corrections policy are documented on the about page.
If sixty seconds feels like a sprint rather than a score, the two-minute typing test shows what you hold once the warm-up fades.
For the endurance number that transcription and data-entry work actually measures, use the ten-minute typing test - a one-minute score overstates it by 5-10 WPM.

faq.q: What is a 1 minute typing test?
faq.a: A 60-second timed round: type the passage shown for exactly one minute, then get your WPM, accuracy and error breakdown instantly. One minute is the most-quoted test length, so scores compare directly across sites and job requirements.

faq.q: How is WPM scored on the 1 minute test?
faq.a: Correct characters divided by 5, divided by the one elapsed minute. Because the test lasts exactly sixty seconds the maths is simple: 300 correct characters equals 60 WPM. The results panel shows both raw WPM and net WPM with errors subtracted.

faq.q: Is 1 minute the right test length?
faq.a: For most people, yes: 60 seconds balances speed bursts against fatigue and matches the length employers and benchmarks use. Take longer 3 or 5 minute tests when you want a steadier, hiring-grade number.

faq.q: Is the 1 minute test free?
faq.a: Yes — unlimited 1 minute rounds, no sign up, no ads in the typing area. Your history stays in your own browser.

faq.q: How can I raise my 1 minute score?
faq.a: Warm up with one throwaway round, then focus on accuracy: at 95%+ accuracy speed follows. Keep your fingers on the home row, look at the text not your hands, and practise daily with typing drills.

faq.q: Is a 1 minute typing test accurate?
faq.a: Yes, for a quick check. Sixty seconds is long enough that one lucky sentence does not decide the result, and it is the length employers and typing certificates use, so your score compares directly. Take a 3 or 5 minute test when you want a steadier number.

faq.q: Is a one minute typing test the same as a 60 second typing test?
faq.a: Yes - one minute and sixty seconds are the same length, and both mean the standard short benchmark. The label changes by site, the measurement does not.

faq.q: What is a good 1 minute typing speed?
faq.a: Around 40 WPM is average, 50-60 is above average, and 70+ on a one-minute round is fast. Because a minute avoids fatigue, expect it to read 5-10 WPM higher than your five-minute score.

faq.q: Can I take a one minute typing test on a phone?
faq.a: You can, but the score will not be comparable. Phone typing averages 36 WPM against 52 on a desktop keyboard, so take any test that counts on a physical keyboard.

pages.title: 2 Minute Typing Test - Free Typing Test 2 Minutes WPM
pages.metaDesc: A 2 minute typing test shows whether speed holds after the first rush. Type for 120 seconds, then compare with your one minute score.
pages.heroP: Test your typing speed over 2 minutes — long enough for a stable WPM score, short enough to stay sharp. A great middle ground between the quick 1 minute test and the full 5 minute test.

seo.h2: 2 minute typing test
p: The 2 minute typing test is a popular middle-ground length. Two minutes is long enough that your score reflects real typing speed rather than one lucky sentence, yet short enough to keep full concentration. Type the passage as fast and accurately as you can — WPM, accuracy and errors are counted automatically.

seo.h2: 1 minute vs 2 minute vs 5 minute
p: A 1 minute test is a quick check, a 2 minute test is a reliable everyday measure, and a 5 minute test is best for serious benchmarking. If you are practising daily, the 2 minute test is a comfortable default that balances speed feedback and stability.

seo.h2: Why a 2-minute typing test
p: Two minutes is the sweet spot between a quick sprint and a full endurance run. It's long enough to settle into a steady rhythm and smooth out a shaky start, yet short enough to retake several times in a sitting. Many employer screening tests use a two-minute format, which makes it ideal practice for job applications.

seo.h2: A daily 2 minute practice routine
p: One reliable routine: open the test at the same time each day, take exactly two rounds with a one-minute stretch break between them, and keep the better score. Two rounds a day is enough to show a trend within a fortnight — most steady practicers gain 5 to 10 WPM in the first month. When progress stalls for a full week, switch to targeted drills for your slowest keys instead of adding more test rounds; our typing tips explain how to find them.

seo.h2: 2 minute typing test vs 1 minute and 3 minute
p: Two minutes is the shortest round where a single bad sentence stops dominating the score. A 1 minute typing test can swing 10-15 WPM on one unfamiliar sentence; across two minutes that swing halves.

• 1 minute - good for daily speed checks and quick warm-ups.
  • 2 minutes - the sweet spot for a repeatable score you can track week to week.
  • 3 minute / 5 minute - endurance and technique, used for screening.
If you are tracking progress, keep the length fixed. Comparing a 2 minute score against a 5 minute score tells you about endurance, not improvement.

seo.h2: How to pace a two minute round
p: Open slightly under your target speed and let the first sentence calibrate you. Most typists gain 3-6 WPM in the second minute simply by relaxing into rhythm; the ones who lose points are those who sprint the first twenty seconds and spend the rest recovering. Keep your eyes one word ahead of the cursor and your hands still between keystrokes.
If you want a stricter reading of the same two minutes, switch the text mode to quotes: capitals and punctuation are where accuracy quietly leaks away, and the result screen will show it.

seo.h2: 2 minute typing test for employment
p: Two-minute formats appear in clerical and customer-service screening because they fit inside a short interview slot. The format that matters is unfamiliar text, one take, and an accuracy floor of 95%. Practise with a passage you have not seen and resist the urge to retake — employers do not offer one. The typing test for jobs page lists the common thresholds by role.

seo.h2: Moving between test lengths
p: Length changes what a score means. A sixty-second round is the format schools, employers and certificates quote most, so it is the number to keep as your baseline: the 1 minute typing test is the reference point every other duration on this site is compared against. Longer rounds then measure how much of that baseline survives, and shorter rounds measure how quickly you can reach it cold.

seo.h2: How this round is scored
p: Each round scores correct characters using the five-character word convention described for words per minute: five characters, spaces and punctuation included, count as one word. A clean round also reports accuracy next to net WPM, because the two numbers answer different questions — how fast your fingers move, and how much of that speed survived contact with the keyboard.

faq.q: How long is a 2 minute typing test?
faq.a: Exactly 120 seconds. When the timer runs out your WPM, accuracy, characters per minute and error count appear instantly.

faq.q: What is a good 2 minute WPM?
faq.a: Around 40 WPM is average, 60+ is good and 80+ is professional. Accuracy above 95% is just as important as raw speed.

faq.q: Is the 2 minute test free?
faq.a: Yes. Free with no sign up; retake the full two minutes as often as you like and every result is stored only on your own device.

faq.q: Can I retry as many times as I want?
faq.a: Yes, there is no limit. Click “Test again” for a fresh passage and your history keeps the last results.

faq.q: Should I use a 2 minute or 3 minute test for job practice?
faq.a: Use the length your employer uses. If the posting does not say, practise on 3 minutes: it is the stricter of the two because endurance decay has time to show up, and a good three-minute score transfers down to a two-minute format.

pages.tldr: Two minutes is the shortest length that shows a stable pace. Most screening tests run one to three minutes, so a two-minute net score is close to what an employer would see.

pages.title: 5 Minute Typing Test - Free 5 Min WPM Test
pages.metaDesc: Five minutes of continuous typing in net WPM with accuracy beside it. Most people sit 5 to 15 percent below their one minute sprint here.
pages.heroP: Measure your sustained typing speed over a full 5 minutes. A longer test averages out lucky bursts and fatigue, giving a more reliable words per minute (WPM) score than a quick 1 minute test.

seo.h2: 5 minute typing test
p: The 5 minute typing test is the best way to measure your real, sustained typing speed. Over five minutes your score settles down: a single fast or slow sentence no longer dominates the result, and natural fatigue is factored in. This is why many employers and typing certifications prefer a 3-5 minute test over a 60 second one.

seo.h2: Who should use a 5 minute test?
p: If you type for a living — data entry, transcription, programming, customer support — the 5 minute test reflects your working speed far better than a short burst. Take it a few times a week and watch your WPM and accuracy trend in the saved history below.

seo.h2: Build typing endurance
p: A five-minute test measures something a quick sprint can't: how well you hold speed and accuracy as your hands tire. Pace yourself, keep your posture relaxed and your wrists level, and breathe. Finishing strong on the five-minute test is a reliable sign your typing is ready for long real-world sessions of writing, coding or data entry. If you want to see how far that endurance goes, run the 10 minute typing test once a month and compare how much of your speed survives to the final minute.

seo.h2: How to prepare for the 5 minute test
p: Treat a five-minute attempt like a short workout: sit with feet flat and wrists floating level with the keyboard, roll your shoulders once, then run a 1 minute typing test as a warm-up. Keep water nearby but skip coffee right before — caffeine jitters tend to show up as extra errors around minute three. During the round, breathe steadily and use sentence breaks as micro-rests for your eyes. Two prepared attempts a week beat seven tired ones.

seo.h2: 5 minute typing test: what a longer round reveals
p: Short tests measure reflexes; a 5 minute typing test measures technique. Most errors that show up here are not typos but fatigue patterns: the left hand drifts off home row, the pinky stops reaching for shift, and accuracy falls before speed does.

• Speed decay - the WPM you hold at minute four is your working speed. Warm-up speed is not.
  • Accuracy drift - watch whether accuracy falls over time. If it does, slow down rather than push.
  • Rhythm breaks - long pauses cluster around punctuation and capitals, which is where drills pay off most.
Best practice once you have a baseline: run 1 minute typing tests daily for speed, and a 5 minute round weekly to confirm the speed is sustainable.

seo.h2: Where the five-character rule comes from
p: Every five-minute score on this page uses the standard five-character word, the same convention summarised by words per minute: a word is five characters, including spaces and punctuation. That is what makes a five minute result comparable with a one minute result taken on a different site — and what makes the endurance drop between the two formats measurable at all.

If you need to know how the speed holds over a real work session rather than a five-minute block, the 10 minute typing test stretches the same measurement to the point where fatigue, posture and pacing dominate the score.
If five minutes feels long for a first run, start with the three-minute test and work up.

faq.q: Is a 5 minute typing test more accurate?
faq.a: Yes. Longer tests average out short bursts of speed and moments of fatigue, so a 5 minute result is more stable and representative of your true typing speed than a 15 or 60 second test.

faq.q: What is a good 5 minute WPM?
faq.a: 40 WPM is average, 60+ WPM is good, and 80+ WPM is professional level. Maintaining high accuracy over 5 minutes matters more than peak speed.

faq.q: Is the 5 minute test free?
faq.a: Yes. Free with no sign up and no limit on retakes; the whole five-minute endurance round costs nothing and uploads nothing.

faq.q: Does the test save my progress?
faq.a: Your last results are saved locally in this browser (localStorage) so you can track improvement over time. Nothing is sent to a server.

pages.tldr: A 5 minute typing test measures sustained speed rather than a sprint: most people type 5 to 15 percent slower over five minutes than over one, and that gap is the number worth tracking. Five minutes is long enough for pacing and fatigue to show, short enough to repeat weekly. Run it after a one minute warm-up, keep wrists level, and compare the result with your own one minute score rather than with someone else's.

pages.title: Capital Letter Typing Test - Shift Key Practice
pages.metaDesc: Capital letter typing test built on shift-key pairs and sentence case, so you can see whether the pinky shift is costing you words.
pages.heroP: Practise uppercase letters and the Shift key with a focused capital letter typing test. Build muscle memory for capitals and symbols while tracking your WPM and accuracy.

seo.h2: Capital letters are a two-hand problem
p: A capital needs Shift pressed with the hand that is not typing the letter, then a quick return to the home row. Most people learn to use the same hand for both, which breaks the hand position and costs three keystrokes of rhythm for every capital.
On a sentence with six capitals in twenty words, that is roughly a 5% speed penalty and a much larger accuracy penalty, because the hand has to find the home row again after each one.

seo.h2: Shift or Caps Lock
p: Shift for a single capital, Caps Lock for a run of them. Anything else mixes habits: Caps Lock for one letter means you press it twice and lose the rhythm either way, and forgetting to turn it off produces a burst of errors.

If your operating system has a sticky-keys or Shift-lock behaviour, turn it off before practising. It masks the exact reach you are trying to build, and it will not be there on the keyboard an employer hands you.

seo.h2: A drill that transfers
p: Type proper nouns and sentence starts for one minute, then check which hand pressed Shift. If the same hand typed the letter, the error is structural, not speed-related - and it will keep appearing in every exam passage.
Then run a two-minute round with normal sentence case and compare the accuracy to your all-lowercase score. A drop of more than 3% means capitals are the weak link.

seo.h2: Where it matters most
p: Names, places, product names, legal defined terms and the start of every sentence. In legal and medical documents a wrong capital can change the meaning; in exam passages it is a scored error.
For the punctuation half of the same skill, see the punctuation test; for the exam context, typing tests for jobs.

faq.q: What is a capital letter typing test?
faq.a: A test using sentence case and proper nouns, so it measures how you handle Shift as well as letter location.

faq.q: Why are capital letters hard to type?
faq.a: They need Shift with the opposite hand plus a return to the home row. Using the same hand for both breaks the hand position and costs rhythm on every capital.

faq.q: Is the capital letter test free?
faq.a: Yes, no account needed, results stored in your browser.

faq.q: Do I use Shift or Caps Lock?
faq.a: Shift for a single capital, Caps Lock for a run of them. Mixing the two creates habits that fail under time pressure.

faq.q: How much speed do capitals cost?
faq.a: About 3-5% on ordinary sentences, and more on text dense with proper nouns. Accuracy usually drops more than speed.

pages.tldr: Capitals need Shift with the opposite hand and a quick return to the home row. Drill them separately, because a broken Shift rhythm costs more words than a slow letter.

seo.h2: What makes this easy
p: Three adjustments: common short words, no digits or unusual punctuation, and a one-minute default so the round ends before fatigue arrives. The point is to remove everything except the skill being built - finding keys without looking.

Easy is not the same as slow. Type at the pace where you make almost no errors; if accuracy is below 95%, slow down further rather than pushing. At this stage speed is a side effect of accuracy, not a separate goal.

seo.h2: The three habits that decide your ceiling
p:
• Looking at the keyboard. Every glance costs a beat and prevents the mental map from forming. Cover your hands once a day, even if it feels slow.
  • Backspacing through every slip. At beginner speeds, corrections cost more than the errors. Practise finishing rounds without correcting.
  • Two-finger typing. It works to about 35-40 WPM and then stops. If you are under 30 WPM, learning the home row now is cheaper than fixing it later.

seo.h2: What to do after the easy test
p: Once you hold 95% accuracy at 30 WPM on easy text, move to the beginner test with normal sentences, then to the one-minute test. The easy page is a starting gate, not a home.
If you are already above 40 WPM, this page will flatter you - switch to the hard typing test, which includes capitals, digits and long words.

faq.q: What makes this an easy typing test?
faq.a: Common short words, no digits or unusual punctuation, and a one-minute default. It isolates key-finding from everything else.

faq.q: I am a slow typist - where do I start?
faq.a: Two 60-second rounds a day, hands covered for one of them, and no backspacing. That combination removes the two habits that cap beginners at 30-40 WPM.

faq.q: Is it free?
faq.a: Yes, with no account and no ads in the typing area. Results stay in your browser.

faq.q: What WPM should I expect first?
faq.a: Most untrained adults start at 20-30 WPM with 90-95% accuracy. Below 20 WPM is usually two-finger typing rather than a lack of ability.

faq.q: When should I move to a harder test?
faq.a: When you hold 95% accuracy at 30 WPM on easy text. Moving earlier just moves the errors to harder text.

seo.h2: Why "English typing test" is its own query
p: For most of the world, an English typing test is simply a typing test. But in South Asia - and especially in India - "English typing test" is a specific exam format: 35 words per minute in English (or 30 in Hindi) for clerical posts, taken on a standard keyboard for ten minutes, with a small error allowance.
That is why this page treats English as one option among several rather than as the default. If you are preparing for an exam, the exam's rules matter more than the language label.

seo.h2: What English asks of your hands
p: English on QWERTY is the best-supported layout in the world, which is why most speed records are set on it. The characters that decide accuracy are not the letters but the punctuation: the apostrophe, the comma, the full stop and the capital that follows it.
A useful drill is sentence case with quotes. Most candidates lose 3-5 WPM there, and it is the exact content of an exam passage. Practise it weekly rather than daily - it is a check, not a workout.

seo.h2: Practising in the exam's conditions
p: Use the same length as the exam (ten minutes for SSC, five for federal), type a passage with full punctuation, and score net WPM plus errors. Then repeat on a different keyboard at least once: exam centres do not provide your laptop.
If your error count is the problem rather than your speed, stop chasing WPM for two weeks and run accuracy rounds at 85% of your pace. A clean 37 WPM passes; a 45 WPM run with 12% errors does not.

faq.q: What is the typing speed required for English typing tests in exams?
faq.a: 35 words per minute for SSC CHSL LDC and JSA posts, over ten minutes, with a small error allowance. US federal clerical roles ask 40 WPM over five minutes with at most three errors.

faq.q: Is English typing speed measured in WPM or KPH?
faq.a: Both, depending on the post. SSC DEO uses 8,000 key depressions per hour; clerical and federal roles use words per minute. 8,000 KPDH is about 27 WPM.

faq.q: How many mistakes are allowed?
faq.a: A small allowance, commonly around 5% of the words typed, and it is stated in the notice for that exam cycle. The federal standard is stricter: three errors in five minutes.

faq.q: Does punctuation count in an English typing test?
faq.a: Yes. Capitals and punctuation are part of the passage and an omitted character is an error. Practise sentence case with quotes, which is where most candidates lose their margin.

faq.q: Can I use my own keyboard in the exam?
faq.a: No. Centre equipment is used. Rehearse on a different keyboard at least twice so key travel and layout are not a surprise.

seo.h2: What Spanish adds to a Latin keyboard
p: Four characters do most of the damage: ñ, the accented vowels á é í ó ú, the inverted marks ¿ ¡, and the dieresis ü in words like pingüino. On a Spanish layout they have dedicated keys; on an English layout they need dead keys or Alt codes, which is a different skill entirely.
If you are preparing for an exam or a job in a Spanish-speaking country, practise on the layout you will actually face. Typing Spanish on an English keyboard trains a workaround, not the skill.

seo.h2: Why the accents matter more than they look
p: Accents change meaning, not just spelling: si (if) and sí (yes), el (the) and él (he), esta and está. Omitting one is a real error in the language, not a typo, which is why Spanish typing tests treat a missing accent as a mistake.

The inverted question and exclamation marks are typed at the start of the sentence, so they require a look-ahead: you have to decide the sentence is a question before you begin it. That is why they show up in error reports.

seo.h2: QWERTY, AZERTY and the Latin American layout

The differences are small but they cost accuracy for the first week. Practise on the layout you will be tested on.

p: Start with sentences that include at least one accent and one punctuation mark per line - that is what ordinary Spanish looks like. Then add a numbers round, because dates and amounts are where Spanish-language office work actually lives.

faq.q: Do accents count as errors?
faq.a: Yes. Accents change meaning in Spanish - si and sí, el and él - so a missing accent is a language error, and Spanish typing tests treat it as a mistake.

faq.q: Should I use a Spanish keyboard layout?
faq.a: If you are preparing for an exam or job in a Spanish-speaking country, yes. Typing Spanish on an English layout with dead keys trains a workaround rather than the skill you will be tested on.

faq.q: Why do the inverted ¿ and ¡ slow me down?
faq.a: They are typed at the start of a sentence, so you must decide the sentence is a question before you begin typing it. That look-ahead is an extra decision per sentence.

seo.h2: Keyboard typing test
p: A keyboard typing test checks how fast you type on your keyboard and how accurate you are. It works the same on laptop, mechanical and full-size keyboards. Measuring regularly shows whether a new keyboard or layout actually improves your speed.

seo.h2: Test any keyboard, not just the one you own
p: A keyboard test answers one question honestly: how fast are your hands on this keyboard? Laptop keyboards, mechanical switches and full-size boards all have different travel and feedback, and your WPM shifts with them. Test the keyboard you use for work, then test the one you game on; the difference tells you which one your hands actually like.

seo.h2: Keyboard typing tips
p: Keep your wrists relaxed and fingers anchored on the home row. Use all ten fingers rather than hunting and pecking. A comfortable keyboard with good key travel helps, but consistent practice matters far more than the hardware.

seo.h2: Works with any keyboard layout
p: This keyboard typing test runs on QWERTY, AZERTY, Dvorak and Colemak alike — it simply measures the characters you type against the target text. Membrane, mechanical or laptop scissor-switch, the physical board doesn't change the score. What matters is muscle memory: knowing where each key sits without looking so your hands stay anchored on the home row.

seo.h2: Build true touch typing
p: Touch typing means typing without watching your fingers. Use the small bumps on the F and J keys to find the home row by feel, then return to it after every reach. The on-screen keyboard below highlights the next key so you can gradually stop looking down at your real keyboard and trust your hands instead.

seo.h2: Is my keyboard working? A key-by-key check
p: If you arrived looking for a way to test whether keys are broken rather than how fast you type, this is the same exercise from the other direction: the test above records which characters you produce, so a key that never registers will show up as a missing character rather than a slow one.

1. Type every character deliberately, including Shift, in a one-minute round: a-z, 0-9, and the punctuation you use.
  2. Read the error report, not the score. A key that produces nothing shows up as an omission on every attempt; a key that double-registers shows as extra characters.
  3. Repeat on a second device if possible - if the same key fails on both, it is the key; if only one, it is that keyboard or its connection.
  4. For a laptop, note whether it fails only on battery - some keyboards behave differently under power management.

This will not diagnose a hardware fault with certainty, and it cannot test keys your operating system intercepts (media keys, function-row shortcuts). For those, use the operating system's own input viewer.

p:

Mechanical (linear)3-4 mmConsistent actuation, no tactile bump; slightly faster for most typists

faq.a: Type every character deliberately in a one-minute round and read the error report: a dead key appears as a repeated omission, a double-registering key as extra characters. Repeat on another device to tell a key fault from a keyboard or connection fault.

pages.heroP: Practise typing numbers fast and accurately. Numeric typing is a separate skill from text — essential for data entry, accounting and finance. This number typing test measures your digit speed and accuracy.

seo.h2: The digit row is a separate skill
p: Letters sit under your fingers. Digits sit on the row above, reached by an extended finger with no tactile landmark to confirm the position. That is why someone who types prose at 60 WPM often drops to 30-35 WPM on numbers, and why data-entry employers test digits separately.

There are two ways to enter numbers and they are not interchangeable. The number row is right when digits are mixed into text (an address, a reference code). The numeric keypad is right when the work is amounts, quantities or codes entered field by field.

seo.h2: What employers actually measure
p:
UnitFormulaTypical requirement
Keystrokes per hour (KPH)characters per minute × 608,000-12,000 for data entry
Key depressions per hour (KDPH)all keys, corrections included8,000 for SSC DEO
Fields per hourcompleted recordsrole-specific
Accuracycorrect fields ÷ total97-99%
A correction costs you twice: once as a keystroke against the hour, and once as a field that has to be re-checked. That is why digit accuracy is worth more than digit speed.

seo.h2: How to practise without a spreadsheet
p: Two minutes of Numbers mode, twice a day, graded on errors rather than speed. Then add the parts that break in real work: decimals, negative signs, and the Tab key between fields.
If you are learning the keypad, use the 4-5-6 home row (index on 4, middle on 5, ring on 6, thumb on 0) and press Enter after each figure, because that is how accounting software behaves.

seo.h2: Where numeric speed pays
p: Data entry, accounting, insurance claims, medical billing, warehouse admin and dispatch all live on digits. Each has its own page on this site with the specific thresholds - see 10,000 KPH for the data-entry benchmark and 10-key typing for the keypad version.

seo.h2: Digits fail differently from letters
p: A letter error is usually visible: the word looks wrong. A digit error looks exactly like a correct number, which is why numeric work is judged on verification rather than on speed. The typical numeric mistakes are transposition (1234 typed as 1324), doubling (11 instead of 1), and a wrong-row slip that turns 4 into 5 or 7 into 8.

Transposition is the most common and the hardest to catch, because both digits are individually valid. It is also the reason numeric drills should be scored on complete fields rather than on character accuracy.

seo.h2: Drills by digit group
p:
GroupWhere it failsDrill
Top row 1-5Left hand reaching up, index finger confusionAlternate 3-4-3-4 and 4-5-4-5 for 30 seconds
Top row 6-0Right hand, weakest fingers7-8 and 9-0 pairs; then 6-7-8-9-0 sequences
Amounts with decimalsThe dot key position, and trailing zerosType 10 amounts with two decimals, verify each
KeypadHome row 4-5-6 and the thumb on 0Enter ten figures, press Enter after each
Two minutes a day on one row beats ten minutes cycling through all of them, because the failure is local.

faq.q: Why is my number typing speed so much lower?
faq.a: Digits sit on the row above the home row and have no tactile landmark, so every digit needs a reach and a visual check. A 40-50% drop from prose speed is normal.

faq.q: Should I use the number row or the keypad?
faq.a: The keypad for amounts and long numeric strings, the number row when digits are mixed into text. Learning ten-key properly takes about a week and pays for itself in data-entry work.

faq.q: What is a good numeric typing speed?
faq.a: 8,000-12,000 keystrokes per hour is the band employers quote for data entry. That is roughly 27-40 WPM equivalent, with accuracy at 97% or better.

faq.q: Do corrections count in a numeric test?
faq.a: In key-depression scoring, yes - every backspace is another keystroke against the hour. That is why typing it right the first time matters more than typing fast.

faq.q: How much practice does it take?
faq.a: Two minutes twice a day for two to three weeks is enough to see a clear gain, mostly from the digit row ceasing to need a visual check.

faq.q: Why do I transpose digits?
faq.a: Both digits are individually correct, so there is no visual signal that anything is wrong. It is the most common numeric error and the reason numeric work is scored on complete fields rather than on characters.

pages.tldr: Numbers are a separate skill: the digit row needs extended reaches with no tactile landmark. Practise in two-minute rounds and score errors, because data-entry work is judged on digit accuracy.

seo.h2: Benefits of an online test
p: Because it's browser-based, you can test your typing speed anywhere — at work, school or home — without software. Your results are saved locally so you can track progress over time, completely private.

seo.h2: How to improve your online typing speed
p: The fastest way to raise your WPM online is short, regular sessions. Five focused minutes a day beats one long weekly grind. Keep your fingers on the home row (ASDF JKL;), glance at the screen instead of the keys, and let your weakest fingers — the pinkies and ring fingers — do their share of the work. Speed follows accuracy, so slow down whenever your error count climbs.

seo.h2: Who uses an online typing test
p: Students check their words-per-minute before online exams, remote workers warm up before a day of emails, call-centre and data-entry applicants rehearse for employer screening tests, and programmers measure how quickly they move through code. Because the test is browser-based and private, anyone can benchmark their speed in under a minute and come back to track steady improvement.

seo.h2: Online typing test vs installed typing software
p: An online typing test needs nothing installed, which matters when you are checking speed on a work laptop, a borrowed machine or a Chromebook.

• No install or admin rights - the test runs in the browser.
  • Same engine everywhere - your score does not depend on which machine you used.
  • Nothing leaves the device - results are stored in your own browser, not uploaded.
The one trade-off is the keyboard itself. Typing on an unfamiliar keyboard can cost 5-10 WPM, so if you are comparing scores, compare them on the same machine.

seo.h2: From testing to practising
p: A test tells you where you are; practice moves you. The online typing practice page turns your score into a daily 10-minute routine with weak-key targeting.

seo.h2: What makes an online typing test trustworthy
p: Four things decide whether a browser typing test gives you a number worth quoting:

1. It reports net WPM, not only gross. A test that counts every character and never subtracts errors will flatter you by 5-10 WPM.
  2. It states the length and lets you change it. A 15-second burst and a five-minute run are different measurements.
  3. It shows accuracy beside speed. Speed without accuracy is not what employers screen on.
  4. It does not reward skipping punctuation. If capitals and full stops are absent from the passage, the score will not transfer to a document.
None of that requires an account. A test that gates the score behind a sign-up is optimising for its own funnel, not for your measurement.

seo.h2: Device and browser caveats
p: Your keyboard changes the result more than your browser does. A laptop board, a mechanical board and a phone screen produce three different scores for the same skill - roughly 51 WPM, similar or slightly higher, and 36 WPM respectively in the published measurements.

Two browser-level things are worth knowing: autocorrect and text-expansion tools can inflate a score without you noticing, and browser zoom changes how much text is visible, which changes how far ahead you can read. Test at 100% zoom, with autocorrect off, on the device you will be tested on.

faq.a: It reports net WPM (errors subtracted), states the test length, shows accuracy beside speed, and includes capitals and punctuation in the passage. Sign-up walls and gross-only scoring are the usual red flags.

faq.q: Does my browser affect the score?
faq.a: Less than the keyboard does, but autocorrect, text expansion and unusual zoom levels all change the result. Test at 100% zoom with those tools off.

pages.title: Punctuation Typing Test - Symbols & Marks Practice
pages.metaDesc: Punctuation typing test with quotes, commas, brackets and symbols at real density. Where most fast typists quietly lose characters.
pages.heroP: Drill commas, periods, quotes and symbols with a punctuation typing test. Punctuation is where accuracy drops most, so train it directly and watch your WPM improve.

seo.h2: Why punctuation is where accuracy breaks
p: Letters sit under your fingers; punctuation does not. The comma, full stop, apostrophe and semicolon need extended reaches and often a Shift press, and none of them appear often enough in normal practice to become automatic.

There is a second reason: punctuation carries meaning. A missing apostrophe changes a word, a wrong comma changes a clause, and a full stop in the wrong place ends a sentence early. Typists who treat it as decoration produce text that has to be re-read.

seo.h2: The marks that cost the most time
p:
MarkWhere it isWhy it slows you down
Apostrophe 'Right of the semicolonRight little finger, already the weakest, with no Shift
Comma ,Right of MSame finger as the apostrophe; frequent in real sentences
Full stop .Right of the commaFollowed by a capital, so it is a two-key rhythm
Shifted symbols : ? ! "Top row with ShiftTwo keys at once, opposite hands, and a return to the home row
If your error report concentrates on the right-hand column of the keyboard, that is not a knowledge problem - it is a reach problem, and it responds to short daily drills.

seo.h2: How to drill punctuation without boredom
p: Use real sentences, not symbol lists. A list of punctuation marks trains the key but not the rhythm; sentences train the transition from word to mark and back, which is what actually fails under time pressure.
Then run one round where you deliberately slow to 80% and check every mark. The next round, type normally and see whether the accuracy carried over. Two rounds is a session; ten minutes is enough.

seo.h2: Where punctuation decides a test result
p: Exam passages include capitals and punctuation, and an omitted character counts as an error on every mainstream test. Candidates who skip punctuation to gain speed usually lose more in the error allowance than they gain in WPM.
For the exam-shaped version, see typing tests for jobs; for the capitals half of the problem, the capital letter test.

faq.q: What is a punctuation typing test?
faq.a: A test using sentences with full punctuation and capitals, so the score reflects how you handle marks rather than only letters.

faq.q: Why do I make so many punctuation errors?
faq.a: Punctuation needs extended reaches, often with Shift, and appears too rarely in normal typing to become automatic. Right-hand marks are the usual weak spot.

faq.q: Is the punctuation test free?
faq.a: Yes, no account, and results stay in your browser.

faq.q: Which punctuation marks slow typists down most?
faq.a: The apostrophe and comma, both under the right little finger, and shifted symbols such as : ? ! which need two keys at once.

faq.q: Do punctuation errors count on exams?
faq.a: Yes. An omitted or wrong mark is an error, and most tests apply an error allowance that a punctuation-skipping strategy will exhaust.

pages.tldr: Punctuation is where fast typists lose accuracy. Run rounds with real sentences and shift-punctuation, then check the error count rather than the speed.

pages.title: Typing Accuracy Test - Free WPM & Accuracy Test
pages.metaDesc: Free typing accuracy test. Measure how accurately you type alongside your WPM, see your error count and improve precision. No sign up.
pages.tldr: A typing accuracy test measures what percentage of your keystrokes are correct, and 95 percent accuracy is the threshold where speed becomes genuinely useful, since below it fixing mistakes costs more time than typing slowly saves. Net WPM subtracts errors from raw WPM, so a fast but sloppy 70 WPM round can score worse than a clean 55 WPM one. Professionals in transcription and data entry hold 97 to 98 percent or more, average typists sit near 92 to 95 percent, and anything under 90 percent signals technique to fix first. Slow down 10 percent, use all ten fingers from the home row, and let speed rebuild on top of clean keystrokes.
pages.heroP: Measure your typing accuracy, not just speed. See your error count and precision alongside WPM. Free, no sign up.

seo.h2: Typing accuracy test
p: A typing accuracy test shows what percentage of characters you type correctly, alongside your WPM and error count. Accuracy is often more valuable than raw speed — a fast typist who makes many mistakes is slower overall once corrections are counted.

seo.h2: How to improve accuracy
p: Slow down slightly and aim for zero errors first; speed follows naturally once your fingers learn the correct movements. Focus on the keys you miss most, and keep your eyes on the screen so you can catch mistakes as they happen.

seo.h2: Why accuracy beats raw speed
p: A blazing WPM means little if half your words need fixing. Every mistake costs a backspace and a retype, so real-world typing speed depends far more on accuracy than on peak pace. This test shows accuracy next to WPM and counts your errors, so you can see exactly where clean typing is quietly slowing you down.

seo.h2: How to type more accurately
p: Start slower than feels natural and let correct keystrokes build muscle memory — rushing only teaches your fingers the wrong moves. Watch for your personal problem keys (often the top row and punctuation), keep a light, even rhythm, and resist the urge to glance at the keyboard. Aim to hold accuracy above 97% before you push for speed.

seo.h2: Sources for the numbers on this page
p: Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.

The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.

Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.

seo.h2: Speed and accuracy together
p: The two metrics feed each other: how to type faster and more accurately explains the error-cost math, and typing speed improvement tips puts accuracy first for a reason.

faq.q: What is a good typing accuracy?
faq.a: Aim for 95% or higher. Professional typists usually stay above 97% accuracy while maintaining good speed.

faq.q: Why does accuracy matter more than speed?
faq.a: Every error needs correcting, which costs time. High accuracy means your effective speed is close to your raw speed.

faq.q: Is this accuracy test free?
faq.a: Yes, free with no sign up. Results are stored only in your browser.

faq.q: What accuracy should I aim for before pushing speed?
faq.a: Hold 97% or higher first; only then add pace. Below 95%, every extra WPM costs more correction time than it saves, so the score looks faster while real output slows down.

pages.title: Online Typing Practice — Free Drills, 15s to 10 Minutes
pages.metaDesc: Free online typing practice with timed drills from 15 seconds to 10 minutes: sentences, quotes, numbers and words, instant WPM. No sign up, progress saved.
pages.tldr: Ten minutes a day beats an hour a week. The plan changes one variable per week: week 1 removes the look-down habit, week 2 fixes accuracy, week 3 adds digits and punctuation, week 4 measures a five-minute score you can reproduce.
pages.heroP: Free typing practice online. Switch between sentences, quotes, numbers and words, pick a longer test, and train every day. Your past results are saved in this browser so you can watch your speed grow.

seo.h2: typing practice
p: Regular typing practice is the only reliable way to get faster. Ten to fifteen minutes a day beats one long session once a week, because your muscles learn the key positions through repetition. Use this page every day: pick a mode, type the text, then compare your result with yesterday. Try to keep accuracy above 95 percent at all times. This doubles as typing test practice: the same engine, the same scoring, so a drill round here is a rehearsal for the real thing.

seo.h2: Start here: today's ten minutes
p:
1. Warm up (2 min) - one round on the current text mode, no target. Just wake the hands up.
  2. Drill the thing you are worst at (5 min) - pick one from the table below. One weakness per session; two at once means you cannot tell which one worked.
  3. Check (3 min) - one timed round and write down net WPM and accuracy. That is the number next week's comparison uses.
If you have no idea where you are weak, take one accuracy test and look at the error list rather than the score. The errors name the drill you need.
This is deliberately short. Ten minutes, done daily, beats an hour on Sunday - the skill is motor memory and it consolidates between sessions, not during them.

seo.h2: A four-week practice plan
p:
WeekDaily 10 minutesCheckpoint (Friday)
1 - Remove the cap2 min warm-up, 5 min home row or covered round, 3 min normal textAccuracy above 92% without looking down
2 - Accuracy2 min warm-up, 5 min accuracy at 85% pace, 3 min normal textThree consecutive rounds above 97%
3 - Digits and punctuation2 min numbers, 3 min punctuation, 5 min sentencesDigits at 97% accuracy, punctuation intact
4 - Length and pace2 min warm-up, two 3-minute rounds, one 5-minute roundA five-minute net score you can reproduce
Each week changes exactly one variable. That is why the plan works: if you change the drill and the length and the text mode at once, a better score tells you nothing about what caused it.

seo.h2: The four bottlenecks practice must target
p: Every slow typist is slow for one of four reasons, and each needs a different drill. Accuracy bottlenecks show as a wide gap between net and raw speed — fix them with controlled rounds at a 98% floor. Speed bottlenecks show as clean but slow rounds — fix them with 15-second sprints that stretch the ceiling. Symbol bottlenecks show as collapses on numbers and punctuation — fix them with dedicated numbers and quotes rounds, because everyday prose never trains those keys.

Stamina bottlenecks show as accuracy decaying in the final third of a long test — fix them with weekly three-to-five-minute endurance rounds. Read your result panel in that order and the panel tells you which bottleneck you have this week. Practice without this diagnosis is just repetition.

seo.h2: Drills by bottleneck
p: Match the drill to the bottleneck — this is the whole art of practice. The table maps each bottleneck to the drill that fixes it and the metric that proves the fix.

BottleneckSymptom on result panelDrillFix metric
AccuracyNet WPM far below raw WPM90% pace, 98% floor roundsNet-raw gap closes
SpeedHigh accuracy, low WPM15-second max-effort sprintsSprint WPM rises
SymbolsCollapses on digits/punctuationNumbers / quotes mode roundsSymbol rounds match prose
StaminaAccuracy decays late in testWeekly 3-5 minute roundsFinal-third errors drop
Specific keysSame keys in weak report15s weak-key bursts dailyKeys leave the report

Notice the fix metric column: every drill has a way to know it worked, usually within one to two weeks. If a drill's metric has not moved in two weeks, the bottleneck moved — re-read the panel and change the drill.

seo.h2: Typing exercises for every skill
p: Change the text mode to target your weak spots. Sentences build everyday typing fluency. Quotes add capital letters and punctuation. Numbers train the top row, which is the slowest part of the keyboard for most people. Words mode drills common English vocabulary so high-frequency words become automatic.

seo.h2: When practice stops working
p: A plateau near 50 or 70 WPM usually means one bottleneck, not general slowness: check your slowest keys in the result panel after each round. Spend a week drilling only those keys in accuracy test rounds at 97%+ before chasing speed again. If accuracy is fine but speed stalls, your rhythm is uneven — try 2 minute tests at a metronome-steady pace instead of sprinting. Most plateaus break within two focused weeks.

seo.h2: How to know your practice is working
p: Weekly, not daily: one measured round under identical conditions, recorded with the date. Three numbers tell you everything — net WPM rising means the system works; accuracy falling means you are pushing too hard; consistency dropping means fatigue or posture drift needs attention before any drill.

Keep the log where you will actually look at it. A simple note with twelve weeks of numbers is more motivating than any badge system, and it is the only reliable way to catch a plateau in week one instead of week six.

seo.h2: Common practice mistakes
p: Practising speed first: every error costs about two correction keystrokes, so sloppy speed practice builds a faster way to be slow. Practising rarely: an hour on Sunday consolidates worse than ten minutes daily, because motor memory forms between sessions. Practising without measurement: if you are not tracking a number, you are rehearsing, not improving.

And the quietest one: practising only what you are already good at. Comfortable text feels productive and fixes nothing. The weak-key report is the opposite of comfortable — and that is exactly where the gains live. For a ready-made weekly structure, the online typing practice plan maps drills to goals, and typing speed exercises lists the full drill menu.

seo.h2: Practising for a specific goal
p: For an employment test: practise the exact format — same duration, unfamiliar text, one take — twice a week, and hold accuracy two points above the gate. For raw speed: alternate sprint days and rhythm days, and accept that gains past 80 WPM come in single points per month. For a new language: practise that language's word pool daily; accuracy habits transfer between scripts faster than vocabulary does.

For school or everyday competence: you need far less than you think. Forty WPM at 97% accuracy covers almost every daily need, and the typing speed requirements table shows what specific jobs actually ask for — most are lower than people fear.

p: Most free typing practice sites are free until you want to see your score, then ask for an account. faq.a: Untimed, repeatable drills across sentences, quotes, numbers and words modes. Unlike a scored test, practice lets you retry weak keys freely and watch per-key accuracy improve before you take a timed test.

faq.q: Can I use this page for typing test practice?

faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes. Short daily sessions build the motor pattern; a single long weekly session mostly builds frustration and fatigue.

pages.heroP: Free typing lessons for every level. Learn touch typing one step at a time: home row first, then every finger, then real speed. Each lesson is a timed practice you can repeat until it feels effortless. No sign up, learn at your own pace.

seo.h2: typing lessons
p: Good typing lessons build speed the safe way: one habit at a time. Touch typing means typing without looking at the keyboard, and it is the single biggest speed upgrade most people can make. Instead of hunting for keys with two fingers, you train all ten fingers so each key has a fixed finger and muscle memory takes over. The result is faster, steadier typing that also frees your eyes for the screen.

seo.h2: Start every lesson with the home row
p: Every typing lesson plan starts in the same place: the home row. Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ; with your thumbs on the space bar. Feel for the small bumps on F and J; they tell your index fingers where to land without looking. Practice typing words made only of home row letters until you never have to think about it, because every other key is reached from this position.

seo.h2: A free four week typing lesson plan
p: Week one: home row only, short one minute lessons, accuracy over speed. Week two: add the top row and the shift keys for capitals, two minute lessons. Week three: cover the bottom row and the number row, then try the number text set. Week four: mix sentences, quotes and punctuation, and test your WPM against week one. Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough; most learners reach 40 to 60 WPM within a month of daily lessons. If you want a full curriculum rather than a weekly plan, the free typing lessons for adults page lays the four weeks out lesson by lesson.

seo.h2: Typing lessons order: what to learn first
p: Lessons only work in the right order. Learning speed before home row is the most common way people stall.

• 1. Home row - asdf jkl; until you can find each key without looking.
  • 2. Top and bottom rows - add one row at a time; accuracy first, speed later.
  • 3. Capitals and punctuation - use the capital letter typing test and punctuation typing test.
  • 4. Numbers - separate skill; the number typing test covers it.
  • 5. Speed and endurance - only now use the 1 minute and 5 minute timed tests as training.
The typing tutorial covers the same ground as a single ordered walkthrough, if you would rather follow one page than pick lessons.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn touch typing?
faq.a: Most people reach a comfortable 40 to 60 WPM with 10 to 15 minutes of daily practice for three to four weeks. Reaching 80 WPM or more takes a few more months of regular use, but the daily time stays the same.

faq.q: Are these typing lessons free?
faq.a: Yes. Every lesson is free, with no sign up, no account and no paywall. You can repeat each lesson as many times as you like, and your results are saved only in your own browser.

faq.q: How often should I take typing lessons?
faq.a: Daily is best, but short. Ten to fifteen minutes every day beats a single long session once a week, because muscle memory is built by frequency rather than by total minutes.

faq.q: Do I need a special keyboard or a paid course?
faq.a: No. Any standard keyboard works, and these free lessons cover the same finger placement as paid typing courses. Start with the home row (A S D F J K L ;) and add one row at a time.

faq.q: What is the difference between touch typing and hunt-and-peck?
faq.a: Hunt-and-peck means looking at the keys and pressing them with one or two fingers, which is slow and tiring. Touch typing uses all ten fingers from the home row without looking, so typing becomes faster, more accurate and far less effort.

pages.tldr: Lessons are ordered by row, not by speed: home row first, then top, then bottom, then capitals and punctuation. Ten minutes a day for two weeks is enough to make the key map automatic.

seo.h2: learn to type faster
p: Most people who want to learn to type faster are already typing every day, so the problem is not volume but method. Two things hold typists back: looking at the keyboard, and fixing mistakes. When you stop looking down, your speed jumps almost immediately, because your eyes stop lagging behind your fingers. When you chase accuracy instead of raw speed, you stop losing time to backspacing, and speed rises on its own.

seo.h2: What slows most people down
p: Three areas cause almost all slow typing: numbers, punctuation, and the shift keys. Most learners are fluent with common words but freeze the moment a digit or a comma appears. Turn your weakness into a drill: spend a few minutes a day on the number and punctuation text sets until they feel as easy as sentences. Also check that you press shift with the opposite hand, never by stretching the same finger across the keyboard.

seo.h2: A four week plan to type faster
p: Week one: one minute tests only, target 98 percent accuracy, ignore speed entirely. Week two: add two minute tests and switch to quotes to train capitals and punctuation. Week three: use the number set daily, and start tracking your average WPM across the week. Week four: push for speed on one minute tests and compare with week one. Most typists add 10 to 25 WPM in a month with ten to fifteen minutes of this training a day.

seo.h2: More ways to get faster
p: Working through the system here? These guides go deeper on specific goals: how to get better at typing with a 4-week system, how to type faster for beginners, and typing speed exercises that target each bottleneck.

faq.q: How fast can I realistically learn to type?
faq.a: With ten to fifteen minutes of daily practice, most people reach 40 to 60 WPM in three to four weeks and 70 to 90 WPM in two to three months. Progress is fastest at the start and then levels off, which is normal.

faq.q: Why has my typing speed stopped improving?
faq.a: A plateau usually means you are practicing what you are already good at. Change the drill: switch text sets, lengthen the test, or focus on accuracy for a week. Speed plateaus break when you rebuild accuracy at the new, higher speed.

faq.q: How long should I practice typing each day?
faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes every day beats a single long weekly session. Short, daily sessions build muscle memory, while your attention stays sharp enough to keep accuracy high.

faq.q: Should I focus on speed or accuracy to get faster?
faq.a: Accuracy first, always. Every error costs a backspace and retype, so fast-but-sloppy typing is actually slower. Aim for 98 percent accuracy; when that feels easy, speed follows without extra effort.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to learn to type?
faq.a: Learn touch typing from the home row (A S D F J K L ;) so you never look at the keyboard, then practice daily with a timed test. Combining proper finger placement with a short daily drill is the quickest path to real speed.

seo.h2: typing tips
p: The best typing tips are the boring ones, because typing is pure muscle memory. Anything you repeat daily becomes automatic, and anything you shortcut becomes a habit you later have to unlearn. Pick two or three tips below and apply them for a week rather than reading all of them once. Small adjustments to hand position and attention add up faster than any speed-typing trick.

seo.h2: Posture and hand position tips
p: Sit with your feet flat, your forearms roughly level, and the top of your screen at eye height so your neck stays relaxed. Curve your fingers slightly and rest them on the home row: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they let your index fingers find home without looking. Keep your wrists floating rather than pressed hard onto the desk.

seo.h2: Accuracy tips that also build speed
p: Look at the text, never your hands. Press every key with the finger that owns it on the home row rather than the nearest finger, even when it feels slower at first. Type to the end of a word before you fix an error, instead of stopping mid-word. And slow down to the speed at which you make almost no mistakes; that is the speed your fingers actually learn, and it rises on its own.

seo.h2: How to type faster and more accurately: a weekly routine
p: Speed follows accuracy, not the other way round. This is the routine that raises both without turning practice into a chore.

• Day 1-2: form only. Run slow rounds at 95%+ accuracy. Ignore WPM entirely.
  • Day 3-4: steady rounds. Hold a pace you can repeat. Use a 2 minute typing test so the score is comparable.
  • Day 5: push one round. Accept lower accuracy to find your ceiling, then go back to form work.
  • Day 6: weak keys. Identify the two or three letters that cost you most and drill them with typing practice.
  • Day 7: rest. Progress in typing is consolidated between sessions.
Two things reliably hold people back: looking at the keyboard, and chasing WPM while accuracy is still below 95%. Fix the second one first, with how to type without looking and typing accuracy test.

p: Beyond general tips: typing speed improvement tips ranked by impact, how to type faster and more accurately with the dual-metric method, and how to type 100 WPM for the elite path. Still deciding where to measure? The best free typing tests compared page covers the alternatives honestly, including this one.

faq.q: What is the single most important typing tip for beginners?
faq.a: Keep your fingers on the home row and look only at the screen. Once your hands learn where the keys are, speed becomes a matter of practice instead of searching.

faq.q: How do I stop looking at the keyboard while typing?
faq.a: Cover your hands with a cloth or dim the room light for a few minutes a day, and use the on-screen keyboard to check positions. The bumps on F and J give your index fingers a landmark, so trust them and keep your eyes on the text.

faq.q: Which finger should press which key?
faq.a: Each key has a home-row finger that owns it. Index fingers cover the middle columns and stretch outward, middle and ring fingers take their own columns, and the pinkies handle the outer edges plus the shift and enter keys. Practice slowly at first so each key keeps its fixed finger.

faq.q: How do I improve my typing accuracy?
faq.a: Slow down until you make almost no errors, finish each word before correcting, and practice the number and punctuation sets, which cause most mistakes. Accuracy is a habit, not a limit, and it is what ultimately raises your speed.

faq.q: What is a good typing posture?
faq.a: Feet flat, back supported, shoulders relaxed, forearms roughly parallel to the floor, and the screen top at eye height. Your wrists should float over the keyboard rather than resting heavily on the desk, which keeps your fingers quick and pain-free.

pages.tldr: The four changes that move the number fastest: stop looking at the keyboard, stop correcting during a test, type sentences instead of random words, and practise five minutes daily rather than once a week.

The fix is simple: use the short round for the fun, and check in with a five-minute round once a week. If the two numbers drift apart by more than 10 WPM, the sprint is flattering you.

seo.h2: words per minute test
p: A words per minute test (WPM test) measures how many words you can type in one minute. The rule is simple: every five characters counts as one word, so longer words add more to your score. Take the test, type the text shown on screen, and your WPM, accuracy and error count are calculated live as you type.

In practice a typing words per minute test is the same measurement under a different name: you type for a fixed time, the test counts correct characters, and dividing that count by five and by the elapsed minutes gives your WPM. Nothing else changes the number, so any result you see here is directly comparable with other typing tests. The name changes with word order too — WPM typing test, typing test WPM and words per minute test all point at the same measurement, so whichever phrasing you searched for, this page scores it the same way.

seo.h2: What is a good WPM score?
p: What counts as fast depends on context, but the bands below hold for most desk work. Around 40 WPM is typical, 60 WPM handles office and writing work comfortably, and 80+ WPM is genuinely fast — professionals land between 90 and 120. New typists should chase 95%+ accuracy first; speed follows on its own.

seo.h2: WPM vs CPM
p: CPM means characters per minute. Some sites show CPM instead of WPM. Because one word equals five characters, you can convert easily: WPM = CPM / 5. This test shows you both numbers on the result panel so you can compare with any other typing test.
Prefer characters per minute? Try the CPM typing test, where CPM = WPM × 5.

seo.h2: Typing words per minute test: what the number means
p: A typing words per minute test reports one number for one minute of typing, using a convention rather than a literal word count: every five characters typed counts as one word, whether those characters formed short words, long words, numbers or punctuation. The Wikipedia entry for words per minute documents the same five-character standard and the reference bands that most tests still quote: professional typists sit around 43 to 80 WPM, and advanced typists go above 120 WPM.

Two numbers come out of a typing words per minute test and they are not interchangeable. Gross (raw) WPM counts every keystroke, including the ones you had to correct. Net WPM deducts those errors, which is why a fast, careless run can post a high raw score and still be the slower run. When a job application or a certificate asks for your speed, the figure they want is net WPM with accuracy reported next to it — anything under about 95 percent accuracy means the speed is not yet usable in real work.

If your target is quoted in keystrokes rather than words — common for data entry and for exam scoring — measure it directly with the CPM typing test, which reports characters per minute and keystrokes per hour from the same round.

seo.h2: Sources for the numbers on this page
p: Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.

The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.

Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.

faq.q: What does a words-per-minute test measure?
faq.a: It converts everything you type into a WPM score using the 5-characters-per-word standard, alongside accuracy and error counts. This page runs the test at 60 seconds, the standard length employers quote.

faq.q: How is WPM calculated?
faq.a: WPM = (correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes elapsed. The industry standard treats every 5 characters as one word, so longer words count more. Raw WPM ignores errors, while net WPM subtracts them.

faq.q: How long should a WPM test run?
faq.a: Sixty seconds is the accepted standard for a reportable score. Shorter sprints flatter you; longer tests (3 to 5 minutes) are steadier. Retake and average three rounds for a number you can quote.

faq.q: How do I raise my WPM score?

faq.q: What is a typing words per minute test?
faq.a: It is a timed typing test that reports your speed in words per minute. You type for 60 seconds (or another length), the test divides your correct characters by five to get words, then divides by the elapsed minutes. A 300-character round is 60 WPM.

faq.q: How many words per minute should I type?
faq.a: Most adults land between 40 and 60 WPM. Office and writing roles usually ask for 60 to 80, data entry and transcription posts 80-plus, and 90 to 120 is professional territory. Anything under 30 WPM is a beginner still building touch typing foundations. Check the average typing speed bands before judging a single round.

faq.q: What is a typing words per minute test?
faq.a: A typing words per minute test measures how many five-character words you type correctly in sixty seconds. Every five keystrokes count as one word regardless of real word length, so the score stays comparable across different passages. Net WPM deducts errors and is the figure to quote; raw WPM ignores them.

faq.q: What does WPM stand for?
faq.a: Words per minute, where one word is five characters including spaces. That convention is what makes scores comparable across passages of different word lengths.

faq.q: Is a free WPM test accurate?

faq.q: What is the difference between WPM and CPM?
faq.a: CPM counts characters per minute, WPM counts five-character words. CPM = WPM x 5, so 60 WPM is 300 CPM.
