seo.h2: What WPM is, and the three ways it is counted
p: WPM is words per minute, where one word is five characters including spaces. That convention exists so a score on a long-word passage and a short-word passage can be compared. Three variants then diverge:

MethodFormulaReads
Gross (raw)all characters ÷ 5 ÷ minutesHighest - counts mistakes
Net(characters − errors) ÷ 5 ÷ minutesWhat employers test
Adjusted (AWPM)all characters ÷ 5 ÷ minutes, errors countedSchool and exam scoring
This page reports net WPM and raw WPM separately, so you can see which one a posting is quoting. A 60 WPM gross score at 94% accuracy nets about 56.

seo.h2: Why an online WPM test is a snapshot, not a verdict
p: One round measures one attempt under one set of conditions: your keyboard, your alertness, the passage you got. The number moves 5-10 WPM between a 15-second burst and a five-minute round, and by a similar margin between morning and end of day.
The honest way to use it is as a trend. Run the same length, at the same time of day, three times a week, and watch the average move. A single high score is a good day, not a new level.

seo.h2: What to compare your score against
p: Use five-minute net scores on sentences, and compare against the measured distribution: mean 51.56 WPM, top 10% above about 78, bottom 10% below about 26 (CHI 2018, 168,960 volunteers). Employer floors cluster at 40 WPM for clerical work and 50-60 for legal and medical support.
Do not compare a one-minute score against a published five-minute average - the difference is systematic, not personal.

seo.h2: Getting a number you can quote
p: Run a five-minute test, read net WPM and accuracy, and keep a screenshot with the date. That is the number to put on a form, a CV or an application - and the one an employer's test will roughly reproduce.
If a posting quotes keystrokes per hour instead, convert: WPM × 300 = KPH, so 45 WPM is 13,500 KPH. The converter does it in both directions.

faq.q: What is the difference between gross and net WPM?
faq.a: Gross counts every character typed; net subtracts errors first. Employers test net, and it always reads equal to or lower than gross.

faq.q: Why is my score lower on longer tests?
faq.a: The first thirty seconds are warm-up pace you cannot hold. Longer rounds also expose attention errors that a short burst hides.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is my WPM?
faq.a: Multiply by 300. 40 WPM is 12,000 KPH, 50 WPM is 15,000 KPH, and 10,000 KPH is about 33 WPM.

seo.h2: How accurate is a 30 second test?
p: A 30 second test is a good snapshot but not the most stable measure - one fast or slow sentence sways the result more than in a longer test. Use it for quick daily checks, and pair it with longer rounds from typing practice to track real progress.

seo.h2: Tips for a faster 30 second sprint
p: Warm up first, keep your eyes on the text rather than your hands, and prioritise accuracy over raw speed since errors cost time to fix. To build real speed, our typing exercises progressively train common words and patterns.

seo.h2: When to choose the 30 second test
p: The 30 second round shines in three situations: a rapid self-check before a job application asks for your WPM, a warm-up lap before a 5 minute typing test, and a low-pressure daily streak you can keep even on busy days. Because one round takes less than a minute including the result screen, it is also the easiest length to repeat — take three back-to-back sprints and average them for a steadier number than any single attempt. Pair it with structured typing practice when one weak key keeps dragging your score down.

seo.h2: What a 30 second score tells you
p: A 30 second round measures peak speed, not sustainable speed. Expect it to land 5-10 WPM above a one-minute result and 10-15 above a five-minute one. That gap is not a flaw in the test — it is the useful part: compare the gap across weeks and you can see whether your endurance is catching up with your top speed.
Use the 1 minute typing test as the reference score and the thirty-second sprint as the check on it. If the two converge, your sustained speed is improving.

seo.h2: The 30 second test as a warm-up
p: Cold starts cost real WPM in the first fifteen seconds. One thirty-second round before a longer attempt raises the score of the round that follows without adding fatigue, which makes this the cheapest warm-up in the set. Pair it with the typing test tips checklist for a repeatable routine.

seo.h2: What thirty seconds actually measures
p: A burst: your top-end keystroke speed before fatigue and before the reading-ahead penalty appears. It reads 5-10 WPM above a five-minute round for the same typist, and that gap is not a flaw - it is the definition of the measurement.

So use it for three things and not for a fourth. Use it to warm up, to train the top end you cannot reach in a longer round, and to compare two keyboards in ten seconds each. Do not use it as the number you quote to an employer.

seo.h2: Using sprints to raise the five-minute score
p: Ten sprints of 15-30 seconds, twice a week, with a slow accuracy round after each set. The sprints pull the ceiling up; the accuracy round stops the ceiling from arriving with a higher error rate attached.

Then check once a week with a five-minute round. If the sprint score rises while the five-minute score stays flat, the extra speed is not transferring - usually because the errors you make at sprint pace are the ones you then spend the long round correcting.

faq.q: Is a 30 second typing test accurate?
faq.a: It gives a reasonable snapshot of your speed, but a short test is more easily affected by a single fast or slow sentence. For a more stable WPM, use a 1, 2 or 5 minute test.

p: The 3 minute typing test hits a sweet spot: it averages out short bursts of speed without the fatigue of a long round, which is why many pre-employment typing screenings use a 3-5 minute window. seo.h2: Why test for 3 minutes?
p: Three minutes filters out the noise of a single lucky sentence while staying short enough to take every day. It reveals whether you can hold speed and accuracy together, the real signal employers care about. Build that endurance with guided typing practice.

seo.h2: What is a good 3 minute WPM?
p: Around 40 WPM is average for adults, 60+ is good, and 80+ is professional. Over 3 minutes accuracy matters as much as speed, so aim to finish with 95% or higher accuracy.

seo.h2: Mistakes that lower your 3 minute score
p: The costliest error is opening at sprint pace: typists who blast the first thirty seconds usually fade below their 1 minute average by minute three. Second is glancing at the keyboard after every mistake, which breaks rhythm and adds hesitation errors. Third is chasing raw speed while accuracy slides under 95% — each error costs both the keystroke and the correction. Hold a pace about 5% under your one-minute speed, keep your eyes on the screen, and let accuracy carry the score.

seo.h2: How to pace a 3 minute round
p: Divide the round into three blocks of sixty seconds. In the first block, settle at about 5% under your one-minute speed and let accuracy lead. In the second, hold that pace — this is where most typists drift upward and start making correctable errors. In the final block, spend the last twenty seconds on whatever is left rather than accelerating; a clean finish usually beats a fast fade by several WPM.
Take a 30 second typing test as a warm-up before the round. Cold hands cost more in the first block than most typists realise, and a warm-up sprint removes that penalty without tiring you out.

seo.h2: 3 minute typing test for job screening
p: Screening tests rarely ask for a 3 minute round in isolation; they use one take on unfamiliar text with no retry, and they care about the accuracy floor more than the headline WPM. Practise in exactly that shape: a passage you have not seen, one attempt, and a result you do not delete. The typing test for interview page walks through the format HR teams commonly use.

seo.h2: 3 minute vs 5 minute vs 10 minute
p: Three minutes is the shortest length that still shows endurance decay; five minutes makes the decay obvious; ten minutes is a transcription-grade stamina test. If your 5 minute typing test score sits more than 8 WPM below your three-minute score, stamina is the bottleneck — train it with weekly long rounds rather than daily short ones.
For daily practice, the 2 minute typing test is easier to repeat. Reserve the three-minute round for weekly measurement so the number stays comparable.

seo.h2: Moving between test lengths
p: Length changes what a score means. A sixty-second round is the format schools, employers and certificates quote most, so it is the number to keep as your baseline: the 1 minute typing test is the reference point every other duration on this site is compared against. Longer rounds then measure how much of that baseline survives, and shorter rounds measure how quickly you can reach it cold.

seo.h2: How this round is scored
p: Each round scores correct characters using the five-character word convention described for words per minute: five characters, spaces and punctuation included, count as one word. A clean round also reports accuracy next to net WPM, because the two numbers answer different questions — how fast your fingers move, and how much of that speed survived contact with the keyboard.

faq.q: Why do employers use 3 minute typing tests?
faq.a: Three minutes is long enough to reflect sustained real-world typing speed yet short enough for screening, so many hiring tests use a 3-5 minute window.

faq.q: What WPM do I need for a typing job?
faq.a: Most data entry and transcription roles ask for 40-60 WPM with 90% or higher accuracy; specialised roles may want 70+ WPM.

faq.a: A 1 minute test measures peak speed and swings 10-15 WPM on an unfamiliar sentence. Three minutes averages that noise out and exposes whether you can hold speed with accuracy, which is why screening tests prefer it.

pages.title: 10 Minute Typing Test - Free 10 Min WPM Test
pages.metaDesc: Ten minutes of unbroken typing measures endurance, not finger speed. Expect to sit 5 to 15 percent below your one minute score at first.
pages.heroP: Test true typing endurance with a full 10 minute typing test. Ten minutes measures how well you hold speed and accuracy over long sessions - the closest test to a real workday of writing or data entry.

seo.h2: 10 minute typing test
p: The 10 minute typing test is the ultimate endurance check. Ten minutes exposes fatigue that short rounds hide: most typists slow 5-15% between minute one and minute ten, so your score here reflects what you can truly sustain. Warm up first with a 1 minute typing test or a 5 minute typing test.

seo.h2: Who needs a 10 minute test?
p: Anyone whose work is long-form typing - transcriptionists, writers, coders, data entry clerks. If you will type for hours, a 10 minute result predicts your real-day speed better than any sprint. Build up to it with structured typing practice sessions.

seo.h2: How to pace a 10 minute test
p: Start about 10% slower than your 1 minute speed and settle into a rhythm you can hold. Sit up, keep wrists neutral, and take micro-pauses at sentence breaks. Finishing strong matters more than an early burst that fades.

seo.h2: Reading your 10 minute result
p: Your ten-minute score tells two stories: the headline WPM, and the fade between your fastest and slowest minutes. A drop under 10% means solid endurance; 10 to 20% is normal and shrinks with practice; more than 20% points to tension — usually raised shoulders or held breath — rather than weak fingers. Check whether errors cluster late in the round, which signals fatigue, or scatter throughout, which signals an accuracy habit; then train the weakness with focused typing practice sessions.

seo.h2: Preparing for a 10 minute typing test
p: A 10 minute typing test is an endurance event, not a sprint. Almost everyone finishes 10-15% slower than their 1 minute speed, and that is expected rather than a failure.

• Set posture first - feet flat, wrists neutral, elbows near 90 degrees. Discomfort at minute three becomes lost accuracy by minute seven.
  • Pace, do not sprint - open at roughly 90% of your comfortable speed and hold it. Sprinting the first minute reliably costs more than it gains.
  • Stop correcting every slip - for an endurance score, constant backtracking costs more WPM than the error itself.
  • Breathe and relax the shoulders - tension is the main cause of late-round slowdown.

seo.h2: What 10 minutes measures that 1 minute can't
p: A one-minute test measures your working speed — fresh fingers, no fatigue, a sprint by any other name. Ten minutes measures something employers actually care about more: whether your speed survives contact with real work. Almost everyone is fast for sixty seconds; the tenth minute is where sloppy posture, death-grip tension and uneven rhythm come due.

Expect your ten-minute score to read 5–15% below your one-minute score. That gap is not a failure — it is your fatigue profile, and it is the most honest single number about your typing. A small gap means your technique is sustainable; a large gap means you are borrowing speed from muscles that will not lend it for eight hours.

seo.h2: The 10 minute decay curve
p: Ten minutes has a shape, and knowing it is half the pacing battle. The table below breaks the test into its natural segments — where speed comes free, where the wall hits, and what to do in each.

SegmentWhat happensWhat to do
Minutes 1–2Warm-up; rhythm formsStart at 90% of sprint pace, settle early
Minutes 3–6Cruise zone; your real speedHold even rhythm, eyes one word ahead
Minutes 7–8The fatigue wall; errors spikeDrop 5% pace, do NOT fight through at full speed
Minutes 9–10Second wind or collapseHold form, finish clean — last-minute errors cost most

Most people lose the test in minutes 7–8, not because they are slow but because they refuse to downshift. The professionals' secret is unglamorous: planned deceleration. Losing 5% of pace for two minutes costs far less than the error cluster that full-speed fatigue produces.

seo.h2: Training for the 10 minute format
p: Endurance is trainable, and the training is boring on purpose: one long round per week at the full ten minutes, watching where your accuracy starts to slip. That slip point moves later and later over a month of weekly rounds — from minute five, to seven, to clear through ten. The decay curve flattening is the clearest progress signal in endurance typing.

Two supporting habits matter more than extra rounds. Posture checks at minute five — shoulders down, wrists floating, grip relaxed — because tension is what you are actually fighting in the back half. And a ten-second hand shake between practice rounds, so you learn to release tension instead of carrying it into the next round.

seo.h2: When employers and exams use long tests
p: Short tests dominate hiring screens, but the long formats show up wherever the job itself is long: transcription and captioning assessments (sustained audio work), data-entry simulations for volume roles, and court or administrative exams in several countries that set five-to-ten-minute passages specifically to measure endurance.

If your target role involves continuous typing, your ten-minute score matters more than your one-minute best — and the typing speed requirements table shows which roles weight endurance heavily. Practise the format you will be tested on: the 5 minute typing test is the natural stepping stone if ten minutes still breaks you today.

seo.h2: Taking a ten minute typing test online
p: This ten minute typing test runs the full 600 seconds in the browser with no sign-up and no round limit, so you can repeat it as often as you like and keep every result in your own local history. Ten minutes is long enough that pacing, posture and fatigue decide the score more than raw finger speed does, which makes it the honest format for testing whether a speed you hit in one minute survives real work.

Use it as an endurance check rather than a daily drill: one ten minute run after a warm-up, compared against your own one minute result from the same week. A gap of 5 to 15 percent below your short-round speed is normal. A gap wider than that is a posture or tension problem, not a speed problem, and the fix is a slower pace with relaxed wrists rather than more force.

seo.h2: Why the five-character word matters for endurance scores
p: Long rounds are only comparable if the unit is fixed. This test scores every five characters as one word, the convention documented for words per minute, so a ten minute result can be set against a one minute result from any other test that uses the same rule. Change the unit and the drop you are measuring stops being fatigue — it becomes an artefact of the formula.
If ten minutes is more than you need, the two-minute test covers the length most interviews use.

faq.q: Will I slow down over 10 minutes?
faq.a: Most people type 5-15% slower by the end of a 10 minute test as fatigue sets in. Pacing yourself and staying relaxed helps limit the drop.

faq.q: Is a 10 minute test better than 1 minute?
faq.a: It measures something different: endurance and consistency rather than peak speed. A 1 minute test shows your top speed; a 10 minute test shows what you can sustain.

faq.q: Is the 10 minute typing test free?
faq.a: Yes, completely free with no sign up and no ads in the typing area, and your results stay private in your browser.

faq.q: What text is used for the test?
faq.a: Real English sentences by default. You can switch to quotes, numbers or words from the panel above the typing area.

faq.q: Why is my 10 minute score lower than my 1 minute score?
faq.a: Almost everyone reads 5–15% lower over ten minutes — that gap is your fatigue profile, not a failure. A small gap means sustainable technique; a large gap means tension and posture issues to fix.

faq.q: How do I train for a 10 minute typing test?
faq.a: One full-length round per week, watching where accuracy starts to slip — that slip point moves later with training. Add posture checks at minute five and downshift 5% at the fatigue wall instead of fighting through at full speed.

pages.tldr: A 10 minute typing test measures endurance, not just speed: expect 5–15% below your one-minute score — that gap is your fatigue profile. The test has a shape: warm up in minutes 1–2, cruise 3–6, downshift 5% at the 7–8 fatigue wall, and finish clean. Train with one weekly long round and posture checks at minute five. Long formats appear in transcription, data-entry and administrative exams where sustained accuracy is the actual job. pages.title: Chinese Typing Test - Free Online Chinese WPM Test
pages.metaDesc: Chinese typing test on real sentences in simplified and traditional characters. Instant WPM, characters per minute and accuracy, no sign up.
pages.heroP: Test your Chinese typing speed with real Chinese sentences. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

seo.h2: Chinese typing is input-method work
p: You do not type Chinese characters directly on a standard keyboard. You type a romanised or structural code - pinyin being the common case - and then choose a candidate from a list. Speed therefore depends on two skills: the keystrokes of the code, and how quickly you pick the right candidate.

That is why a Chinese WPM figure is not comparable to an English one at face value. A pinyin typist producing 40 characters per minute is typing maybe 120-160 keystrokes, and the character count is what gets reported.

seo.h2: The three things that decide your speed
p:
• Candidate selection. Common words appear first; rare characters require scanning or extra keystrokes. Practising your own vocabulary beats practising random text.
  • Phrase versus character input. Typing whole phrases (词) rather than single characters roughly halves the candidate selections, which is where most of the gain is.
  • Homophones. Pinyin maps many characters to one syllable, so accuracy depends on choosing correctly rather than on hitting the right key. An input-method error is a wrong character, not a typo.

seo.h2: Other input methods, and when they are faster
p: Structural methods - Wubi (五笔), Cangjie (倉頡), Zhengma - encode the shape of a character rather than its sound. They have a much steeper learning curve but avoid candidate selection almost entirely, which is why professional Chinese typists often use them.

For most people pinyin is the right choice: it is already installed, it matches how you think, and the ceiling is high enough for office work. Switch only if you type Chinese for hours a day and the candidate list is demonstrably your bottleneck.

seo.h2: How to practise and how it is scored
p: Use the Sentences mode and type the characters as they appear, committing each phrase with the space or number key your IME uses. The score panel reports characters per minute; multiply by 60 for characters per hour, and remember that the five-characters-per-word convention was designed for alphabetic scripts.

For a job that quotes words per minute, ask whether they mean characters or words. A 60 WPM requirement in a Chinese-language role usually means 60 characters per minute, which is a different target from 60 English words per minute.

faq.q: How is Chinese typing speed measured?
faq.a: Usually in characters per minute, because each character carries a syllable. Multiply by 60 for characters per hour. The five-characters-per-word convention was designed for alphabetic scripts.

faq.q: Is pinyin or Wubi faster?
faq.a: Wubi and other structural methods have a higher ceiling because they avoid candidate selection, but they take far longer to learn. For office work, pinyin's ceiling is usually enough.

faq.q: Why does my accuracy drop on rare characters?
faq.a: Rare characters sit deep in the candidate list, so you scan or type extra keystrokes to reach them. Input-method errors produce a wrong character rather than a typo, which is why they are harder to notice.

faq.q: What is a good Chinese typing speed?
faq.a: 40-60 characters per minute is comfortable for office work with pinyin; experienced typists reach 80-120. Professional structural-method typists exceed that, but they are a different population.

faq.q: Does the test include punctuation?
faq.a: Yes - the Chinese comma and full stop (， 。) are part of the passage, and in full-width form they are separate keystrokes from their Latin counterparts.

pages.tldr: Chinese practice uses simplified characters typed through an IME. WPM is reported for the committed text, so the number reflects IME fluency as much as key location.

pages.title: Hindi Typing Test - Free Online Hindi WPM Test
pages.metaDesc: Hindi typing test in Devanagari, including matras and conjuncts where most errors happen. Get WPM, accuracy and your weakest keys at once.
pages.heroP: Test your Hindi typing speed with real Hindi sentences in Devanagari script. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

seo.h2: Devanagari is not a one-key-per-letter script
p: Hindi is written in Devanagari, where consonants carry an inherent 'a' vowel and other vowels appear as matras - marks placed before, after, above or below the consonant. A single written syllable can require two or three keystrokes, so your characters-per-minute is not the same as your syllable rate.

Add conjuncts (क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ) and the nasal marks (ं ँ) and you have a script where accuracy depends on sequence, not just key location. That is why Hindi typing tests feel different from English ones even at the same WPM.

seo.h2: Krutidev, Remington and Mangal
p: Indian typing exams usually specify a layout, and the three you will meet are Krutidev, Remington (often called the typewriter layout) and Mangal/InScript. They map Devanagari to the keyboard in completely different ways: Krutidev and Remington are legacy layouts built for typewriters and phototypesetting, while InScript follows the script's logical order.

LayoutWhere you meet itLearning cost for a QWERTY typist
KrutidevMany state government exams, court workHigh - keys do not match the script order
RemingtonOlder exams, some typing institutesHigh - typewriter-era mapping
InScript / MangalModern government and Unicode workModerate - follows the script logically
Check the notice before you practise. Learning the wrong layout is worse than not practising, because the reflexes conflict.

seo.h2: The exam requirements
p: Hindi typing tests commonly ask 25-30 words per minute, with 30 WPM the figure used where English requires 35. Some posts quote key depressions per hour instead, and the mistake allowance is usually around 5%.

Because the same passage can be scored as WPM or as key depressions, convert before comparing yourself to a friend's score: 30 WPM is 9,000 key depressions per hour under the five-character convention.

seo.h2: Practising that transfers
p: Practise on the layout your exam uses, on a keyboard you do not own, with a passage that includes the danda (।) and the numerals. Then time yourself for the full ten minutes rather than in one-minute bursts: conjunct errors cluster late, when attention thins.

If you are starting from English touch typing, expect two to four weeks before the Devanagari reflexes stop interfering with your Latin ones. Do not alternate layouts within a session; the interference is real and it slows both.

faq.q: What typing speed is required for Hindi typing tests?
faq.a: Commonly 25-30 words per minute, with 30 WPM where an English requirement would be 35. Some posts quote key depressions per hour instead, usually with a 5% error allowance.

faq.q: Which layout should I learn for Hindi typing?
faq.a: Whichever your exam notice specifies - Krutidev, Remington or InScript/Mangal. They map Devanagari completely differently, and learning the wrong one creates conflicting reflexes.

faq.q: Why is Hindi typing slower than English at the same skill level?
faq.a: Matras and conjuncts mean one written syllable can take two or three keystrokes, so characters per minute and syllables per minute diverge. Accuracy also depends on sequence rather than single key location.

faq.q: Does the danda count as an error if I omit it?
faq.a: Yes. It is part of the passage, like a full stop in English, and an omitted character counts as an error on every mainstream test.

faq.q: Can I practise Hindi typing on a normal keyboard?
faq.a: Yes, once the layout is installed in your operating system. The physical keyboard stays the same; only the mapping changes.

pages.tldr: Hindi practice uses Devanagari with matras and the danda. It is the drill shape used by Indian typing exams; layout conventions differ by test centre, so check which layout your exam uses.

pages.title: Arabic Typing Test - Free Online Arabic WPM Test
pages.metaDesc: Arabic typing test with right-to-left rendering and real sentences. Live WPM, accuracy and characters per minute as you type.
pages.heroP: Test your Arabic typing speed with real Arabic sentences. Measure your words per minute and accuracy instantly. Free, no sign up.

seo.h2: What makes Arabic different to type
p: Arabic is written right to left and the letters join, so what you see on screen is not one glyph per keystroke: most letters have isolated, initial, medial and final forms, and the renderer picks the form as you type. Your speed is still one keystroke per letter - the joining is the font's job, not yours.

Four features decide accuracy: the hamza forms (أ إ آ ؤ ئ), ta marbuta (ة) versus ha (ه), the alif maqsura (ى) versus ya (ي), and the Arabic comma ، and semicolon ؛ which sit where a Latin keyboard puts different characters. None of these are optional if the text is right-to-left formal writing.

seo.h2: Keyboard layout and the RTL cursor
p: The standard Arabic layout keeps the Latin letters on the same physical keys and adds Arabic legends, so touch typists can switch between languages without moving their hands - the muscle memory transfers, only the output changes. That is good news for anyone who already types English.

The part that catches people is direction. In a right-to-left field the cursor moves left as you type, and mixing Arabic with Latin words or numbers reverses the visual order of the run. If your accuracy collapses when a sentence contains a number or an English product name, that is bidi handling, not typing speed.

seo.h2: How Arabic speed is measured
p: Most Arabic typing tests report words per minute using the same five-characters-per-word convention as English, so the two numbers are broadly comparable - with one caveat: Arabic words are shorter on average than English words, so a text of equal character count contains more words. Compare CPM rather than WPM when you are comparing across languages.

CPMWPM (÷5)Reading
15030Beginner, hunt-and-peck
20040Comfortable office speed
25050Fast for Arabic formal text
300+60+Professional, transcription level

seo.h2: Practising for real Arabic text
p: Start with sentences without tashkeel (diacritics), because everyday writing omits them and typing them slows you down for no gain. Add them only if your work requires vocalised text - religious, educational or children's material.

Then practise the pairs that cause errors: ة versus ه at word ends, ى versus ي, and the hamza carriers. Ten repetitions of one word beat one pass through ten words, because the goal is a corrected reflex rather than exposure.
For the English side of the same skill, see the English typing test; for the general benchmark, average typing speed.

seo.h2: Where Arabic typing speed is tested
p: Government and clerical posts in the Gulf and Egypt commonly ask for a certificate or a timed sample, often 20-30 words per minute for data entry and higher for secretarial work. Because the requirement is set per employer, read the posting rather than assuming a national standard exists.

If a test is proctored, expect an unfamiliar keyboard with Arabic legends. Practise at least twice on a different machine: key travel and legend placement change your error rate more than practice volume does.

faq.q: Does Arabic typing count characters or letters?
faq.a: Letters - one keystroke per letter. The joined forms you see on screen are produced by the font, not by extra keystrokes.

faq.q: Why does my accuracy drop when a sentence contains numbers?
faq.a: Mixing right-to-left Arabic with left-to-right digits reverses the visual order of that run. It is a bidirectional text issue rather than a typing-speed problem; check your output rather than your speed.

faq.q: Should I practise with tashkeel (diacritics)?
faq.a: Only if your work needs vocalised text. Everyday Arabic writing omits them, and typing them slows you down without improving the result.

faq.q: What is a good Arabic typing speed?
faq.a: 200-250 characters per minute (40-50 words per minute) is comfortable office speed. Government and clerical tests commonly ask 20-30 words per minute for data entry.

faq.q: Do I need a special Arabic keyboard?
faq.a: No. The Arabic layout keeps Latin letters on the same keys, so you can add it in your operating system and switch with a shortcut. Touch typing transfers directly.

pages.tldr: Arabic practice runs right to left with the hamza forms and the ta marbuta. Speed is reported as WPM and CPM; the script is joined, so character counts run differently from Latin text.

seo.h2: touch typing test
p: A touch typing test measures how fast and how accurately you type without looking at the keys. p: Muscle memory is built by frequency, not by marathon sessions. A daily 60 second touch typing test is enough to keep the home row fresh and to expose the two or three keys that always slow you down. Track your WPM across a week and you will see the pattern: accuracy climbs first, and speed follows a few days behind. When your accuracy passes 98 percent, you know the keyboard has finally moved into your fingers.

p: Start by resting your index fingers on the small bumps on F and J, with the other fingers curling onto the home row beside them. Type the sentence on screen without glancing down; if you must look, look only after the line is finished. Keep your wrists floating and your shoulders down. After the test, read the error report: those keys, not your fastest ones, are your next practice targets.

seo.h2: Measuring progress without fooling yourself
p: Three numbers, once a week, same test length and time of day: net WPM, accuracy, and consistency (how much your speed varies second to second). Progress in touch typing usually shows up in accuracy first, then consistency, then speed - in that order.

If speed rises while accuracy falls, you are trading one for the other and the net result is flat. That is the most common false plateau, and the fix is a week of accuracy-only rounds rather than more speed work.

faq.q: What is a touch typing test?
faq.a: A touch typing test measures your typing speed and accuracy while you type without looking at the keyboard. This one runs for 60 seconds and reports live WPM, accuracy, and a per-key error summary.

faq.q: Is this touch typing test free?

faq.q: How fast is good touch typing?
faq.a: A comfortable touch typing speed is 40 to 60 WPM, and 70 to 90 WPM is considered fast. Above 100 WPM is competitive territory. Accuracy matters first: most people reach their best speed only after their accuracy passes 97 to 98 percent.

faq.q: How long until I can touch type at full speed?
faq.a: Expect the home row within a week and 40 to 60 WPM in three to four weeks of 10 to 15 minute daily sessions. Full speed takes longer, but this test doubles as training since every round uses real lesson sentences.

faq.q: Should I look at the keyboard while testing?
faq.a: No. Cover the keyboard with a piece of paper if you have to, and let the bumps on F and J guide your index fingers. Every glance down is a habit that costs speed later, so train the eyes to stay on the screen.

faq.q: What is the home row?
faq.a: The home row is the middle letter row: A S D F G H J K L ; with the thumbs on the space bar. Every finger owns a small group of keys around the home row, and every finger returns home after each keystroke.

faq.q: How do I know my touch typing is improving?
faq.a: Track net WPM, accuracy and consistency weekly at the same length. Accuracy improves first, then consistency, then speed; if speed rises while accuracy falls, the net result is flat.

p: This is a competitive typing game in its purest form: one minute, one text, and a score that stays on this device until you beat it. There is no lobby and no opponent to wait for, so the race starts the moment your first keystroke does. Compete against yourself daily, or share your WPM and race a friend on the same keyboard; every session is a new heat.

seo.h2: How to race your fastest typing sprint
p: Treat the first sentence like a warm up, not a launch: start at 80 percent of your top speed and build into the race. Keep your eyes on the text two or three words ahead of your fingers, so your hands never stall mid-sentence. Keep your wrists light and your rhythm even, because most typing races are lost in the last ten seconds when fatigue makes fingers sloppy.

The third race usually produces your best WPM, because chasing accuracy is what unlocks the top speed. Come back daily and the leaderboard of your own history does the rest.

seo.h2: Racing yourself is the only comparison that holds
p: A race against another person adds a variable you cannot control: their speed. A race against your own last round adds only one: you. That is why the useful version of this page is a sequence of attempts at a fixed length, tracked over weeks.
Run three 30-second attempts and record all three. The one that matters is the middle one - the fastest is a lucky draw, the slowest is often a fumble at the start.

seo.h2: Sprint speed and working speed are different numbers
p: A 30-second sprint typically reads 8-12 WPM above a five-minute round for the same typist. Neither is wrong; they measure different things. Sprints train the top end you cannot otherwise reach, and the five-minute round tells you what you can actually sustain.

Use races to raise the ceiling, and a five-minute test once a week to check that the ceiling is moving the average. If sprint speed rises while the five-minute score stays flat, you are training a skill you do not use.

faq.q: What is a typing race?

faq.q: What is a good WPM for a typing race?
faq.a: Around 50 to 70 WPM is a solid race speed, 80 to 100 WPM is fast, and anything above 100 WPM is competitive. Remember that accuracy multiplies speed: a race with no corrections almost always beats a faster race full of fixes.

seo.h2: What to skip, and in what order
p: Skip alternative layouts (Dvorak, Colemak) until you are past 60 WPM on QWERTY. Switching early means paying the learning cost twice and measuring neither. Skip code typing until you can type sentences without looking, because brackets make a hard task harder.
Do not skip the digits stage even if your job seems prose-only. Every real document contains a date or an amount, and the number row is where untrained typists lose the most accuracy.

seo.h2: A four-week schedule that fits a working day
p: Week 1: two minutes home row, three minutes normal text, one minute covered. Week 2: add the row you miss most, keep the covered round. Week 3: punctuation and capitals in sentences, plus a numbers round every other day. Week 4: five-minute rounds and one full test as a checkpoint.
Fifteen minutes a day is enough. The variable that predicts progress is not session length but the number of days you show up.

seo.h2: How to know the tutorial worked
p: Two checks. First, you can type a sentence with your hands covered at 90% of your normal accuracy. Second, your five-minute net score improved by at least 5 WPM since the start.
If neither happened, the cause is almost always that the covered round got dropped. It is the least pleasant part of the tutorial and the only part that removes the ceiling.

seo.h2: When a stage will not click
p: Every stage has a characteristic failure, and each has one fix that works better than repeating the same drill:

SymptomWhat it usually meansFix
Accuracy collapses when you cover your handsThe key map is visual, not spatialTwo weeks of covered rounds at 30 seconds, no target
Speed rises but errors rise fasterYou are typing ahead of the bufferDrop to 85% pace for a week; one error per round allowed
Fine on sentences, lost on digitsThe number row was never drilledTwo minutes of Numbers mode daily, graded on errors
Good in practice, worse in testsThe countdown itself is the problemPractise with the timer visible every session, same length as the test

seo.h2: How long each stage actually takes
p: These are typical ranges for an adult practising fifteen minutes a day, not guarantees. The spread between people is wide, and the variable that predicts progress is how many days you show up, not how long each session is.

• Home row secure: 1-2 weeks.
  • All rows without looking: 3-4 weeks.
  • Capitals and punctuation not breaking rhythm: 5-6 weeks.
  • 45 WPM sustained on normal text: 2-3 months.
  • 60 WPM: 4-6 months for most adults starting from two-finger typing.
If you are outside those ranges by a lot, the cause is almost always one of the four symptoms above rather than talent.

faq.q: How long does a typing tutorial take?
faq.a: Four to six weeks at 15 minutes a day to go from two-finger typing to sentences without looking. Speed beyond that comes from months of regular practice rather than more lessons.

faq.q: Should I learn Dvorak or Colemak instead of QWERTY?
faq.a: Not before 60 WPM on QWERTY. Switching early doubles the learning cost and prevents a clean comparison.

faq.q: Do I need to learn the number row?
faq.a: Yes. Dates, amounts and reference codes appear in almost every real document, and the number row is where untrained typists lose accuracy first.

faq.q: What is the most important drill?
faq.a: The covered round. It is the only one that removes the look-at-keyboard habit, which is what caps most people at 35-40 WPM.

faq.q: Is this tutorial free?
faq.a: Yes, with no account. Each stage links to the test mode it needs, and results stay in your browser.

faq.q: What if I get stuck at a stage?
faq.a: Each stage has a characteristic failure: a visual key map (fix with covered rounds), typing ahead of the buffer (drop to 85% pace), undrilled digits (two minutes of Numbers mode), or test anxiety (practise with the timer visible).

seo.h2: What a tutor does that software cannot
p: Software measures output: WPM, accuracy, which keys you miss. A tutor watches process: posture, whether the same hand presses Shift, whether you look down before or after an error, whether you tense your shoulders when the timer starts.

That distinction matters because most adult blockers are process problems. A typist who types at 45 WPM with all ten fingers and no looking has a posture or tension problem, and no amount of drill volume fixes it.

seo.h2: What a diagnosis should contain
p:
• Baseline: five-minute net WPM, accuracy, and the same on a numbers round.
  • Technique observations: finger assignment, Shift hand, looking frequency, wrist position.
  • Error pattern: which characters cluster in the error report, not just how many.
  • Prescription: two or three drills, not a course. Anything more will not be done.
If an assessment gives you a number and a course to buy, it is a sales funnel rather than a diagnosis.

seo.h2: Choosing a tutor, or self-tutoring
p: A good tutor will ask what you type and why before testing you, and will spend most of the first session watching rather than timing. Ask whether they teach touch typing from scratch or fix existing habits - the second is harder and rarer.

Self-tutoring works if you follow three rules: measure the same way every week, change one variable at a time, and keep a covered round in every session. The data does the diagnosing; you just have to write it down.

seo.h2: Using this site as the measurement layer
p: Run a five-minute test at the start of each week and record net WPM, accuracy and the two slowest keys from the results panel. That is enough data to see whether a drill is working after three weeks.
For the drills themselves, the touch typing course is structured, and the typing speed exercises page covers the ones that target specific weaknesses.

faq.q: Do I need a typing tutor?
faq.a: Not if you are progressing: weekly measurements and a covered round are enough. A tutor helps when you are stuck at the same speed for months with correct technique, or when posture and tension are the problem.

faq.q: What should a first session cover?
faq.a: Mostly observation: a baseline five-minute score, finger assignment, Shift hand, how often you look down, and where your errors cluster. A number alone is not a diagnosis.

faq.q: Can software replace a tutor?
faq.a: For measurement, yes - it is more consistent than a person. For technique and posture, no: software cannot see your hands or your shoulders.

faq.q: How often should I be re-tested?
faq.a: Weekly, always the same length and time of day. Every six weeks, add a numbers round and one unfamiliar-keyboard round.

faq.q: Is this page a tutor service?
faq.a: No. It is the test and measurement layer. There is no account, no coaching product and no data leaving your browser.

seo.h2: learn to type
p: To learn to type you only need two things: the home row, and the patience to be slow for a week. This free course teaches touch typing from absolute zero, and every practice sentence is a lesson about learning itself, so your practice text coaches you while you type it. Sixty seconds a day in your browser, with live WPM and accuracy feedback, no account and no cost.

seo.h2: Your first lesson in learning to type
p: Rest your left fingers on A S D F and your right fingers on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Feel the small bumps on F and J; they are the only map a beginner needs. Type words made from the home row only, slowly, and let each finger return home after every key. If you must look, look after the word, never in the middle of it. That is the entire first lesson, and everything after it is just practice.

seo.h2: How long does it take to learn to type?
p: Most people own the home row in a week and reach a comfortable 40 to 60 words per minute in three to four weeks of daily practice. The mistake beginners make is chasing speed early; accuracy is the foundation and speed is the building that arrives later. End every session on your slowest, most careful line, and your hands will learn faster than you expect.

seo.h2: Learn to type without looking
p: Looking at your hands feels faster for about a week and caps you near 30 WPM forever, because every glance breaks the loop between what your eyes read and what your fingers do. Break the habit deliberately: cover your hands with a cloth for one short round a day, accept the slower score, and let the home row do the work. The full method is on the how to type without looking page.

seo.h2: A one-week learn-to-type plan
p: Day one: home row only, slow, eyes on the screen. Day two: add the top row with the correct fingers. Day three: bottom row and the shift key. Day four: short common words. Day five: full sentences at a comfortable pace. Day six: numbers and punctuation. Day seven: one timed round to see where you are — not to pass a target. Fifteen minutes a day is enough; the schedule matters more than the minutes.
When the week ends, move to structured typing practice and check the result panel for the keys that are slowing you down.

seo.h2: Learn to type on a laptop keyboard
p: Laptop keys have shorter travel, which makes light, quick presses easier and heavy presses slower. The home row is the same, but the keyboard is often narrower, so your hands sit closer to centre. If the built-in keyboard is uncomfortable, the mechanical keyboard for typing guide covers what actually matters — key travel and actuation force — without the marketing.
For a step-by-step version of this page, the typing tutorial runs the same five stages with a checkpoint at each one.

faq.q: Can I learn to type for free?
faq.a: Yes. This course is completely free, with no sign up, no account, and no paywall. Every lesson is a timed practice you can repeat as often as you like, and your results stay in your own browser.

faq.q: I have never touched a keyboard. Can I still learn to type?
faq.a: That is exactly who this page is for. It starts at the home row, assumes nothing, and adds one row at a time. Being slow in the first week is not a setback; it is the lesson.

faq.q: What is the first thing I should learn?
faq.a: The home row: A S D F J K L ; with your thumbs on the space bar. Find the bumps on F and J with your index fingers, and practice words made only from those keys until you never look down.

faq.q: How long until I can type without looking?
faq.a: Usually one to two weeks for the home row, and three to four weeks before the whole keyboard feels automatic. Covering the keyboard with a cloth speeds this up, because it removes the option of cheating.

faq.q: Should I focus on speed or accuracy while learning?
faq.a: Accuracy, always. Speed is a byproduct of accurate repetition. A fast wrong keystroke teaches your hand the wrong address for a key, which you then have to unlearn.

faq.q: How many minutes a day should I practice?
faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes every day. Short daily practice builds muscle memory far better than one long weekly session, because the hands learn by frequency, not by total minutes.

faq.q: Can I learn to type in a week?
faq.a: You can learn the correct finger positions in a week, and most people reach a usable 30-40 WPM within three to four weeks of daily practice. Reaching 60 WPM usually takes two to three months of consistent short sessions.

pages.tldr: Start at the home row and add one row per week. Typing slowly and correctly for ten minutes a day beats an hour of fast, corrected typing, and the habit is what carries over.

seo.h2: The trainer's four week plan
p: Week one is diagnosis: run three drills a day and read the error report without trying to fix anything. Week two, drill your two weakest keys twice as often as the rest. Week three, run the full minute at a speed where you make no errors, and live there. Week four, chase your personal best once a day and log it. Five words per minute each week is the only target, because tendons keep their own pace.

seo.h2: Why training beats practice
p: Practice is typing a lot; training is typing the right thing a lot. The difference is the log. When you record your WPM and accuracy side by side each day, a speed that costs accuracy shows up immediately as a bad trade, and the drill that fixed your weak keys shows up as a permanent step up. Your hands will plateau; the trainer's answer is variety and rest, not more effort.

faq.a: Yes, completely free, with no sign up and no account. Your best scores are stored only in your own browser.

faq.q: What is the difference between a typing trainer and a typing test?
faq.a: A test measures you once. A trainer gives you drills sized for daily use, keeps your best score so you always have a target, and points your next session at your weakest keys.

faq.q: How long should a training drill be?
faq.a: Sixty seconds per set, with short rest between sets. Keep total training under thirty minutes a day; a tired hand practices its own mistakes.

faq.q: How fast can a typing trainer make me?
faq.a: Most people add five to ten words per minute per month with daily drills. The reliable ceiling for daily practice is around 80 to 100 WPM, and accuracy above 95 percent is what makes that speed stick.

faq.q: Should I train when my hands hurt?
faq.a: No. Stop, rest, and check your posture and wrist position. Rest days are part of the training program, because muscle memory is written during recovery, not during strain.

faq.q: How do I know the training is working?
faq.a: Log your WPM and accuracy side by side each day. Speed that drops accuracy is not progress. The clearest sign is your error report shrinking week over week, because fewer errors always precede faster speed.

p:

  • Weak-key drilling - paste the words you keep missing, twenty times each, and run a minute on them.

seo.h2: What to paste, and what not to
p: Paste plain text. Formatting, smart quotes and non-breaking spaces can all produce characters your keyboard cannot type, which turns a practice round into a hunt for a Unicode symbol.
Keep it between 100 and 400 words. Shorter and the round repeats, which makes memorisation inflate your score; longer and you will never finish a five-minute round.

SettingUse it when

seo.h2: Limits worth knowing
p: A custom test cannot tell you whether the passage is representative. If you paste easy words, you will score higher than on an employer's test and believe you are ready.
Use it for targeted practice, and the standard tests for benchmarking. For the benchmark itself, see the one-minute test or the five-minute test.

seo.h2: When a custom test is the right measurement
p: A custom test is valid for practising a specific text. It is not valid for comparing yourself to a benchmark, because the passage you chose is not a neutral sample.

Use it for: rehearsing the exact format of an employer's test, drilling your own domain vocabulary, and reproducing a text you keep mistyping. Do not use it to decide whether you are fast enough for a job - use a standard sentence test at the same length as the employer's, because that is what their test will be.

seo.h2: How pasted text behaves in the engine
p: The text is split on whitespace and typed word by word. Punctuation inside a word (hyphens, apostrophes, brackets) is counted as part of that word, so a passage full of citations will score lower than the same character count of plain prose - correctly, because it is harder to type.

Two things to watch when pasting: smart quotes and non-breaking spaces from a word processor can produce characters your keyboard does not have a key for, and a very long single line will wrap in a way that makes the cursor jump. Paste plain text, and keep paragraphs under about 400 words.

faq.q: What is a custom typing test?
faq.a: A test where you supply the text - your own vocabulary, a sample passage or an interview-style document - and the engine measures speed and accuracy on it.

faq.q: How much text should I paste?
faq.a: 100-400 words. Under 100 the round repeats and memorisation inflates the score; over 400 you will not finish a five-minute round.

faq.a: No. It stays in the browser for the session; there is no server-side storage and no account.

p: Our typing tests in other languages give you the same timed test, the same live WPM and accuracy feedback, and the same instant results, in eight languages: English Typing Test, Spanish Typing Test, Chinese Typing Test, Hindi Typing Test, Arabic Typing Test, Japanese Typing Test, Korean Typing Test and Urdu Typing Test. If you write in more than one language, your typing speed is not one number; it is five, and the only way to know each one is to test it in that language.

seo.h2: Why test typing in your own language
p: Most typing tests assume English, but a keyboard is not the same in every language. Chinese and Hindi use input methods that add a composition step between keystroke and character. Arabic reverses direction and changes letter shapes mid-word. Spanish adds accented vowels. Testing in the language you actually write in is the only way to measure the speed that matters to you.

seo.h2: How to compare across languages
p: Run the same one minute test in each language on the same day, and write the five numbers down. Most people are fastest in their dominant language and ten to twenty percent slower in the others, and the gap shrinks fast with a few minutes of daily practice in the weaker languages. Re-run the same set next month and the comparison is honest, because the test itself never changed.

seo.h2: What changes between languages, and what does not
p: The measurement does not change: five characters count as a word, errors are subtracted, and the length is whatever you chose. What changes is the input mechanism, and that is what makes cross-language scores incomparable.

LanguageMechanism that changes the score
English, Spanish, German, French, Turkish, IndonesianDirect key-per-letter; accents and umlauts on dedicated keys (or dead keys)
VietnameseTelex or VNI: tone and quality marks are typed after the word and the IME reorders them
Chinese, JapaneseIME conversion: you type romaji or pinyin, then choose characters from a candidate list
KoreanJamo assembly into syllable blocks - two to four keystrokes per visible character
Hindi, Arabic, Urdu, ThaiScript-specific shaping and matras/vowel marks; layout conventions vary by exam board
So compare CPM within a language over time, and compare languages only on the same mechanism. An English 60 WPM and a Chinese 60 characters per minute are not the same achievement.

seo.h2: Choosing which language test to use
p: Use the language you are actually tested in, or the one you actually type. Practising on a language you do not write daily measures nothing useful - the script may be slower and the vocabulary unfamiliar, and neither tells you about your typing.
If you work across two languages, keep two separate benchmarks and never average them. The benchmarks page explains why a single number cannot span different input mechanisms.

faq.q: How does WPM work in Chinese, Hindi or Arabic?
faq.a: WPM is still correct characters divided by five, divided by minutes. For Chinese and Hindi the count reflects composed characters through an input method, which is the speed that matters when you actually write.

faq.q: Do the non-English tests render correctly?
faq.a: Yes. Arabic renders right-to-left with correct letter shaping, and each page declares its own language and hreflang alternates so search engines route the right version.

faq.a: Only if the input mechanism is the same. Chinese and Japanese involve IME conversion, Korean assembles jamo into blocks, Vietnamese reorders tone marks - so compare CPM within a language over time instead.

p: This page generates a typing certificate from your most recent round. It is free, needs no account, and is produced entirely in your browser - nothing is uploaded, which is also why there is no verification code on it.

The certificate is a printable record of one test: who typed, when, at what speed and accuracy, on what test length. It is a convenience for applications that want a number, not an accredited credential. The honest version of that distinction is spelled out on the certificate acceptance page.

p:

If the result panel is still open, the certificate uses that round. If you have closed it, take a new round first: the certificate is generated from the round in the current session, not from your history.

If your accuracy is below 97%, run an accuracy round before generating the certificate. A certificate showing 55 WPM at 92% invites the question of how many of those words were right.

Plan for the re-test: if your certificate says 58 and their test reads 52, that is normal and consistent. If it says 70 because you quoted a 15-second burst, it looks like a discrepancy.

seo.h2: dvorak typing
p: Most typing tests show a QWERTY keyboard, which is useless when you practice Dvorak typing: the label you need to find is not on the key you press. This test flips the on screen keyboard to the Dvorak layout, keeping the physical key positions of QWERTY and relabelling every key, so the hand you need to move matches the finger guide on screen exactly as a Dvorak user sees their own keyboard.

Nothing is installed and nothing changes your system: the test only draws the Dvorak keyboard on this page. Switch your operating system input to Dvorak, start typing, and the test scores you exactly as it would in QWERTY, because the measuring logic reads the characters your layout produces, not the keys.

seo.h2: Why switch to Dvorak
p: August Dvorak designed the layout in the 1930s so the most common letters sit on the home row, which means less finger travel between rows for almost every English word. Typists who switch usually report less strain in long sessions, and many reach a higher comfortable speed once the new muscle memory settles, which takes roughly two to four weeks of daily practice.

The honest trade off: Dvorak helps most for people who type a lot of English prose. Shortcuts that assume QWERTY positions stay where they were physically, and shared or public keyboards are QWERTY by default, so most Dvorak users keep a fast way to switch back.

seo.h2: How to practice Dvorak typing
p: Set your operating system layout to Dvorak first, otherwise you would be typing QWERTY text while looking at a Dvorak keyboard. Start with short sessions of two to five minutes, and resist the urge to look at your hands: the finger guides on this page exist exactly to replace that habit.

Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week; that drop is the switch cost, not a sign Dvorak is wrong for you. Track your WPM here each day and compare accuracy rather than raw speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it.

seo.h2: Before you switch layouts
p: Considering the switch? Dvorak vs QWERTY weighs the evidence honestly — and why technique usually beats layout.

faq.q: Does this test switch my keyboard to Dvorak?
faq.a: No. The test only shows a Dvorak keyboard on this page; you switch your own operating system input to Dvorak in its keyboard or language settings. The test then scores what your layout produces.

faq.q: Do I need an account or install anything?
faq.a: No. The Dvorak keyboard is drawn by the page itself, the test runs entirely in your browser, and your results are stored only in this browser.

faq.q: Will my Dvorak WPM be lower than my QWERTY WPM?
faq.a: At first, yes, usually much lower. That is the cost of rebuilding muscle memory and it passes in a few weeks. Measure accuracy first; once accuracy is back to your normal level, speed follows.

faq.q: Can I switch back to QWERTY on this page?
faq.a: Yes. The keyboard toolbar has a QWERTY and Dvorak switch and your choice is remembered in this browser, so the same page works for either layout.

faq.q: Which keys move in Dvorak?
faq.a: The vowels A, O, E, U, I move to the middle row under the left hand, and common consonants like T, N, S and H move to the right hand. The full relabelling is drawn on the on screen keyboard above.

faq.q: Is Dvorak faster than QWERTY?
faq.a: Evidence is mixed: most studies show a modest speed gain at the high end and clearer reductions in finger movement and strain. The main benefit people report is comfort in long typing sessions rather than a guaranteed speed jump.

pages.title: One Hand Typing - Free Single-Handed Speed Test
pages.metaDesc: Free one hand typing practice and speed test. Type with one hand using the standard keyboard, with drills and a WPM test. No sign up.
pages.heroP: Learn and measure one hand typing on a normal keyboard. Whether you type with one hand because of an injury, a permanent condition, or simply a hand that is busy holding a coffee, the technique below lets you reach useful speeds without special hardware or chording software. Take the test with one hand and see where you are today.

seo.h2: one hand typing
p: One hand typing on a standard QWERTY keyboard is a real, learnable skill. The idea is not to hunt and peck with one finger, but to assign each finger a fixed zone of the keyboard so your hand develops a repeatable map of where every letter lives. With practice, single hand typists reach 40 to 70 WPM, which is fast enough for almost all desk work.
You do not need a one handed keyboard or chord input software. The regular keyboard you already own is enough, because the technique is about hand position and practice, not hardware.

seo.h2: Hand position for one hand typing
p: Put your four fingers on the home row of the side you use: left hand on A S D F, right hand on J K L semicolon. The thumb works the space bar. Each finger owns the keys in its column plus the row above and below, and the index finger stretches across the middle column to cover the keys on the far side.

The stretch is the hard part at first, especially the keys farthest from your little finger. Slow drills at first are normal; speed comes from accuracy, because a hand that returns to home row after every key does not need to look down.

seo.h2: How fast can one hand typing get
p: Beginners hunting with one finger sit near 15 to 25 WPM. With proper finger zones and a few weeks of short daily sessions, 35 to 50 WPM is common. Experienced one hand typists who type all day reach 60 to 70 WPM and occasionally higher.

Measure honestly with the test on this page: run a one minute test with one hand only, and record your accuracy beside your WPM. Accuracy below 90 percent usually means you are reaching for speed before the map is settled, so slow down until accuracy rises and let speed follow.

faq.q: Can I really type fast with one hand?
faq.a: Yes. With fixed finger zones and practice, one hand typists commonly reach 40 to 60 WPM and experienced ones 70 WPM or more. The key is using all fingers of that hand, not one finger hunting.

faq.q: Do I need a special one handed keyboard?
faq.a: No. The technique works on any standard QWERTY keyboard. Specialised hardware can help for some people, but it is not required to reach useful speeds.

faq.q: Should I learn left hand or right hand typing?
faq.a: Use the hand you have. The finger zone method works symmetrically for either side; the test here does not care which hand presses the keys.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn one hand typing?
faq.a: Basic fluency in two to four weeks with fifteen to twenty minutes a day. Getting back to your two hand speed takes longer, but useful working speed arrives faster than most people expect.

faq.q: Is this test suitable for injured hands?
faq.a: The test is self paced and as short as 15 seconds, so you can use it within whatever your recovery allows. It is not medical advice; follow your clinician's guidance about how much to type while healing.

faq.q: How do I track progress?
faq.a: Results are saved in this browser automatically, so run a one minute test every few days and watch the history table for your WPM and accuracy trend.

pages.title: Average Typing Speed: What Is a Good WPM in 2026?
pages.metaDesc: Average typing speed is 51.56 WPM in the largest published study, not the 40 WPM figure copied everywhere. What good, fast and top-10% mean, by age and job.
pages.tldr: The largest measured sample (136 million keystrokes, 168,960 people) puts mean typing speed at 51.56 WPM. The commonly quoted 40 WPM comes from older office-worker samples. Top 10% exceed about 78 WPM; bottom 10% are under 26.
pages.heroP: The average typing speed is about 40 to 50 words per minute (WPM) with roughly 92% accuracy. 45–60 WPM is good, 60–80 WPM is above average, and only about 1% of people type faster than 100 WPM. Test your own speed below, then compare it with the benchmarks.

seo.h2: The number, and where it comes from
p: The most-cited modern measurement is Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson and Oulasvirta, "Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes" (CHI 2018). It recorded 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers and reports a mean of 51.56 WPM with a standard deviation of 20.2, an uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and 1.173 keystrokes per character. The paper is open at doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220.

Most pages still quote 40 WPM. That figure comes from older, smaller samples of office workers and students, and it has been copied forward without being re-measured. Both describe real populations: 40 WPM is closer to "typical office worker on a work task", 51.56 WPM to "person who chose to take an online typing test".

seo.h2: Why published averages disagree
p: Search "average typing speed" and you will find 40, 45, 50, 52 and 60 WPM on the first page. They are not all wrong - they describe different populations, measured different ways. This is the table that reconciles them:

FigureWhat it describesWhere it comes from
~40 WPMOffice workers on work tasks, older and smaller samplesThe legacy figure quoted in most business and career articles; no single modern study
51.56 WPMPeople who chose to take an online typing testDhakal et al., CHI 2018 - 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers, doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220
36.17 WPMThe same task on a touchscreenPalin et al., MobileHCI 2019 - 37,370 volunteers, doi.org/10.1145/3338286.3340120
60-70 WPM"Good typists" in job advertisingAdvertised requirements, not a measured population

So the honest answer to "what is the average" is: 51.56 WPM if you mean people who take typing tests, about 40 WPM if you mean office workers on work tasks, and 36 WPM if you mean phones. None of those is a national average, and nobody has measured one recently.

Which should you use? For a job application, use the figure in the posting - employers compare against their own floor, not against a population. For a personal target, use the percentile table above, because it tells you where you sit among people who actually type for a measured minute.

seo.h2: What counts as good, fast and exceptional
p:
BandNet WPMPercentile (approx.)What it means
Slowunder 26bottom 10%Hunting for keys; typing is the bottleneck
Below average26-4010th-28thTwo-finger or untrained touch typing
Average40-5228th-50thEnough for most office work
Good52-6550th-75thComfortable all-day typing
Fast65-7875th-90thAbove most job requirements
Top decile78-10090th-99thProfessional typists, developers, transcribers
Exceptional100+top 1%Competitive typing, world-record territory

The percentile column is a normal approximation of that distribution, and it reproduces the study's own reported deciles to within about one point. The percentile page does the arithmetic for any score.

seo.h2: Average typing speed by age
p: Speed peaks in the late teens to thirties in most published samples and declines slowly after that, but the spread within an age band is far larger than the difference between bands. A 55-year-old who touch types beats a 20-year-old who does not, every time.

The practical reading: age is a weak predictor compared with whether someone was ever taught to touch type. If they were not, the gap is trainable at any age - the age breakdown has the numbers by decade.

seo.h2: Average typing speed by profession
p:
• Data entry: 45-65 WPM, often quoted as 13,500-19,500 KPH, with 97-98% accuracy.
  • Administrative and secretarial: 50-70 WPM depending on seniority.
  • Transcription: 65-80 WPM sustained over audio, which is harder than the same speed over visible text.
  • Software developers: no formal requirement; most sit above 70 WPM, and code typing differs because of brackets and symbols.
  • Writers and journalists: 60-80 WPM, where the limit is usually thinking rather than typing.
Role-by-role figures, in the units employers actually use, are on the typing speed requirements page.

seo.h2: Why your score differs from these numbers
p: Test length: a 15-second burst reads 5-10 WPM higher than a five-minute run. Text type: random words score lower than sentences, code lower again, digits are a different skill. Scoring: gross WPM is higher than net. Keyboard: a laptop chiclet keyboard is slower than a mechanical one for most people.

So before concluding you are below average, check what you measured. A five-minute net score on sentences is what this page's bands refer to; a one-minute gross score on random words is not comparable.

seo.h2: Test yourself against the bands
p: Run a five-minute sentence test, then read net WPM and accuracy from the results panel. Compare the net figure against the table above, and check whether accuracy is inside the 97-98% band most employers require - a fast score at 92% accuracy is not the same asset as a slightly slower clean one.
The source table behind these bands, plus the phone average and the raw CSV, is on the typing speed benchmarks page.
Reading about averages is not the same as measuring yours - a free typing test on this site reports net WPM and accuracy against these bands in one minute.

faq.q: What is the average typing speed?
faq.a: 51.56 WPM in the largest published measurement, from 136,857,600 keystrokes recorded from 168,960 volunteers (Dhakal et al., CHI 2018). The older 40 WPM figure reflects office-worker samples rather than self-selected test takers.

faq.q: Is 40 WPM good?
faq.a: It is around the 28th percentile of the CHI 2018 distribution and clears the floor for most clerical and reception roles. It is below the 50-70 WPM band that legal, medical and transcription roles ask for.

faq.q: What is a fast typing speed?
faq.a: Above 78 WPM puts you in the top 10% of the measured population. Above 100 WPM is roughly the top 1%, and competitive typists exceed 130 WPM in short bursts on known text.

faq.q: Does typing speed decline with age?
faq.a: Slightly, and far less than the variation between people of the same age. Whether someone was taught touch typing predicts speed much better than age does.

faq.q: Why do I score lower on longer tests?
faq.a: The first thirty seconds are warm-up pace you cannot hold. A five-minute net score is typically 5-10 WPM below a 15-second burst, and the longer number is the one that reflects a working day.

faq.q: How is typing speed measured?
faq.a: Correct characters divided by five, then divided by the minutes elapsed. Five characters count as one word. Net WPM subtracts errors first; gross WPM does not.

faq.q: What is the average WPM for an adult?
faq.a: 51.56 WPM in the largest published measurement (168,960 volunteers, CHI 2018). The commonly quoted 40 WPM comes from older office-worker samples rather than self-selected test takers.

faq.q: What is the average typing speed for a beginner?
faq.a: 20-30 WPM with 90-95% accuracy is typical for an untrained adult. With ten minutes of daily practice, 35-45 WPM within three months is a realistic progression.

faq.q: Why do different sites quote different average typing speeds?
faq.a: They measure different populations: about 40 WPM for office workers on work tasks (the legacy figure), 51.56 WPM for people who take online typing tests (CHI 2018, n=168,960), and 36.17 WPM for phones (MobileHCI 2019).
