pages.title: CPM Test — Characters Per Minute Typing Test, Free
pages.metaDesc: Take a CPM test to see characters per minute beside WPM from the same one-minute round. 200 CPM equals 40 WPM. Built for data entry and exams.
pages.heroP: This CPM typing test measures your speed in characters per minute. CPM counts every correct keystroke, so because one word is five characters, CPM = WPM × 5. Type the passage below to see your live CPM, WPM and accuracy.

seo.h2: What is CPM (characters per minute)?
p: CPM counts how many characters you type in one minute — every letter, number, space and symbol you produce. It is the rawest possible measure of typing output, which is why data-entry and transcription work quote speed in CPM or its hourly sibling KPH (keystrokes per hour) rather than in words.

On this site the conversion is the standard one used across the typing industry: five characters count as one word. So CPM is simply your WPM multiplied by five — no rounding tricks, no alternate formulas.

seo.h2: CPM to WPM calculator
p: 200 CPM = 40 WPM = 12,000 keystrokes per hour
Type in any box: CPM, WPM or keystrokes per hour. The conversions are CPM ÷ 5 = WPM, WPM × 5 = CPM, and CPM × 60 = KPH, so the three boxes always agree.

The unit that matters depends on the posting: typing tests quote WPM, data-entry adverts quote keystrokes per hour, and exam notices in some countries quote characters per minute. Converting before you compare avoids the most common application mistake - quoting a number in the wrong unit.

seo.h2: WPM, CPM and KPH: the conversion table
p: Use this table to convert between the three units employers and exams quote. The formula is exact: CPM = WPM × 5, and KPH = CPM × 60.

WPMCPM (WPM × 5)KPH (CPM × 60)
201006,000
301509,000
4020012,000
5025015,000
6030018,000
8040024,000
10050030,000
12060036,000

Two reference points make the table easy to use: an average adult types about 40 WPM, which is 200 CPM or 12,000 KPH; the office-standard 60 WPM is 300 CPM or 18,000 KPH. Data-entry job postings asking for '8,000–10,000 KPH' are therefore asking for roughly 27–33 WPM — much less intimidating than the big number sounds.

seo.h2: CPM vs WPM: which should you use?
p: Use WPM when you are comparing yourself with the classic typing benchmarks — schools, résumés and most online tests all quote it. Use CPM when the work itself is measured in keystrokes: numeric data entry, transcription, coding-adjacent tasks, and any language where 'word' is a fuzzy concept.

That last case matters more than it seems. In Japanese or Chinese, one character carries the meaning of a whole English word, so WPM understates the real work; CPM stays honest across scripts. The same is true for number-heavy documents, where a 'word' of five digits is far denser than a word of prose. If your job involves mixed text and figures, track both numbers for a week and see which one predicts your real output better.

seo.h2: How this CPM test measures you
p: The timer starts on your first keystroke, and the live display tracks your character rate as you type. When the clock stops you get two figures: net CPM, which is your correct characters per minute with errors deducted at the standard weighting, and raw CPM, your gross keystroke rate before any penalty. The site uses the same five-characters-per-word standard across every page, so your CPM here converts directly to the WPM shown elsewhere with no second-guessing.

You also get the consistency score, which measures how even your keystroke timing is, and the per-key report showing which letters you miss and which ones slow you down. For character-rate work the slow-key list is gold: a single hesitant key — a bracket, a digit, a shifted symbol — taxes every word that contains it. Drill that one key and the whole character rate lifts.

Results save privately in your browser, building a history you can compare week to week. Because CPM is more granular than WPM, real progress shows up in the numbers sooner — a five-CPM gain is visible long before a one-WPM gain would be.

seo.h2: The hidden cost of errors in CPM
p: Errors hurt twice in a character-based score. The mistyped character does not count, and the correction costs further keystrokes — a backspace and a retype at minimum, roughly two extra keystrokes for every mistake you actually fix. Unfixed errors are worse: they sit in the text and get deducted from your net figure at the end.

Run the arithmetic and the pattern is obvious. A raw 310 CPM at 94% accuracy nets below a controlled 290 CPM at 99%, and the cleaner run also produces better real documents. This is why every experienced data-entry trainer gives the same advice: find the speed where your accuracy stays above 97%, hold it until the character rate climbs on its own, then lift the ceiling a little. Accuracy is not the enemy of speed — it is the mechanism of it.

One more reason CPM deserves a place on your dashboard: it reacts to practice faster than WPM does. Because the unit is five times finer, a genuine improvement shows up as a visible CPM gain within days, while WPM might not tick over for weeks. That faster feedback loop keeps motivation honest — you can see the practice working, in keystrokes, almost as it happens.

seo.h2: What is a good CPM typing speed?
p: Scaled from the standard WPM bands: around 200 CPM is the average adult, 300 CPM is good office-standard speed, 400 CPM is fast — the top ten percent — and 500 CPM or more is elite territory. The accuracy rule scales too: whatever your CPM, keep it above 97% accuracy, because every corrected error costs far more time than it saves.

WPMCPM (= WPM × 5)Level
20 WPM100 CPMBeginner
40 WPM200 CPMAverage adult
60 WPM300 CPMGood / office standard
80 WPM400 CPMFast
100 WPM500 CPMTop ~1%

Watch your net figure, not the raw one. This test shows net CPM with errors deducted alongside your raw keystroke rate; the raw-minus-net gap is the clearest signal of whether you should push speed or tighten accuracy.

seo.h2: How to raise your CPM
p: CPM rewards exactly one thing: more correct keystrokes per minute. Anything that removes hesitation raises it — home-row discipline, eyes on the screen, and drilling the specific keys your weak-key report flags after each round. Anything that creates backspaces lowers it, so type a touch slower than your panic speed and let accuracy do the compounding.

Symbols and digits carry more CPM weight than people expect, because they break letter rhythm. A few rounds in numbers or quotes mode each week keeps punctuation from collapsing your character rate. Short daily rounds on the 1 minute typing test build the base speed; then check the same run here to see it expressed in keystrokes.

seo.h2: Drills that move your CPM
p: Different text types train different parts of your character rate. Numbers mode is the fastest way to raise digit-heavy CPM — the kind that data-entry and spreadsheet work actually measure. Quotes mode drills the punctuation and capitals that break letter rhythm in prose. Words mode strips away sentence flow and measures pure per-word burst speed, which is useful for diagnosing whether your ceiling is vocabulary or technique.

Structure the week around your weak-key report. Two or three 15-second sprints as a warm-up, one full minute for the measurement, then five minutes drilling whichever keys the report flagged. Alternate prose days with numbers days if your work involves figures. Once a week, take a longer run — three or five minutes — and watch how your character rate decays; stamina is trainable, and the decay curve flattening over weeks is the clearest sign of real progress.

seo.h2: CPM and KPH benchmarks for jobs and exams
p: Data-entry job postings usually quote KPH — keystrokes per hour — with typical requirements between 8,000 and 12,000 KPH, plus an accuracy cutoff near 98%. Converted at the standard rate, that is roughly 130 to 200 CPM, or 27 to 40 WPM: demanding for a hunt-and-peck typist, comfortably reachable for anyone with a few weeks of touch-typing practice. Clerk, banking and court exams in several countries score short passages the same way, in keystrokes with an accuracy threshold.

Transcription and captioning sit higher, often expecting the equivalent of 300 CPM or more with near-perfect accuracy, because the work is continuous. Wherever a target is quoted in keystrokes, practise in CPM so the number on test day needs no mental conversion. Because this site uses the industry-standard five-character word, scores you measure here transfer directly to those requirements.

seo.h2: CPM for data entry, exams and language typing
p: Data-entry employers quote KPH targets — typically 8,000 to 12,000 keystrokes per hour — and exams for clerk and banking posts often score passages in keystrokes with an accuracy cutoff. Practising directly in CPM removes the mental conversion on test day. The keystrokes per hour test shows the same score in KPH, and the typing speed calculator converts any result between the three units instantly.

If you type in more than one language, CPM is also the only fair cross-language scoreboard: WPM shifts with each script's idea of a 'word', while characters are characters everywhere. The words per minute test page explains the word-based view in more detail.

seo.h2: CPM for non-English and symbol-heavy typing
p: Words are a comfortable unit in English, but they get slippery elsewhere. Japanese and Chinese text has no spaces between words, so a 'word count' depends on a segmentation algorithm, not anything a typist can see. Agglutinative languages like Turkish or Finnish pack whole phrases into single long words, pushing WPM down even when finger speed is high. Code and data files invert the problem: brackets, operators and digits are dense with keystrokes but sparse with 'words'.

Characters never have this problem. A keystroke is a keystroke in every script and every file type, which is why CPM travels where WPM cannot: comparing your speed across languages, across prose and numbers, or across a week that mixed emails with spreadsheets. If you work in more than one language, CPM is the only scoreboard that treats them all fairly.

The same logic applies to accuracy. One mistyped character costs exactly one character of net score whether it sits in English prose, a Hindi conjunct or a line of figures — so the accuracy habits that raise your CPM transfer to every script you type.

seo.h2: CPM test: take a characters-per-minute test in one minute
p: A CPM test scores the same one-minute round as a WPM test, but reports characters instead of words — which is why CPM appears roughly five times larger than the equivalent WPM figure. Take the test above, type for sixty seconds, and the result panel shows characters per minute, words per minute and accuracy side by side so you never have to convert by hand.

CPM is the fairer unit when your language or your work is not English prose. WPM depends on an arbitrary five-character word, so scripts that write without spaces, and data entry that is mostly digits and symbols, produce WPM numbers that cannot be compared across languages. Character counts have no such convention: 200 CPM means 200 characters typed correctly, in Tokyo, Berlin or Bangalore alike.

seo.h2: Why characters are the more portable unit
p: The five-character word is a convention, not a measurement: words per minute standardises a word to five characters including spaces and punctuation precisely so that different passages produce comparable numbers. Character counts skip the convention entirely, which is why a CPM score travels across languages and across numeric keypad work, where the numeric keypad contributes most of the keystrokes.

seo.h2: Sources for the numbers on this page
p: Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.

The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.

Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.

seo.h2: About this page
p: Last updated 2026-10-20. Written and maintained by the Typing.Rerivo team; scoring formulas, sources and corrections policy are documented on the about page.

faq.q: What does CPM mean in typing?
faq.a: CPM stands for characters per minute — the number of correct characters you type in one minute, counting letters, numbers, spaces and symbols. It is a finer-grained measure of typing speed than WPM.

faq.q: How do you convert CPM to WPM?
faq.a: Divide CPM by 5, because a word is defined as five characters. So 300 CPM equals 60 WPM and 200 CPM equals 40 WPM. To go the other way, WPM × 5 = CPM.

faq.q: What is a good CPM typing speed?
faq.a: The average adult types about 200 CPM (40 WPM). A good CPM is 250–300 (50–60 WPM), and 400+ CPM (80+ WPM) is fast. Numeric data-entry roles often require at least 165 CPM.

faq.q: Why do data entry jobs use CPM?
faq.a: Numeric data entry is done on the number keypad where whole words do not apply, so speed is measured in characters (or keystrokes) per minute. Employers commonly ask for at least 165 CPM with 95%+ accuracy.

faq.q: Is CPM better than WPM?
faq.a: Neither is better — they measure the same thing on different scales (CPM = WPM × 5). WPM is the standard for prose typing; CPM is more common for numeric and data-entry work.

faq.q: Does this site count errors in CPM?
faq.a: Yes. The headline CPM is a net figure with errors deducted, so it matches what an employer measures. Your raw keystroke rate is shown separately, and the gap between the two tells you whether to push speed or accuracy.

faq.q: Is a CPM test the same as a WPM test?
faq.a: It is the same one-minute test reported in different units. CPM counts every correct character; WPM divides that count by five and by the elapsed minutes. A 300 CPM result equals 60 WPM, so neither number is more accurate — only differently scaled.

faq.q: How do I convert CPM to WPM quickly?
faq.a: Divide by five. 200 CPM is 40 WPM, 300 CPM is 60 WPM. The calculator on this page does CPM, WPM and keystrokes per hour at once, in either direction.

pages.tldr: CPM (characters per minute) counts every keystroke you produce in a minute and converts exactly to WPM at 5 characters per word: 40 WPM is 200 CPM, 60 WPM is 300 CPM, and 100 WPM is 500 CPM (KPH = CPM × 60, so 300 CPM is 18,000 keystrokes per hour). Average adults type around 200 CPM, office standard is 300, and 500+ is elite. CPM is the fairest speed metric for data entry, KPH-quoted jobs, and languages like Japanese or Chinese where a 'word' is ambiguous. pages.title: How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
pages.metaDesc: Learn to type without looking at the keyboard. Master the home row, the right finger for each key, and short daily practice.
crumbs: How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
pages.h1: How to Type Without Looking at the Keyboard
pages.heroP: To type without looking, rest your fingers on the home row — left hand on ASDF, right hand on JKL; — feel the small bumps on F and J, and let each finger own its own keys. The skill is called touch typing, and it comes from short daily practice, not talent. Here is exactly how to build it, then test yourself below.

seo.h2: The three stages of not looking
p:
1. You look because you do not know where the key is. Fix: the on-screen keyboard and home-row drills, with the guide visible.
  2. You know the key but look anyway to confirm. Fix: covered rounds. This is the stage that lasts longest, and the only cure is typing with the hands hidden.
  3. You look when you make a mistake. Fix: finish the word before checking. Most "looks" happen after errors, not before them.

Most people are stuck in stage two and believe they are in stage one. The test is simple: type a sentence with your hands under a cloth. If accuracy collapses, you are in stage two and the fix is covered practice, not more key drills.

seo.h2: Why looking is so expensive
p: Each glance costs an eye movement, a re-focus and a re-orientation - roughly a quarter of a second, plus the risk of losing your place in the text. At one glance per word, that is 15-25 seconds of lost typing per minute.
It also prevents the mental map from forming. The map is built by reaching for a key and being right, which is exactly what looking replaces with a visual shortcut.

seo.h2: A two-week plan
p: Days 1-3: one covered round a day, 30 seconds long, no target. Just get through it. Days 4-7: two covered rounds, 60 seconds. Days 8-11: covered rounds on the words you miss most, then a normal round to compare. Days 12-14: one covered round per session, permanently.
Expect accuracy to fall by 10-20% during the covered rounds. It recovers within a week and the resulting speed is higher than where you started, because the glance was the ceiling.

seo.h2: What to do when you get stuck
p: If a particular key keeps failing, practise that key in isolation for thirty seconds, then return to text. If the whole round collapses, shorten it - a 15-second covered round you finish beats a 60-second one you abandon.
And keep one normal round per session. The goal is to type without looking, not to type under a cloth forever.

faq.q: How long does it take to stop looking at the keyboard?
faq.a: Two to four weeks of covered rounds, at 30-60 seconds a day. Accuracy dips 10-20% for the first week before recovering above where you started.

faq.q: Why do I look at the keyboard even when I know the key?
faq.a: That is the confirmation habit, and it is the longest stage. Key drills do not fix it; only typing with the hands hidden does.

faq.q: Should I cover my hands completely?
faq.a: Yes for the covered rounds - a cloth or a sheet of paper. Partial covering lets you cheat by peeking, which keeps the habit alive.

faq.q: Will covering my hands make me slower permanently?
faq.a: No. Accuracy drops for about a week, then speed rises above your previous ceiling because the glance was the limiting factor.

faq.q: I keep losing my place in the text. What helps?
faq.a: Shorten the round and read one word ahead rather than one line ahead. Losing place is usually a reading-ahead problem, not a typing problem.

seo.h2: Why Colemak
p: Colemak was published in 2006 as a middle path between QWERTY and Dvorak. It keeps the common shortcut keys Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places and changes only 17 keys, so the switch is far gentler than Dvorak while still putting the most-used letters under your fingers.

Less finger travel usually means more comfort over long sessions; it does not guarantee a higher top speed, which still depends mostly on practice.

Expect your speed to drop well below your QWERTY speed for the first week or two; that is the switch cost, not a verdict on Colemak. Track accuracy here before speed, because accuracy recovers first and speed follows it. Compare Colemak with Dvorak and QWERTY on the keyboard layouts page.

faq.a: For most QWERTY typists, yes. Colemak changes only 17 keys and keeps Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY positions, so common shortcuts and much of your muscle memory still apply. Dvorak moves almost every key.

pages.title: Keyboard Layouts Compared - QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak
pages.metaDesc: QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak vs Workman compared: home-row use, finger travel and same-finger rate in one table. Test each free.

seo.h2: QWERTY vs Dvorak vs Colemak vs Workman
p: A keyboard layout is just the map of which letter sits under each key. QWERTY has been the default since the 1870s, but alternative layouts rearrange the letters so the most common ones sit on the home row, cutting finger travel. Here is how the four best-known layouts compare on the same English text.

LayoutIntroducedFinger travel*Home-row useSame-finger
QWERTY1870s153 m (baseline)36%7.9%
Dvorak193688 m (−42%)71%3.2%
Colemak200689 m (−42%)73%1.5%

Home-row share and same-finger figures below are modelled from a fixed English passage. For the documented history and design intent of each layout, see keyboard layout, Dvorak keyboard layout (patented 1936) and Colemak (released 2006, 74% of typing on the home row against 32% for QWERTY).

seo.h2: Which keyboard layout is best?
p: There is no single best layout, because less finger movement is not the same as faster typing. QWERTY wins on familiarity: it is on every shared computer and every shortcut assumes it. Dvorak alternates hands the most (about 67% of keystrokes), which many typists find rhythmic for long English prose. Colemak keeps the most letters on the home row (73%) and the fewest awkward same-finger presses (1.5%) while leaving Z, X, C, V and most shortcuts in place, so it is the usual pick for QWERTY users who want to switch. Workman trims total finger travel the most by also minimising sideways stretches.

For almost everyone, practice and accuracy move your WPM far more than the layout does. A fast QWERTY typist will beat a beginner on any layout. Switch for comfort and reduced finger travel, not for a guaranteed speed jump.

seo.h2: Should you switch keyboard layout?
p: Switching costs you one to four weeks of slower, deliberate typing while new muscle memory forms, and shared or public machines will still be QWERTY. The payoff is less finger travel and, for many people, more comfort in long sessions. It is worth it mainly if you type a lot of English every day and own the keyboards you use most.

If you want the gentlest change, start with Colemak because it keeps your common shortcuts. If you love hand-alternation, try Dvorak. The honest answer for casual typists is that staying on QWERTY and practising is the higher-return move.

p: You can practise two of these layouts right now with a matching on-screen keyboard and finger guide: take the Colemak typing test or the Dvorak typing test, or measure your current speed on QWERTY with the main typing speed test. Each shows WPM, accuracy, consistency and a per-key heatmap so you can compare how a layout feels for you.

seo.h2: Choosing a layout
p: Layout decisions: Dvorak vs QWERTY — evidence, retraining cost, and who should switch.

faq.q: Which keyboard layout is the fastest?
faq.a: No layout is reliably fastest for everyone. Modeling shows Dvorak, Colemak and Workman cut finger travel by roughly 42 to 45% versus QWERTY, but measured typing speed depends far more on practice and accuracy than on the layout. The world's fastest typists use several different layouts, including QWERTY.

faq.q: Is Dvorak better than QWERTY?
faq.a: Dvorak puts about 71% of letters on the home row versus QWERTY's 36% and alternates hands more, which many typists find more comfortable for long English text. Studies show modest speed gains at best, so the main benefit is reduced finger movement and comfort, not a guaranteed speed jump.

faq.q: Is Colemak better than Dvorak?
faq.a: Colemak keeps more letters on the home row (about 73%) and the lowest same-finger rate (about 1.5%), and it changes only 17 keys while keeping Z, X, C and V in their QWERTY places, so it is easier to switch to than Dvorak. Dvorak alternates hands more. Which feels better is personal.

faq.q: What is the best keyboard layout for programming?
faq.a: Code uses far more punctuation, brackets and symbols than English prose, so prose-optimised layouts help less. Programmer variants such as Programmer Dvorak and Workman Programmer rearrange the number and symbol rows. Many developers stay on QWERTY because editors, shortcuts and pair-programming all assume it.

faq.q: How long does it take to switch keyboard layouts?
faq.a: Most people reach usable speed again in one to four weeks of short daily practice, and return to their old speed over one to three months. Accuracy recovers before raw speed, so track accuracy first.

faq.q: Can I practise Dvorak and Colemak online for free?
faq.a: Yes. This site has a free Dvorak typing test and a free Colemak typing test, each with an on-screen keyboard relabelled to that layout and a matching finger guide, so you can practise and measure your WPM without installing anything.

pages.tldr: Keyboard layouts trade finger travel against retraining cost. QWERTY puts about 32 percent of typing on the home row; Colemak puts about 74 percent there and Dvorak a little less, while keeping most shortcuts where your hands already expect them. Layout changes rarely beat consistent practice in the short term, so switch only if the travel figures matter more to you than the three to six weeks of slower typing a switch costs.

It is the standard speed test for data entry, accounting and finance work. Take the timed number-pad test below and get your speed instantly.

seo.h2: What is a 10 key typing test?
p: 10 key typing (also written ten key typing or 10-key) is touch typing on the numeric keypad: the number, arithmetic and Enter keys on the right of a full-size keyboard. Instead of hunting for digits across the top row, a 10 key typist keeps the right hand anchored on 4 5 6 with the index, middle and ring fingers, and reaches every other key from there. It is the skill behind fast data entry, bookkeeping and banking work.

This page runs a numpad typing test in numbers mode, so the practice text is digits, decimals, dates and amounts — exactly the characters a 10 key operator types all day. Switch the Time chips to 15 or 30 seconds for a quick check, or run 3–5 minutes for a stable result.

seo.h2: The 10 key home row (4 5 6)
p: Rest your index finger on 4, your middle finger on 5 and your ring finger on 6 — these three usually have a raised bump or a dot so you can find them without looking. The index finger also covers 1 and 7, the middle covers 2 and 8, the ring covers 3 and 9, and the little finger handles 0, . and Enter. Your thumb rests on the 0 key on many layouts.
The golden rule of ten key typing is the same as touch typing on the letter keys: eyes on the screen, fingers always returning to 4 5 6 between digits. Speed comes from never looking down.

seo.h2: How is 10 key speed measured?
p: 10 key speed is usually quoted in keystrokes per hour (KPH) or characters per minute (CPM), not words per minute. A comfortable 10 key speed for data entry is about 8,000–10,000 KPH (roughly 130–165 CPM), and strong operators reach 12,000–15,000 KPH with 99%+ accuracy.

Level10 key speed

seo.h2: Why practise the number pad separately?
p: The top number row and the numeric keypad use completely different muscle memory. Typing letters fast does not make you fast at the number pad, and many people lose a data entry job interview on the 10 key portion alone. Practising the numpad on its own trains the right hand to hit 0–9 and the decimal point without a single glance at the keyboard.
If you need both, warm up with this 10 key typing test and then check your general speed on the number typing test or the main typing speed test.

seo.h2: Keystrokes, characters and words are three units
p: Numeric keypad work is usually scored in keystrokes per hour, but the same minute of typing can be read three ways: keystrokes per hour, characters per minute, and the five-character words per minute used by general typing tests. Because digits and operators are single characters, ten key speeds look far higher in KPH than the same effort looks in WPM — convert before comparing yourself with anyone quoting a different unit.

faq.q: What is a 10 key typing test?
faq.a: A 10 key typing test measures how quickly you type on the numeric keypad (the number pad on the right of a full-size keyboard) using your right hand, keeping the fingers anchored on the 4, 5 and 6 keys.

faq.q: What is a good 10 key speed?
faq.a: For data entry work, aim for at least 8,000 keystrokes per hour (about 133 characters per minute). Experienced operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy or better.

faq.q: Is 10 key the same as touch typing?
faq.a: It is touch typing applied to the numeric keypad. You keep your eyes on the screen, rest the fingers on 4 5 6, and let each finger own its column of digits.

faq.q: How do I improve my 10 key speed?
faq.a: Practise a few minutes a day with your eyes off the keyboard, keep the index, middle and ring fingers on 4, 5 and 6, and prioritise accuracy — errors cost more time than a slightly slower but clean run.

faq.q: Does this work on a laptop without a number pad?
faq.a: On laptops with no dedicated keypad you can use an external USB numeric keypad, or practise the digits with the number-typing mode instead, which uses the top number row.

pages.tldr: A 10 key typing test measures speed on the numeric keypad (the number pad on the right of a full keyboard), not the letter keys. Data-entry and accounting roles often require 8,000 to 10,000 keystrokes per hour, roughly 30 to 40 words per minute, with accuracy above 97 percent. seo.h2: What speed does data entry require?
p: Data entry and clerical jobs usually expect 50–70 WPM with 97%+ accuracy. Numeric-heavy roles are often measured in keystrokes per hour instead, where the bar is about 8,000–10,000 KPH. Some employers use a 10 key (numeric keypad) test rather than a text passage.

seo.h2: Accuracy matters more than raw speed
p: In data entry, a wrong digit is worse than a slow one, so most employers score net speed — your speed after errors are subtracted — and many set a hard accuracy floor. Practise typing clean the first time rather than relying on backspace, and let speed rise on its own as the keystrokes become automatic.
Take the test at the length the employer uses. Most screening tests run 1 to 5 minutes, so warm up with a 1 minute test and then do a 3 minute or 5 minute run.

seo.h2: How to prepare for a data entry typing test
p: Practise with real text that includes numbers, punctuation and capitals, because that is what the passage will contain — not a clean word list. If the role is numeric, train the number pad separately with the 10 key typing test. Sit comfortably, keep your fingers on the home row, and do two or three warm-up runs before your scored attempt so you are at your normal speed.
Every result here is saved in your browser, so you can watch both WPM and accuracy improve over the days before an interview. Your history is private and stays on your device.

seo.h2: What KPH do data entry jobs require?
p: Most data-entry postings quote 8,000–12,000 keystrokes per hour with ~98% accuracy — about 27–40 WPM — and professional numeric roles can reach 12,000–15,000 KPH. For the full requirements table across every scenario, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.

seo.h2: Prepare for data entry hiring tests
p: Before the real test: data entry practice with a two-week KPH plan, and data entry job requirements translated into plain numbers.

seo.h2: Why data entry is measured in keystrokes, not words
p: A data entry record is a set of fields - a name, a reference, a date, an amount - and none of them is a word. Counting characters is the only unit that survives that, which is why postings quote keystrokes per hour or key depressions per hour instead of WPM.

The conversion is arithmetic: 8,000 KPH ≈ 27 WPM, 12,000 KPH ≈ 40 WPM. But the two numbers measure different things in practice, because a character count includes the digits, punctuation and corrections that a prose test quietly ignores.

seo.h2: The drill that matches the job
p: Type records, not passages. A realistic record is four fields and takes about twelve seconds: name, reference, date, amount. Run ten of them, verify each against the source, and count how many are completely clean - that number, not WPM, is what a data entry manager is buying.

Add the two skills the prose test cannot see: the numeric keypad for amounts (4-5-6 home row, thumb on zero), and Tab to move between fields. Typing a clean record and then pressing the wrong key to advance is a lost record just the same.

faq.q: What is a good speed for data entry?
faq.a: Most data entry jobs ask for 50 to 70 words per minute with 97% or higher accuracy. Numeric-heavy roles are often measured in keystrokes per hour, where 8,000 to 10,000 KPH is the usual requirement.

faq.q: How accurate do you need to be for data entry?
faq.a: Aim for 97% to 99% accuracy. Many employers score net speed (errors subtracted) and set a minimum accuracy threshold, so a clean 60 WPM beats a sloppy 75 WPM.

faq.q: How long is a data entry typing test?
faq.a: Employer screening tests are usually 1 to 5 minutes. Practise at 3 minutes for a balanced check, and use shorter runs to warm up.

faq.q: Do data entry jobs use a 10 key test?
faq.a: Many do. Roles that are mostly numeric use a numeric keypad (10 key) test measured in keystrokes per hour, while text-heavy roles use a words-per-minute passage.

faq.q: How can I improve my data entry typing speed?
faq.a: Practise daily with text that includes numbers, punctuation and capitals, prioritise accuracy over speed, and train the number pad separately if the job is numeric.

faq.q: Why is data entry measured in keystrokes rather than WPM?
faq.a: Because a record is a set of fields - name, reference, date, amount - and none of them is a word. Characters per hour is the only unit that survives that, which is why postings quote 8,000-12,000 KPH.

pages.title: Keystrokes Per Hour Test - Free KPH Typing Test

pages.heroP: A keystrokes per hour (KPH) test measures typing speed the way many data entry employers do — in keystrokes over an hour, not words per minute. Data entry roles commonly require 8,000–10,000 KPH. Type the passage below and convert your result to KPH instantly.

seo.h2: What is keystrokes per hour?
p: Keystrokes per hour (KPH or KSPH) counts how many individual key presses you make in an hour, counting every character including spaces. It is the standard measure for data entry and numeric keypad work because it does not depend on how long the words happen to be. A fast data entry operator reaches 10,000–15,000 KPH.

If you know your characters per minute (CPM), multiply by 60 to get KPH: a steady 160 CPM equals 9,600 KPH. This test shows your characters per minute live, so you can read your KPH straight off the result.

seo.h2: KPH vs WPM vs CPM
p: All three describe the same typing, just at different scales. WPM counts words (5 characters each) per minute; CPM counts characters per minute; KPH counts keystrokes per hour. Because a ‘word’ is standardised as 5 characters, the conversions are fixed:

Your speedWPMCPMKPH
Average4020012,000
Good6030018,000
Fast8040024,000
Elite10050030,000
The table assumes no error penalty; employers usually apply a net-accuracy penalty, so your effective KPH is lower than the raw figure.

seo.h2: What KPH do data entry jobs require?
p: Job postings for data entry and clerical work often ask for 8,000–10,000 KPH with a high accuracy rate; some set the bar at 12,000 KPH. Numeric roles may test the number pad specifically, so pair this test with the 10 key typing test. Measure your text speed here and your WPM on the words per minute test, then check the requirements in the typing test for jobs page.

seo.h2: How do KPH requirements convert to WPM?
p: Divide by 300: WPM = KPH ÷ 300, so a 10,000 KPH posting is asking for about 33 WPM. For the complete table of KPH, CPM and WPM requirements by job and exam, see typing speed requirements by job and exam.

seo.h2: Where KPH scores lead
p: Put your KPH to work: online typing jobs that quote KPH, and data entry job requirements by the numbers.

seo.h2: Sources for the numbers on this page
p: Speed and accuracy figures quoted here follow the largest published study of everyday typing: Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes, which measured 136,857,600 keystrokes from 168,960 volunteers. It reports a mean of 51.56 WPM (SD 20.2), a mean uncorrected error rate of 1.17%, and a mean keystrokes-per-character rate of 1.173. Those are the numbers this page's bands are checked against.

The claim that finger consistency and keypress preparation predict speed — more than which finger presses which key — comes from Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta, CHI 2016, a motion-capture study of 36 typists. The two studies disagree on how much formal touch-typing training matters, and this page says so where it matters rather than picking the tidier result.

Where a figure is an estimate rather than a measurement — job requirements, age bands, exam cut-offs — it is drawn from the ranges employers and exam boards publish and is labelled as an estimate. Nothing on this page is a benchmark we ran ourselves.

seo.h2: Keystrokes, characters and words are three units
p: Numeric keypad work is usually scored in keystrokes per hour, but the same minute of typing can be read three ways: keystrokes per hour, characters per minute, and the five-character words per minute used by general typing tests. Because digits and operators are single characters, ten key speeds look far higher in KPH than the same effort looks in WPM — convert before comparing yourself with anyone quoting a different unit.

seo.h2: What is the average keystrokes per hour?
p: Around 12,000 KPH is the middle of the working population, because that is what 40 WPM produces and 40 WPM is close to the median office speed. The bands below convert the WPM distribution into keystrokes per hour using KPH = WPM × 300.

Keystrokes per hourWPM equivalentReading
6,00020Beginner; hunt-and-peck
9,00030Below average, workable for simple entry
12,00040The common data-entry floor and close to the median
15,00050Above average; comfortable for full-time entry
18,00060Fast; upper band for entry work
24,00080Top decile; numeric-heavy roles

The distribution behind those WPM figures is the CHI 2018 sample (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2, n = 168,960), summarised on the benchmarks page. The conversion is arithmetic, so the uncertainties are in the WPM band, not in the multiplication.

seo.h2: 8,000 key depressions per hour in WPM
p: 8,000 KPDH ÷ 300 = 26.7 WPM (or 133 keystrokes per minute). That is the figure Indian SSC DEO posts use, and it is deliberately modest because the scoring counts every keypress - including backspaces.

That distinction is the whole difficulty. In a keystroke-per-hour test, a correction is another keystroke against your hour, so a typist who produces 35 WPM but backspaces constantly can score below someone at 30 WPM who types it right first time. If you are preparing for a KPDH test, practise without correcting: alphanumeric drills are the closest format.

Key depressions per hourWPM (÷300)Keystrokes per minute

seo.h2: Key depression and keystroke are not always the same thing
p: A keystroke in this site's measurement means a character typed correctly. A key depression in examination scoring means any key pressed down, including Shift, Tab, Enter and backspace. The two numbers differ most for typists who correct a lot.

So when a posting says "8,000 key depressions per hour", assume it counts everything, and treat your KPH score from this page as an optimistic version of it. When a posting says "keystrokes per hour" without qualification, ask - the difference is worth several WPM.

faq.q: What is a good keystrokes per hour score?
faq.a: For data entry work, 8,000 to 10,000 KPH is the usual requirement, and fast operators reach 12,000 to 15,000 KPH with 99% accuracy. General office roles often accept lower KPH because typing is only part of the job.

faq.q: How do I convert KPH to WPM?
faq.a: WPM = KPH ÷ 300. Because 1 word is 5 characters and there are 60 minutes in an hour, 60 WPM equals 18,000 KPH.

faq.q: How do I convert CPM to KPH?
faq.a: Multiply characters per minute by 60: 160 CPM equals 9,600 KPH.

faq.q: Does this test score accuracy too?
faq.a: Yes. It reports your characters per minute live and, like every test on this site, gives your accuracy and error count after the run, so you can judge net rather than gross speed.

faq.q: Is KPH used for 10 key tests?
faq.a: Yes. Numeric keypad (10 key) tests are almost always scored in keystrokes per hour, which is why data entry applicants are often asked for a 10 key KPH figure.

faq.q: What is the average keystrokes per hour?
faq.a: About 12,000 KPH, which is what 40 WPM produces and roughly the median office speed. 15,000 KPH (50 WPM) is above average and 24,000 (80 WPM) is top-decile.

faq.q: How many WPM is 8,000 key depressions per hour?
faq.a: 26.7 WPM. 8,000 ÷ 300 = 26.7, or 133 keystrokes per minute. Corrections count as key depressions, so backspacing lowers the effective score.

pages.tldr: Keystrokes per hour (KPH) measures total key presses in an hour and is the standard metric for numeric data-entry jobs, where 8,000 to 10,000 KPH is common. Because one word averages five characters, KPH is roughly WPM multiplied by 300; this page measures your KPH live and converts it to WPM and CPM.

seo.h2: Calculate your speed from what you typed
p: 60 WPM gross / 59.4 WPM net / 300 CPM / 18,000 KPH / 66th percentile

Enter the characters you typed, the errors you left uncorrected, and the seconds elapsed. The calculator returns gross WPM, net WPM, CPM, keystrokes per hour and the approximate percentile of the net score.

The percentile uses a normal approximation of the CHI 2018 distribution (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2). It is an approximation - real typing speed is mildly left-skewed - and it reproduces the study's reported deciles to within about one point. The percentile page has the full curve.

seo.h2: How to calculate typing speed (WPM)
p: Typing speed in words per minute (WPM) is worked out with one simple formula: WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes. Every five characters count as one ‘word’, so longer words are worth more. Net WPM subtracts your errors first: net WPM = ((correct characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes). Employers use net WPM, because a mistake you have to fix costs time.
To get your own numbers, just take the timed test above — it computes WPM, raw WPM, CPM and accuracy for you, so you can read your result straight off the scoreboard.

seo.h2: WPM, CPM and KPH conversions
p: The three common typing-speed units are all fixed multiples of each other, so you can convert any of them by hand:

FromToFormula
CPMWPMWPM = CPM ÷ 5
WPMCPMCPM = WPM × 5
CPMKPHKPH = CPM × 60
WPMKPHKPH = WPM × 300
WPMWPM = (characters ÷ 5) ÷ minutes
So 60 WPM = 300 CPM = 18,000 KPH. These are the standard conversions used by typing certificates and data entry employers.

seo.h2: Worked examples
p: If you type 300 characters in 1 minute, that is 300 ÷ 5 = 60 WPM (or 18,000 KPH). If you type 1,200 characters in 3 minutes, that is (1,200 ÷ 5) ÷ 3 = 80 WPM. If you make 12 mistakes over that run, your net speed is (1,200 − 12) ÷ 5 ÷ 3 = 79 WPM.
Want the measured number instead of the maths? Run the words per minute test for WPM, the CPM typing test for characters per minute, or the keystrokes per hour test for KPH.

faq.q: How do I calculate my typing speed in WPM?
faq.a: WPM = (characters typed ÷ 5) ÷ minutes elapsed. Every 5 characters count as one word, so 300 characters in 1 minute is 60 WPM.

faq.q: How do I convert CPM to WPM?
faq.a: Divide characters per minute by 5. So 250 CPM is 50 WPM, and 400 CPM is 80 WPM.

faq.q: How do I convert WPM to KPH?
faq.a: Multiply WPM by 300. For example, 60 WPM equals 18,000 keystrokes per hour.

faq.q: What is the difference between gross and net WPM?
faq.a: Gross WPM counts every character you typed; net WPM subtracts your errors first. Employers almost always use net WPM because it reflects usable output.

faq.a: Yes. The typing speed calculator and every typing test on this site are completely free, with no sign-up and no account.

pages.tldr: Gross WPM = characters ÷ 5 ÷ minutes. Net WPM subtracts errors first. CPM = characters ÷ minutes, and KPH = CPM × 60. The calculator below does all five figures at once, including the percentile.

pages.title: Quick Brown Fox Typing Test - Free Pangram Practice
pages.metaDesc: Free quick brown fox typing test. Practise the classic pangram that uses every letter of the alphabet, and check your typing speed and accuracy.
pages.heroP: The ‘the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog’ sentence is the most famous pangram in typing practice — a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. Typing it is the traditional warm-up and a quick way to check that every key on your keyboard works. Take the test below and measure your speed and accuracy.

seo.h2: What is the quick brown fox sentence?
p: ‘The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog’ is a pangram: a sentence that uses all 26 letters of the alphabet at least once. Because it covers the whole keyboard it has been the standard typing drill for over a century, and it is still used to test typewriters, keyboards and fonts. Practising it warms up every finger before a longer typing test.
Type it a few times here — the test scrolls through alphabet-rich sentences in the same spirit, so your warm-up trains every letter rather than only the common ones.

seo.h2: Why practise with pangrams?
p: Ordinary sentences repeat the same handful of common letters and rarely touch q, z, x or j. A pangram forces every key into the run, which is exactly what you need before a speed attempt: it surfaces the awkward keys while the stakes are low. That is why ‘quick brown fox’ games appear in almost every typing tutor and school typing class.
For a targeted version, the keyboard typing test highlights the next key and the correct finger, and the easy typing test uses simple high-frequency words if the pangram still feels hard.

seo.h2: Quick brown fox and keyboard checking
p: Because the pangram contains every letter, typing it is the fastest way to confirm that no key is broken or stuck: if a letter is missing from the output, that key is faulty. Try it with capitals and punctuation too — ‘The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.’ — to exercise the shift keys and the full stop. Then move on to a full typing speed test to get your WPM.

seo.h2: Where the sentence comes from
p: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog is a pangram - it contains every letter of the English alphabet at least once. Sentences like it were used from the late nineteenth century to test typewriters and telegraph equipment, because a single line could exercise every key.
That history is why it is still the default demo text on keyboard and font sites. It is short, it is memorable, and it touches every letter without needing a paragraph.

seo.h2: What it is good for, and what it is not
p:
Good forNot good for
Warming up every key in 15 secondsMeasuring your real speed - it is short and you memorise it
Checking that every key registersTesting punctuation, capitals or digits
A first typing test for a beginnerComparing yourself to a benchmark

The memorisation point is the important one. By the fifth attempt you are recalling the sentence rather than reading it, and the score rises without your skill changing. Use it as a warm-up, then measure on text you have not seen.

seo.h2: Other pangrams worth rotating
p: Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow; Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs; How vexingly quick daft zebras jump; Waltz, bad nymph, for quick jigs vex. Each is a different length and a different letter distribution, which is exactly what stops memorisation from inflating the score.
Two or three is enough. Rotating through sixteen is entertainment; rotating through three is practice.

faq.q: What is the quick brown fox sentence?
faq.a: ‘The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog’ is a pangram — a sentence that contains every letter of the alphabet. It has been the classic typing-practice sentence for over a century.

faq.q: Why is the quick brown fox used for typing?
faq.a: Because it uses all 26 letters, it exercises every key and finger in one short line, making it an ideal warm-up and a fast way to check that your keyboard works.

faq.q: Is the quick brown fox test good for beginners?
faq.a: It is a good warm-up, but the unusual letters (q, z, x) make it harder than common-word practice. Beginners may prefer the easy typing test first.

faq.q: How many words are in the quick brown fox sentence?
faq.a: The classic sentence is nine words: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. It contains 35 letters.

faq.q: Can I use it to test a keyboard?
faq.a: Yes. If a letter is missing from what you type, that key is faulty. Include the full stop and capitals to test shift and punctuation keys as well.

faq.q: Why do typing tests use the quick brown fox?
faq.a: It is a pangram - it contains every letter of the alphabet - so one short line exercises every key. It has been used to test typewriters and keyboards since the late nineteenth century.

faq.q: Is the quick brown fox a good speed test?
faq.a: No, for measurement. It is short and quickly memorised, so the score rises without skill changing. Use it as a warm-up or a key check, and measure on unseen text.

pages.tldr: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" is a pangram, a sentence that uses every letter of the alphabet at least once, which is why typing tests use it to exercise the whole keyboard. This page lets you type the quick brown fox and other pangrams to warm up and check every key works.

pages.heroP: The home row is the row of keys your fingers rest on — A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right. Every key on the keyboard is reached from here, which is why home-row practice is the first lesson in touch typing. Take the timed test below to drill the home row and track your progress.

seo.h2: What is the home row?
p: The home row (also called the home keys) is the middle row of the keyboard where your fingers rest between keystrokes: A S D F for the left hand and J K L ; for the right hand. The F and J keys have small raised bumps so your index fingers can find home by feel alone, without looking down.

Home-row typing is the foundation of touch typing. Each finger owns a column of keys and always returns to its home key, so the hand never has to hunt for a letter. Start by typing only home-row letters until they feel automatic, then add the rows above and below.

seo.h2: Which finger types which home key?
p:
Home keyFingerAlso reaches
ALeft pinkyQ, Z, 1
SLeft ringW, X, 2
DLeft middleE, C, 3
FLeft indexR, T, G, V, B, 4, 5
JRight indexY, U, H, N, M, 6, 7
KRight middleI, comma, 8

The thumbs rest on the space bar. Keeping this assignment is what lets you type without looking — see the full method on how to type without looking.

seo.h2: Home row drills and practice
p: Effective home-row practice repeats the eight home keys in short, varied bursts rather than long paragraphs, so your fingers build the exact movements they need. Run this test for 1 or 2 minutes a day, aiming first for perfect accuracy and only then for speed. When the home row feels natural, move on to the touch typing test and the keyboard typing test, which introduce the surrounding rows with an on-screen finger guide.

seo.h2: Hand and finger fundamentals
p: Placement done right: proper hand position for typing and the typing finger chart.

faq.q: What are the home row keys?
faq.a: A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, ; for the right hand, with the thumbs on the space bar. F and J have raised bumps so you can find the row without looking.

faq.q: Why is the home row important?
faq.a: It is the base position of touch typing. Every key is reached from home and the fingers return there, so you never have to look down to find a letter.

faq.q: Which fingers type the home row?
faq.a: Left hand: pinky on A, ring on S, middle on D, index on F. Right hand: index on J, middle on K, ring on L, pinky on ;.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn the home row?
faq.a: Most people feel comfortable within a few days of short daily practice, but full touch typing across all rows takes a few weeks of consistent practice.

faq.q: Should I look at the keyboard when practising?
faq.a: No. Keep your eyes on the screen and use the F and J bumps to find home. Looking down slows the muscle memory you are trying to build.

pages.tldr: The home row is the middle letter row: A, S, D, F for the left hand and J, K, L, semicolon for the right, with raised bumps on F and J to find it by touch. Touch typists keep their fingers anchored there and return after each reach, which is the foundation of all typing speed. This page drills the home row with a finger guide.

pages.heroP: This typing test for adults is built for grown-ups who want a quick, no-nonsense check of their typing speed and accuracy — no lessons, no cartoon mascots, no account. The average adult types around 40 WPM; take the test below and see where you land.

seo.h2: What is a good typing speed for an adult?
p: The average adult typing speed is about 40 WPM. Reaching 60 WPM puts you comfortably above average and is enough for most office work; 80 WPM is fast, and 100 WPM+ is top-tier. Age or when you learned to type matter far less than how much you practise.

These bands come from published typing-speed studies; see the full average typing speed breakdown by age and profession.

seo.h2: You can still learn to type faster as an adult
p: It is a common myth that only children can build typing speed. Adults usually improve faster than children because they follow instructions, understand why accuracy comes before speed and can practise deliberately. The catch is unlearning years of two-finger habit: the fix is to slow down, keep the fingers on the home row, and look at the screen instead of the keyboard.
Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough. Start with the home row typing test, then the touch typing test, and only push for raw speed once your accuracy is steady.

seo.h2: How to use this test as an adult
p: Decide what you need. For a job application, run a 1–3 minute test and check the requirement table in the typing test for jobs. For everyday comfort, test once a day at 1 minute and watch the trend in your saved history. For data entry or accounting work, add the 10 key typing test. Your results are stored only in your browser, so nothing is uploaded.

seo.h2: Why adults usually start below where they could be
p: Almost every adult who types slowly learned by using a computer, not by being taught. That means the habits formed were whatever got the work done: two fingers, looking at the keyboard, backspacing through errors. None of those are permanent, but all of them are invisible until you try to type without looking.

The encouraging part is that adults learn the key map faster than children do - you already read and write fluently, so the bottleneck is motor habit rather than language. Two weeks of covered rounds typically produces the first real jump.

seo.h2: Reasons adults actually have for improving
p:
• A job requirement - clerical, reception, dispatch, legal and medical support postings quote 40-60 WPM and often test it.
  • A return to work - the test is usually a five-minute sample with an accuracy floor, not a race.
  • Career change into admin or support - the typing bar is modest but the accuracy expectation is not.
  • Writing volume - reports, emails and documentation that used to be someone else's job.
  • Comfort - less hunting means less wrist and shoulder tension by the end of a day.

seo.h2: What to expect in the first month
p: Week 1 is slower and frustrating: you are replacing a working habit. Weeks 2-3 bring accuracy up and speed back to where it started. Week 4 usually produces the first measurable gain, often 5-8 WPM, mostly from no longer looking down.
If you are over 50, add one thing: a five-minute break every half hour during practice, and stop at the first sign of hand or wrist discomfort. The skill builds fine at that pace; strain does not.

faq.q: What is a good typing speed for an adult?
faq.a: Around 40 WPM is average for adults, 60 to 80 WPM is good and enough for most jobs, and 100 WPM or more is elite. Consistent practice matters more than age.

faq.q: Can adults learn to type faster?
faq.a: Yes. Adults often improve faster than children because they can practise deliberately. Focus on accuracy and touch typing rather than raw speed at first.

faq.q: How much practice do adults need?
faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes a day is enough to see steady improvement within a few weeks, as long as you keep your eyes off the keyboard.

faq.q: Do adults need to learn touch typing?
faq.a: Not everyone, but touch typing removes the speed ceiling of two-finger typing and reduces strain during long sessions, so it pays off for anyone who types daily.

faq.q: Is this typing test free for adults?
faq.a: Yes, completely free, with no sign-up and no ads in the typing area. Your results are saved only in your own browser.

faq.q: Can adults learn to touch type?
faq.a: Yes, and often faster than children on the key map, because reading and writing are already fluent. The slower part is replacing the two-finger habit, which takes about two weeks of short daily covered practice.

faq.q: What typing speed do adult job seekers need?
faq.a: 40-50 WPM with 97% accuracy covers most clerical, reception and admin postings. Legal, medical and transcription roles ask 60-75, and public-sector tests often require a proctored certificate.

pages.tldr: The average adult types about 40 words per minute; 40 to 60 WPM is comfortable, 60 to 80 is fast and above 100 is rare. Adults can still add 10 to 20 WPM with deliberate practice, so this free adult typing test sets realistic targets by skill level rather than competitive leaderboards.

pages.heroP: This typing test for students measures your WPM and accuracy in one minute and shows how you compare with other students. Typing quickly and accurately saves time on essays, notes and online exams — and many courses and jobs now expect 40–60 WPM.

seo.h2: What typing speed should a student have?
p: Most students type between 30 and 50 WPM, and schools increasingly expect 40–60 WPM by the end of secondary school so that typing stops being a bottleneck for essays and exams. College students and anyone writing long assignments benefit most from reaching 60 WPM+.

StageTypical / target WPM
Primary / elementary15–30
Middle school30–40
High school40–60
College / university60+
Targets vary by school and country; the bands above reflect commonly published guidance. See the full average typing speed table for more detail.

seo.h2: Why students should type faster
p: Typing speed is study efficiency. At 60 WPM you can keep up with a lecturer in real time, transcribe notes without falling behind, and finish essays in less time while staying in flow. For out-of-class and online exams, slow typing can cost marks simply because you run out of time — not because you do not know the answer.
If you type with two fingers, the ceiling is low. Learning touch typing is a one-time investment: practise the home row, then the touch typing test, and your speed will follow.

seo.h2: How to practise as a student
p: Ten minutes a day beats an hour once a week. Warm up with a short drill, take a 1-minute test to record your WPM, then spend the rest of the time on whichever is weaker — speed on the typing practice page, or precision with the typing accuracy test. Every result is saved in your browser so you can chart your progress before an exam or application.

seo.h2: Where students actually lose time
p: Not in essays. Students lose time in the small, repeated typing tasks: searching a database for a citation, writing lab notes, replying to a seminar email, formatting a bibliography by hand. Each is two minutes of typing, five times a day.

The measurable consequence is that typing speed correlates with how much written work gets finished, not with how good it is. A student at 35 WPM spends roughly twice as long on the same written output as one at 70 WPM, and that gap comes out of reading time.

seo.h2: Exam and coursework contexts worth rehearsing
p:
ContextWhat is timedWhat to rehearse
Timed online exam with typed answersThe whole paper, including thinkingTyping while composing, not copying - practise answering a question in 200 words at pace
In-class laptop notesNothing, but you fall behind the lectureSpeed with abbreviations and no backspace; lectures run 130-150 words a minute
Referencing and formattingYour own patienceRepeat the same citation ten times rather than ten citations once
Language or typing exam (e.g. SSC, school boards)A fixed passage at a fixed speedThe exact format: length, punctuation, error allowance

seo.h2: A term-long plan that fits around coursework
p: Ten minutes, four days a week, for twelve weeks. Weeks 1-4: home row and covered rounds - this is the only part that feels like a step backwards. Weeks 5-8: accuracy at speed, 30-second sprints plus one slow round. Weeks 9-12: real material - lecture notes, your own essay paragraphs, a citation style you actually use.
Do not practise on random word lists in week 9. By then the constraint is your vocabulary and your punctuation habits, and those only appear in your own subject's text.

faq.q: What is a good typing speed for a student?
faq.a: Most students type 30 to 50 WPM. Schools often target 40 to 60 WPM by the end of secondary school, and college students writing long assignments benefit from 60 WPM or more.

faq.q: Why should students learn to type faster?
faq.a: Faster typing means keeping up with lectures, finishing essays sooner and not losing marks to the clock in timed or online exams.

faq.q: What typing speed do I need for exams?
faq.a: It depends on the exam, but 40 to 60 WPM is a comfortable target for written exams and coursework. Check your own requirement with a teacher or in the syllabus.

faq.q: Can students learn to type without looking?
faq.a: Yes, and they usually learn fastest. Practise the home row and touch typing a little each day, keeping the eyes on the screen rather than the keyboard.

faq.q: Is this typing test suitable for school use?
faq.a: Yes. The test is free, needs no sign-up and stores results only in the browser, which makes it suitable for classroom or homework practice.

faq.q: Does typing speed matter for grades?
faq.a: Indirectly. Timed exams, coursework volume and note-taking all convert typing speed into time. A student at 70 WPM writes the same essay in roughly half the keystrokes' worth of time as one at 35 WPM.

faq.q: What typing speed should a university student have?
faq.a: 45-60 WPM with 97% accuracy covers essay writing, notes and referencing comfortably. Below 35 WPM, the keyboard becomes the bottleneck for written coursework.

pages.tldr: Students are expected to grow with their grade: roughly 20 to 30 WPM in primary school, 30 to 40 in middle school, 40 to 50 in high school and 50 or more at university. Typing well cuts note-taking and essay time, so this free student typing test measures WPM and accuracy with targets for each stage.

pages.title: Typing Skill Test - Free Online Typing Skills Test
pages.metaDesc: Free typing skill test. Check your typing skill level online with a timed WPM and accuracy test, and see the scores that count as good for jobs and exams.
pages.heroP: A typing skill test tells you how good you are at typing: your words per minute (WPM), your accuracy and your error rate, combined into one clear picture of your typing skill level. It is the same kind of test used for job applications and typing exams. Take it below and get your score instantly.

seo.h2: What a typing skill test actually measures
p: Three figures, not one. Net speed is the number employers quote. Accuracy is what they weight when the job involves records, codes or names. Consistency - how much your speed varies second to second - predicts whether the speed survives a five-minute test.
A single WPM number hides all of that. Two typists at 60 WPM can be a careful 99% accuracy operator and a 91% risky one, and the second is a liability in any role where a wrong digit matters.

seo.h2: Skill bands, and what each one opens
p:
BandNet WPMAccuracyWhat it clears
Entry25-3592-95%Some dispatch and call-centre floors; personal use
Clerical35-4595-97%Data entry at 8,000-12,000 KPH; county clerk roles
Office standard45-5597%Reception, admin, general office postings
Fast55-7098%Legal secretary, medical admin, transcription entry
Professional70-8598-99%Transcription upper band, dispatch supervisor, court support
These bands come from advertised requirements, not from a certification body - no one certifies a typing skill level. They are useful because they match the numbers employers actually print.

seo.h2: How to test your skill fairly
p: Use a five-minute round on sentences, in one sitting, at the same time of day each time. Then repeat it on a second day before you believe the number: single-round scores move by 5-10 WPM for reasons that have nothing to do with skill.
If you only ever test on one-minute rounds, you are measuring your burst, not your skill. Five minutes is long enough for the warm-up advantage to fade and short enough to repeat weekly.

seo.h2: What employers do with the score
p: Most screen against a floor - 40 WPM is the common one - and then watch the work sample. A few use a platform test with a cut score, and public-sector roles often require a proctored result.

In practice the accuracy figure decides more outcomes than the speed figure, because it is the one that predicts rework. If you are choosing which number to improve, improve accuracy first: it is faster to move and it is what the job punishes.

seo.h2: Improving the weakest of the three
p: Speed low? Work the habit ceiling - covered rounds and no-backspace rounds (see the plateau guide).
Accuracy low? Slow to 85% of your pace for two weeks and refuse to correct during rounds; the error list, not the score, is the thing to read.
Consistency low? Type ten rounds and look at the spread. Slow-hold rounds narrow it faster than any speed drill - the consistency page has the method.

faq.q: What is a typing skill test?
faq.a: A timed test that reports net speed, accuracy and often consistency, rather than a single WPM figure. It is meant to show what you can sustain, not your best burst.

faq.q: What is a good typing skill level?
faq.a: 45-55 WPM at 97% accuracy clears most office requirements. 55-70 at 98% opens legal, medical and transcription entry roles; above 70 with high accuracy is professional territory.

faq.q: How long should the test be?
faq.a: Five minutes on sentences, repeated on a second day. A one-minute round measures a burst, and a single round moves 5-10 WPM for reasons unrelated to skill.

faq.q: Does accuracy matter more than speed?
faq.a: For most jobs, yes. Accuracy predicts rework, and the roles that quote speed also quote an accuracy floor - typically 95-98%.

faq.q: Is there an official typing skill certification?
faq.a: No universal one. Public-sector exams and some agencies issue certificates for their own requirements, but no body certifies a general typing skill level.

pages.tldr: A skill test measures three things at once: net speed, accuracy, and how steady the speed is. A 55 WPM typist at 99% accuracy with a flat curve is more employable than a 65 WPM typist at 92% who swings 20 WPM between rounds.

seo.h2: What typing speed do government jobs require?
p: Government typing requirements vary by post and country, but the common shape is: a minimum of 30–40 WPM for entry-level administrative roles, and 40–60 WPM with high accuracy for clerical, secretarial and data entry positions. Where the job is mainly data entry, the test may be a numeric one scored in keystrokes per hour instead.

Post typeTypical requirement
Entry / general clerical30–40 WPM
Clerical / admin40–50 WPM
Secretarial / stenography50–70 WPM
Data entry8,000–10,000 KPH

Speed is only half of it: government tests usually require 95–98% accuracy, and some subtract errors, so a clean run beats a fast messy one. Requirements differ by department and country — always check the official notification for your exam.

seo.h2: How government typing tests are scored
p: Government typing tests are timed, commonly 3 to 5 minutes, and scored on net speed — the words per minute remaining after errors are deducted. Many use a fixed passage, and some allow no backspace, so typing it correctly the first time is essential. Because the standard is net speed, accuracy training is the fastest route to passing, not raw bursts of speed.
Practise at the exam length. Warm up with a 1 minute test, then run 3 and 5 minutes to build the stamina a scored attempt needs.

seo.h2: How to prepare for a government typing test
p: Work on accuracy until you can complete a passage cleanly, then raise speed. Train the home row and touch typing so you are not watching your hands, and if the post is data entry, drill the keypad with the 10 key typing test. Test yourself under the same conditions as the exam — same length, no restarts — and check your standing against the average typing speed. Your practice history stays in your browser.

seo.h2: What typing speed do government exams require?
p: Government clerk and assistant exams usually qualify on a short timed passage around 25–35 WPM with capped errors. For the complete scenario-by-scenario table with conversions, see typing speed requirements by job and exam. For country-specific exam formats such as SSC, IBPS and court clerk tests, see the government jobs typing test guide.

seo.h2: The three formats you will actually meet
p:

Read the notice rather than a general guide: the same country runs all three formats, and the notice is the only document that states which one applies to you.

seo.h2: What the day itself is like
p: You will type on unfamiliar equipment, usually a basic membrane keyboard, with the passage on screen or on paper beside you. The clock starts when the proctor says so, not when you are ready.

Three practical habits: type one warm-up sentence before the clock if allowed; do not watch the timer, because the countdown costs more accuracy than it buys speed; and if the format allows corrections, fix only the errors that change meaning - a scrawl of backspaces at minute four is how candidates fail a qualifying test.

faq.q: What typing speed do government jobs require?
faq.a: Entry-level government and clerical roles commonly require 30 to 40 WPM, while clerical, secretarial and data roles ask for 40 to 70 WPM with high accuracy. Check the official notification for your specific exam.

faq.q: How long is a government typing test?
faq.a: Government typing tests are typically 3 to 5 minutes long and are scored on net words per minute after errors are deducted.

faq.q: Is accuracy important in government typing tests?
faq.a: Yes. Most government tests require 95% to 98% accuracy, and many subtract errors from your score, so accuracy matters as much as speed.

faq.q: Do government jobs use a numeric typing test?
faq.a: Data entry posts often use a numeric keypad (10 key) test scored in keystrokes per hour, while general clerical posts use a text passage measured in words per minute.

faq.q: How do I pass a government typing test?
faq.a: Practise at the exam length, prioritise accuracy over raw speed, learn to touch type so you do not look at the keyboard, and train the number pad if the post is data entry.

faq.q: What is the difference between government typing test formats?
faq.a: Three: a fixed short standard (US federal, 40 WPM over five minutes with at most three errors), a post-specific speed over a longer sample (SSC 35 WPM English / 30 Hindi, 8,000 key depressions for DEO), and a proctored certificate with an employer-set floor. The notice states which applies.

pages.tldr: Government and clerical typing tests are usually qualifying rounds with a fixed pass mark, commonly around 35 to 50 words per minute with strict accuracy limits. This free practice page runs a timed passage, most exams use three to five minutes, so you can rehearse the exact format before the real test.

seo.h2: Paragraph versus word-list tests
p: A word-list test (the monkeytype style) shows one word at a time and rewards raw reaction. A paragraph test shows continuous prose, so it also measures reading ahead, punctuation, capitals, and the ability to hold a rhythm across sentences.

Employers test with paragraphs because that is what the job looks like: continuous text with full stops, names, commas and the occasional number. A word-list score is a training metric; a paragraph score is a work metric.

seo.h2: Why paragraphs are harder
p: Three reasons. Punctuation and capitals add keystrokes that a word list omits. Sentence structure means the next word is predictable, but only if you read ahead - which most typists do not. And length means fatigue enters: errors in the fourth minute are usually attention, not technique.
The result is a score typically 5-15% lower than the same typist's word-list number, and 5-10 WPM lower than a one-minute burst on the same text.

seo.h2: Choosing a length
p:
LengthWhat it measuresUse it when
1 minuteBurst speedDaily warm-up, quick comparison
3 minutesCommon screening lengthInterview practice, exam rehearsal
5 minutesWorking paceThe number you quote; matches most job standards
10 minutesEnduranceTranscription, data entry, long document work

seo.h2: How to use this page
p: Start with one minute to warm up, then run a five-minute round and record net WPM plus accuracy. If accuracy is under 96%, stop chasing speed and run accuracy rounds for a week - it is the cheaper fix.

For exam-style practice, use the same length as the exam and include punctuation. For a written job test, add one round of the quotes test, which is the closest thing to real document text. A paragraph score is only useful if you can reproduce it on a second attempt, at a different time of day, on a keyboard you have not warmed up on.

faq.q: What is a paragraph typing test?
faq.a: A test using continuous prose rather than a word list, so it measures reading ahead, punctuation and capitals alongside raw speed.

faq.q: Why is my paragraph speed lower than my word-list speed?
faq.a: Punctuation and capitals add keystrokes, sentence structure requires reading ahead, and length introduces fatigue. A 5-15% lower score is normal.

faq.q: How long should the paragraph be?
faq.a: Five minutes for a number you can quote, three minutes to match most screening tests, ten minutes for transcription and data-entry work.

faq.q: Do employers use paragraphs or word lists?
faq.a: Paragraphs, because that is what the work looks like. Word-list scores are useful for training but they are not what screening tools measure.

faq.q: Is this the same as a passage typing test?
faq.a: Yes. Paragraph, passage and prose tests all mean continuous text; the differences are length and difficulty, not format.

pages.tldr: A paragraph typing test uses connected sentences with capitals and punctuation, the format real exams and employers set, rather than a list of single words. Paragraph scores run a little lower than word-list scores because of the extra reaches, but they reflect your true working speed; this page offers 1, 5 and 10 minute passages.

pages.title: Beginner Typing Test - Free Test for Typing Beginners
pages.metaDesc: A free beginner typing test for people just starting out. Short passages and instant feedback so you can see your first WPM score with no pressure.
pages.heroP: New to typing? Start here: an easy, forgiving test that measures where you are today so you can watch yourself improve.

seo.h2: A first test that does not punish you
p: The default round is short, the words are common, and the score is reported with accuracy beside it. A beginner's first number should be a baseline, not a verdict - most untrained adults start at 20-30 WPM with 90-95% accuracy, and that is normal.
If your accuracy is below 85%, the speed number is not meaningful yet. Slow down until errors are rare; the speed will follow within two weeks and it will be a real number rather than a lucky one.

seo.h2: What a beginner should actually practise
p:
• Home row first. asdf jkl; until the fingers return without looking.
  • No looking down. One covered round a day. This is the single largest gain available at this stage.
  • No backspace. Finish rounds with mistakes in them. Corrections cost more than errors at beginner speed.
  • Ten minutes daily. Short and frequent beats a long weekly session, because the skill is motor memory.

seo.h2: Your first realistic targets
p:
StageWPMAccuracyWhat it unlocks

First month25-3595%Comfortable email and messaging

Six months45-6097%+Most clerical job floors
These are typical progressions for someone practising ten minutes a day, not guarantees. The variable that matters is consistency, not talent.

seo.h2: What to do after your first month
p: Move to the one-minute test for the classic benchmark, and add the home row test as a weekly check on technique. When you can hold 95% accuracy at 35 WPM, the 40 WPM plan is the next step.
Avoid jumping to hard text or code typing before the map is automatic - it moves the errors rather than removing them.

seo.h2: Your first week, day by day
p:
Day10 minutesWhat to notice
1Find F and J by touch; type the home row slowlyWhether you can return to the home row without looking

3Top row added; short real wordsWhich finger reaches wrong first
4Bottom row added; one minute of normal textWhether you are backspacing more than typing
5No-backspace round, then a slow accuracy roundHow much the corrections were costing you
