The population behind the distribution - who was measured, on what device, and why the numbers differ between sources - is on the average typing speed page.

seo.h2: What the percentile does not tell you
p: The sample is self-selected: people who choose to take an online typing test are not a random sample of the population, and they are disproportionately young, educated and comfortable in English. A 60 WPM score being the 66th percentile here does not mean it is the 66th percentile of all office workers.

The study also measures transcription typing — copying displayed text — on a desktop keyboard in English. Phone typing, dictation, code and non-Latin scripts are different tasks with different distributions, so a percentile from this table describes one specific skill.

seo.h2: Using the percentile for a decision
p: For job applications, percentiles are persuasive but not what screeners check: they check against a fixed threshold such as 40 or 50 WPM. Use the percentile to decide whether you are in the band, and the raw net WPM to report it.

For practice targets, aim at the next decile rather than the mean. Moving from the 50th to the 66th is roughly 10 WPM and takes weeks; moving from the 90th to the 99th is 22 WPM and takes months of deliberate practice on specific key sequences.
Every figure on this page, with its source and a downloadable CSV, is collected on the typing speed benchmarks page.

faq.q: What percentile is 60 WPM?
faq.a: About the 66th percentile, using the CHI 2018 distribution with mean 51.56 and standard deviation 20.2. In other words, faster than roughly two thirds of the volunteers in that study.

faq.q: What percentile is 100 WPM?
faq.a: About the 99th. The study's fastest decile exceeded roughly 78 WPM, so 100 WPM sits well inside the top 1% of that sample.

faq.q: What is the average typing speed?
faq.a: 51.56 WPM, from 136,857,600 keystrokes recorded from 168,960 volunteers (Dhakal et al., CHI 2018). Older sources often quote 40 WPM, which reflects office workers rather than self-selected test takers.

faq.q: How accurate is a percentile from a normal approximation?
faq.a: Within about one point across the middle of the distribution, and it reproduces the study's reported 10th and 90th percentile thresholds (about 26 and 78 WPM). Extreme tails above 130 WPM are less reliable.

faq.q: Does the percentile include errors?
faq.a: It is based on speed as the study measured it, with errors reported separately at 1.17% uncorrected. A net score with heavy corrections would rank lower than the raw WPM suggests.

faq.q: Is a percentile the same as a ranking?
faq.a: No. A percentile describes position in a sample; a ranking in a job test compares you to that employer's applicants. The thresholds employers use — 40, 50, 60 WPM — are usually fixed, not percentile-based.

pages.tldr: Using the CHI 2018 study (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2): 40 WPM is about the 28th percentile, 60 WPM the 66th, 80 WPM the 92nd, 100 WPM the 99th. The approximation reproduces the study's own deciles within about one point.

pages.title: Typing Test for Nurses — Charting Speed You Need
pages.metaDesc: Nursing documentation rewards 35-45 WPM with near-perfect accuracy on drug names and dosages. What to practise, why digits matter, and a shift-length test.
pages.heroP: Nurses do not type fast for a living; they type accurately under interruption. Charting notes, medication names and dosages are short, frequent and unforgiving. Practise at 35–45 WPM with accuracy above 98%.

seo.h2: What nursing documentation actually demands
p: A shift note is a few hundred characters typed between tasks: assessment findings, interventions, a time, a signature. The volume is modest. What breaks is the detail — a dose written as 10 instead of 100, a drug name auto-corrected into a different drug, an identifier attached to the wrong patient.

That is why nursing informatics training emphasises verification over velocity, and why the typing requirement in job ads is usually a modest 35–45 WPM. Speed matters because charting happens at the end of a twelve-hour shift when everyone wants to go home; accuracy matters because the error is clinical.

seo.h2: Where the errors come from
p:
• Digits. Dosages, vitals, weights and times are numeric. The number row is typed with a different reach than the home row and it is where most slips happen.
  • Look-alike drug names. Hydralazine and hydroxyzine, prednisone and prednisolone. Autocomplete is not your friend here; type the name rather than accepting a suggestion.
  • Interruption. You type half a sentence, answer a call bell, come back and continue in the wrong field. The typing skill is resuming without losing the thread.

seo.h2: A practice routine that fits a shift
p: Five minutes, twice a day. One 60-second sentence round for rhythm, one Numbers round for digits, then stop. Short daily rounds beat a weekly marathon because the skill you are training is availability under fatigue, not peak output.
Once a week, take one five-minute test and record net WPM and accuracy. Five minutes is roughly the length of a focused charting session, so it is the honest number to compare month to month.

seo.h2: Benchmarks to aim at
p:
LevelNet WPMAccuracyWhat it supports
Minimum for most postings3597%Short shift notes, care plans
Comfortable4598.5%Full assessment charting, discharge summaries
Fast55+99%Admissions, triage notes, telephone orders
These bands come from the ranges printed in nursing and medical-administration job advertisements; they are a target, not a licensure standard. No nursing board certifies a typing speed.

seo.h2: If you are switching from paper charting
p: The people who struggle most are usually experienced clinicians, not new typists. Twenty years of handwriting produces efficient note language and a hunt-and-peck relationship with the keyboard. The fix is not a typing course; it is ten minutes a day of copying your own note style, not textbook sentences.

Type the phrases you actually write — "alert and oriented", "denies chest pain", "afebrile" — until they are automatic. Domain vocabulary is where speed comes from once the keys stop needing attention.

faq.q: What typing speed do nurses need?
faq.a: Most nursing and medical-administration postings ask for 35–45 WPM with high accuracy. The number is modest because notes are short; the accuracy expectation is high because dosages and identifiers are clinical data.

faq.q: Is typing speed tested when applying for nursing jobs?
faq.a: Sometimes, especially for roles with heavy electronic documentation such as triage, admissions or telehealth. More often it is assumed rather than tested, which is why a low speed shows up later as unpaid overtime.

faq.q: Why does accuracy matter more than speed in charting?
faq.a: A wrong digit in a dose or a wrong patient identifier is a clinical incident, not a typo. Corrections also cost more time than typing slightly slower, so a 45 WPM run at 99% finishes a shift ahead of 60 WPM at 94%.

faq.q: How should I practise digits?
faq.a: Use the Numbers mode for two minutes a day and grade yourself on errors rather than speed. Dosages, vitals and times are the content that matters, so numeric accuracy is the skill to build first.

faq.q: How long should a practice test be?
faq.a: Five minutes once a week for the benchmark, plus 60-second bursts daily for rhythm. A five-minute round approximates a charting session; a 15-second round measures a sprint you will never use on a ward.

pages.tldr: Nursing job ads commonly list 35-45 WPM. The binding constraint is accuracy on medication names, dosages and patient identifiers, not raw speed. Practise 60-second bursts plus one Numbers round daily, and test at five minutes to match a charting session.

pages.title: Typing Test for Court Reporters — 225 WPM Explained
pages.metaDesc: Court reporting certification is 225 WPM on a stenotype, not a keyboard. What each tier means, how keyboard rates compare, and how to train for it.
pages.heroP: Court reporting certification is 225 words per minute — on a stenotype machine, not a QWERTY keyboard. The two numbers are not comparable, and confusing them is the most common mistake applicants make.

seo.h2: Two different skills with two different ceilings
p: A stenotype writes syllables, not letters: multiple keys are pressed together and a chord resolves into a word or phrase. That is how 225 WPM is reachable at all. A QWERTY keyboard writes letter by letter, and the fastest competitive typists in the world top out around 200 WPM in short bursts on text they can see.
So the 225 WPM requirement is not a claim that court reporters can type 225 WPM on a laptop. It is a test of realtime dictation capture through a machine built for it.

seo.h2: Speed tiers and what they qualify you for
p:
SpeedMachineTypical meaning
180 WPMStenotypeOften the floor for graduation from a reporting program
200 WPMStenotypeEntry-level freelance work in many markets
225 WPMStenotypeThe certified reporter standard, tested on live dictation
260 WPMVoice or stenotypeHigher-tier certification for fast proceedings
60–90 WPMQWERTYTranscript editing, scoping, proofreading support roles
The lower bands are programme requirements rather than universal law: schools and states vary. Check the specific certification body before planning a timeline around one number.

seo.h2: Why a keyboard test still matters
p: Most working hours are not spent on the machine. They are spent editing: correcting names, fixing speaker attribution, verifying exhibit numbers and formatting the transcript. That work happens on a keyboard, and it is where a reporter's day actually goes.
Scoping and proofreading roles, which are the usual entry point while certification is pending, are keyboard jobs outright. A 60–80 WPM editing speed with clean accuracy is the practical requirement.

seo.h2: Training toward the exam
p: Dictation practice, not typing practice, moves the stenotype number: five minutes at a speed where you can write every word, then a speed where you cannot. The second set is where the growth happens, provided you review the strokes you fumbled.

Use a keyboard test for the editing half of the job. Ten minutes of 10-minute rounds at 98% accuracy will make transcript cleanup painless, and it is the part candidates neglect because it is not the number they are chasing.

faq.q: Do court reporters really type 225 WPM on a keyboard?
faq.a: No. 225 WPM is a stenotype standard, achieved by chording syllables on a purpose-built machine. Keyboard typing at that speed is not what the certification measures.

faq.q: What is a good QWERTY speed for a court reporter?
faq.a: 60–90 WPM is comfortable for transcript editing, scoping and proofreading, which is where most keyboard time goes. Accuracy matters more than speed because transcript corrections are billable work.

faq.q: How long does it take to reach 225 WPM?
faq.a: Reporting programmes typically run two to four years, and speed is the usual reason people take longer. The machine skill is built by daily dictation practice at the edge of your current speed.

faq.q: Can I become a court reporter without a stenotype?
faq.a: There are voice-writing and digital reporting routes, and some jurisdictions accept them. They have their own certification requirements, so confirm with the body that governs your state or country.

faq.q: Is a 10-minute typing test relevant?
faq.a: For the editing side, yes — it measures sustained keyboard accuracy rather than a burst. It will not predict your steno speed, which is a different motor skill.

pages.tldr: The NCRA certified reporter exam tests 225 WPM live dictation on a stenotype. A QWERTY typist at 100 WPM is fast but is not training the same skill. Keyboard tests are still useful for transcript editing and scoping work, which is where most keyboard time goes.

pages.title: Typing Test for 911 Dispatchers — Speed & Multitasking
pages.metaDesc: Dispatcher posts ask for 35-45 WPM with clean digit accuracy while taking a call. What agencies test, why the number row decides it, and how to rehearse.
pages.heroP: Dispatch is typing while talking, under a clock. Agencies commonly ask for 35–45 WPM, but the deciding factor is whether a plate number, an address or a callback number survives contact with a stressed caller.

seo.h2: What dispatch agencies screen for
p: A dispatcher enters an address, a name, a phone number and a plate while the caller is still explaining. The typing is short, numeric and immediately consequential. Public postings typically list 35–45 WPM, and the assessment usually adds a multitasking or call-taking simulation on top of the typing score.

No single national typing standard applies to dispatch; requirements are set per agency. Treat published ranges as the target band and check the specific posting, because a state police dispatch centre and a small municipal one often differ by ten WPM.

seo.h2: Digits and addresses are the real test
p: Prose typing rewards rhythm. Dispatch typing rewards the number row, the ten-key area and the ability to spell an unfamiliar street name correctly the first time. That is a different practice target.

• Numbers mode for two minutes a day, graded on errors not speed.
  • Listen to a podcast and type the numbers you hear — times, prices, years — in one pass.
  • Type addresses from a map app, including postcodes, without looking down.

seo.h2: Speed bands in context
p:
RoleTypical WPM floorAdded assessment
Call taker35–40Structured call interview, data capture
Dispatcher40–45Radio simulation, multitasking test
Supervisor or trainer45+Quality assurance, report writing
The typing test is rarely the only gate. Agencies also test hearing, memory, prioritisation and stress tolerance, and a 60 WPM score will not offset a failed call simulation.

seo.h2: Practice that transfers
p: Two-minute rounds are the right length: long enough to feel the pressure of a call, short enough to repeat. Two minutes at 45 WPM net with 99% accuracy on digits is a stronger signal than five minutes of prose at 55.

Then rehearse the split-attention part. Read a sentence aloud, type it from memory in one pass, and check character by character. Five repetitions a day for two weeks is enough to feel the difference in how you hold digits in working memory.

faq.q: What WPM do 911 dispatcher jobs require?
faq.a: Usually 35–45 WPM, with accuracy weighted heavily. Requirements are set per agency rather than nationally, so the posting is the authority.

faq.q: Is typing the hardest part of the dispatch test?
faq.a: No. The call-taking simulation and multitasking assessment usually eliminate more candidates. Typing is a floor you clear so the rest of the assessment can be scored.

faq.q: Should I practise numbers or sentences?
faq.a: Both, but lead with numbers. Plate numbers, addresses and callback numbers are the content that fails in real calls, and the number row is where untrained typists lose the most accuracy.

faq.q: How accurate do I need to be?
faq.a: Aim for 99% on digits. A transposed digit in an address sends responders to the wrong place, which is the failure mode agencies screen hardest for.

faq.q: Does the test include typing while listening?
faq.a: Often the assessment includes a simulated call where you must enter data as it is spoken. Rehearse that directly: audio in, one-pass typing out, then verify.

pages.tldr: Most dispatch postings list 35-45 WPM with high accuracy. The realistic test is capturing digits and addresses in real time while a caller talks, so practise the Numbers mode and audio copying rather than prose speed.

pages.title: SSC CHSL Typing Test — 35 WPM & 8000 KPH Rules
pages.metaDesc: SSC CHSL typing rules: 35 WPM English or 30 WPM Hindi for LDC/JSA, 8000 key depressions per hour for DEO, plus the error allowance and a plan.
pages.heroP: Two different skill tests sit inside SSC CHSL: 35 WPM English or 30 WPM Hindi for LDC and JSA posts, and 8000 key depressions per hour for DEO posts. They are scored differently and rehearsed differently.

seo.h2: The two tests, side by side
p:
PostStandardDurationScoring
LDC / JSA35 WPM English or 30 WPM Hindi10 minutesWords per minute with an error allowance
DEO / DEO Grade A8000 key depressions per hour15 minutesTotal key depressions against an 8000/hour rate

8000 key depressions per hour is about 26.7 WPM under the five-character convention, but it is measured as raw keystrokes including corrections you make, so a typist who backspaces constantly loses ground even at a good words-per-minute rate.

seo.h2: Error allowance is where candidates fail
p: The typing test is qualifying: you either clear the standard or you do not, and the score does not add to your merit total. That changes the strategy completely. A candidate chasing 45 WPM with 12% errors fails; a candidate at 37 WPM with 3% errors passes.

Practise with the error budget in view: type at a pace where you can hold mistakes under the allowance, and never let a correction spree eat the clock. On the 10-minute LDC test, thirty seconds lost to backspacing is roughly 18 words you never typed.

seo.h2: Keyboard and layout rules
p: The test is taken on a standard QWERTY keyboard provided at the centre. Hindi candidates may opt for Krutidev or Remington layout depending on the notice in force, and the layout is usually chosen at the application stage — check your admit card and the current notice rather than assuming.
Because the machine is not yours, rehearse on something other than your laptop at least twice before the exam. Key travel and spacing change your error rate more than practice volume does.

seo.h2: A four-week plan
p: Week 1: ten-minute rounds at a comfortable pace, recording accuracy only. Week 2: same length, push until errors cross the allowance, then back off 3 WPM — that is your exam pace. Week 3: alternate sentences and passages with punctuation, because the actual passage includes capitals and full stops. Week 4: full-length simulations at the same time of day as your shift, with no pause button.
The DEO candidate should add a daily 15-minute numbers round, since key depressions include digits and the numeric reach is the slowest part of the keyboard for most people.

faq.q: What is the typing speed required for SSC CHSL?
faq.a: 35 words per minute in English or 30 words per minute in Hindi for LDC and JSA posts, and 8000 key depressions per hour for DEO posts. Both are qualifying tests.

faq.q: Is the SSC CHSL typing test qualifying or merit?
faq.a: Qualifying. It does not add marks to your total; you either meet the standard or you do not. That is why accuracy matters more than a high raw speed.

faq.q: How long is the SSC CHSL typing test?
faq.a: Ten minutes for LDC and JSA, fifteen minutes for DEO. Practise at the full length rather than in one-minute bursts, because the error rate at minute nine is what decides the result.

faq.q: How many mistakes are allowed?
faq.a: A small error allowance applies, commonly around 5% of the words typed, and it is specified in the notice for that cycle. Check the current notice: the allowance and the passage length change between years.

faq.q: Can I use my own keyboard?
faq.a: No. The test is conducted on centre equipment. Rehearse on a different keyboard at least twice so key travel and spacing are not a surprise on the day.

pages.tldr: LDC/JSA: 35 WPM English, 30 WPM Hindi, 10 minutes, error allowance around 5%. DEO: 8000 key depressions per hour, 15 minutes, on a standard keyboard. Both are qualifying, not merit-ranking, so accuracy beats speed.

pages.title: Typing Test for 5th Graders — Target WPM by Grade
pages.metaDesc: What a reasonable 5th grade typing speed looks like, how it compares with grades 3 and 8, and a 10-minute routine that does not become homework.
pages.heroP: By fifth grade most children can type 25–35 WPM if they have had regular practice, and accuracy matters far more than the number. Here is what the grade bands look like and how to practise without tears.

seo.h2: Grade bands, with a caveat
p: Classroom benchmarks vary by district and by how much keyboarding time a school actually provides, so treat any table as a rough band rather than a standard. The pattern that holds across published curricula is steady growth of roughly 5 WPM per grade once formal instruction begins.

GradeTypical rangeWhat to focus on
3rd10–20 WPMHome row, not looking down
4th15–25 WPMAll letters, capitals with Shift
5th25–35 WPMAccuracy above 90%, punctuation
6th–8th30–45 WPMSustained paragraphs, editing

seo.h2: Why accuracy is the only goal at this age
p: A child who types 35 WPM by hunting for keys with two fingers has hit a ceiling that will cost years later. A child at 22 WPM with all ten fingers on the home row is on a curve that reaches 50 by secondary school with no extra lessons.
So score the round on errors, not words per minute. If accuracy is below 90%, the speed number is fiction — it is measuring how fast the child can produce text that has to be retyped.

seo.h2: A routine a ten-year-old will actually do
p: Ten minutes, three times a week, is enough. One minute of warm-up, five minutes of the actual test, then two minutes of the child's own choice — quotes, pangrams, numbers. Stop while it is still fun; the failure mode is a forty-minute session that ends in an argument and no practice for a month.

Use the on-screen keyboard and finger guide on this site so the child can see which finger owns which key without an adult narrating it. Cover the hands with a light cloth for one round a week if looking down has become a habit — it is uncomfortable for two days and then it works.

seo.h2: What to do about games
p: Games are legitimate practice if the child is typing rather than watching. The test that matters: are the fingers moving on the home row, or is one finger stabbing at the keyboard while the other hand rests? If it is the second, the game is entertainment and the drill still has to happen separately.
A reasonable split for a fifth grader is one game session for every two test sessions. The test gives the number; the game gives the motivation.

faq.q: How fast should a 5th grader type?
faq.a: Roughly 25–35 WPM with 90% or better accuracy if they have practised regularly. Bands vary by school and by how much keyboarding instruction the child has actually had.

faq.q: Is 20 WPM bad for a 5th grader?
faq.a: No. It is normal for a child who has not had formal keyboarding instruction. What matters is whether the fingers are on the home row and whether accuracy is climbing.

faq.q: How long should practice be?
faq.a: Ten minutes, three times a week. Short and frequent beats a long weekly session, and it keeps practice from becoming a punishment.

faq.q: Should my child look at the keyboard?
faq.a: Not while testing. Looking down is the habit that caps speed. Cover the hands for one round a week so the child is forced to build a mental map of the keys.

faq.q: Do typing games help?
faq.a: Yes when the child is genuinely typing with correct fingers. If the game rewards speed with two fingers, it teaches a habit that has to be undone later.

pages.tldr: Fifth graders who practise regularly typically sit around 25-35 WPM with 90%+ accuracy. The useful goal is accuracy and home-row habit, not speed: children who type accurately at 25 WPM overtake fast, sloppy typists within a year.

pages.title: Typing Test for Legal Secretaries — 60-70 WPM
pages.metaDesc: Legal secretarial work screens higher than general office typing: 60-70 WPM with near-perfect accuracy on names, citations and formatting. What to rehearse.
pages.heroP: Legal support is the top of the clerical typing band: 60–70 WPM with accuracy high enough for citations, party names and numbered paragraphs. Speed alone will not pass the formatting half.

seo.h2: Why the bar is higher than general office work
p: A legal document is read by people who will quote it back. Party names must be exact, citations must be punctuated correctly, and a paragraph number that shifts breaks every cross-reference after it. That combination pushes the requirement to 60–70 WPM in job advertisements, above the 40–50 WPM typical of general clerical roles.
The speed figure exists because documents are long. A 40-page agreement at 45 WPM is two days of typing; at 65 WPM it is a day and a half with time left for checking.

seo.h2: The skills the test does not capture
p:
• Numbered paragraphs. Auto-numbering that renumbers on paste is the single most common formatting failure.
  • Capitalisation of defined terms. "the Company" is not "the company", and a find-and-replace will not fix it safely.
  • Citations. Italics, full stops and abbreviations follow a house style; consistency is the whole job.
  • Track changes. Typing inside a tracked document is slower and less forgiving than typing into a blank page.

seo.h2: Benchmarks by setting
p:
SettingTypical WPMAccuracyNotes
Small general practice55–6598%Letters, forms, correspondence
Corporate legal department60–7098.5%Contracts, board papers
Litigation support65–7599%Court filings, exhibits, indexes
Transcription-heavy role70+99%Dictation, hearing notes
Ranges reflect what appears in legal recruitment advertising; a firm that tests will usually set its own floor and tell you before the test.

seo.h2: How to rehearse for the real thing
p: Stop practising plain sentences after the first week. Type a real contract clause, complete with defined terms and numbered sub-paragraphs, and check it against the source line by line. That is a slower exercise and a far better predictor.

Then add the time pressure: five-minute rounds of dense text with punctuation, targeting 98.5% accuracy. If your accuracy falls below that at 70 WPM, work at 60 until it holds — a legal document with two errors per page costs more to check than it saved to type.

faq.q: What typing speed do legal secretaries need?
faq.a: Commonly 60–70 WPM with accuracy near 98.5%, which is above the 40–50 WPM typical of general clerical roles. Firms that test usually state their own floor.

faq.q: Is 55 WPM enough for legal work?
faq.a: For a small general practice handling letters and forms, often yes. Corporate and litigation roles usually screen at 60 and above because documents are long and reference-heavy.

faq.q: Does the test include formatting?
faq.a: A plain typing test does not, but the job is mostly formatting. Rehearse numbered paragraphs, defined terms and citations separately, because those are the errors that get noticed.

faq.q: How do I improve accuracy on capitals and citations?
faq.a: Type real clauses rather than random sentences, then proof against the source. Capitals, full stops and italics are pattern work, and patterns only build on realistic text.

faq.q: Should I learn to touch type for this role?
faq.a: Yes. At 60+ WPM sustained over long documents, looking at the keyboard is the limiting factor. Two weeks of home-row drills typically adds more than months of hunt-and-peck speed work.

pages.tldr: Legal secretary postings commonly ask for 60-70 WPM and near-perfect accuracy. The differentiator is not raw speed but consistency with capitals, citations and numbered lists, which is what the work is made of.

pages.title: Federal Typing Test — The 40 WPM Standard Explained
pages.metaDesc: US federal clerical jobs use a five-minute typing sample at 40 WPM with no more than three errors. How the standard works and how to rehearse it exactly.
pages.heroP: The US federal clerical standard is 40 words per minute on a five-minute sample with no more than three errors. It is a pass or fail gate, not a score to maximise, and it is easier than most commercial tests if you rehearse the exact format.

seo.h2: What the standard actually says
p: Federal clerical and office-automation positions are commonly advertised with a typing requirement of 40 words per minute, demonstrated on a five-minute sample, with no more than three errors. Some agencies accept a self-certification on the application; others ask for a certificate from a testing centre or an approved online test.

The arithmetic is simple: 40 WPM for five minutes is 200 words, or about 1,000 correct characters at five characters per word. Three errors in that sample is 1.5% - so the real requirement is roughly 98.5% accuracy at a moderate speed, not a fast run.

seo.h2: Why candidates fail it
p:
• They practise one-minute bursts. A five-minute sample has a different error profile: fatigue, drifting attention, and the temptation to speed up when the end is in sight.
  • They correct too much. Three errors are allowed; twelve corrections in a panic can push you under 40 WPM even though your accuracy was fine.
  • They have never seen the format. Some tests show the passage continuously and scroll; others replace line by line. Rehearse both.

seo.h2: A rehearsal that matches the format
p: Run a five-minute sentence test with the passage visible and no pause. Then count: net WPM must exceed 40 and uncorrected errors must stay at or below three. Do this three times in a week; if all three pass, the format is not going to surprise you.
If you are failing on errors rather than speed, slow to about 45 WPM indicated and hold it. The extra five WPM of headroom is what absorbs a bad sentence.

seo.h2: Certificate versus self-certification
p: A self-certification is the fastest route: you state your speed on the application and the agency may verify later. A proctored certificate costs money and takes a visit, but it never expires in the middle of a hiring cycle and some postings require it outright.
Read the announcement carefully. If it says "must submit a typing test with your name and date", a self-certification will be rejected, and a certificate older than a year is often refused as well.

seo.h2: What to do with the number afterwards
p: Once you clear 40 WPM, stop optimising it. Federal screening is qualifying: a 70 WPM score does not add points that a 45 WPM score misses. Put the remaining effort into the rest of the application, where the competition actually is.
Keep one dated record of a passing five-minute run so you can attach it to future applications without re-testing.

faq.q: What is the federal typing requirement?
faq.a: Commonly 40 words per minute from a five-minute sample with no more than three errors for clerical and office-automation roles. Individual announcements state their own version, so read the posting.

faq.q: Is 40 WPM hard to reach?
faq.a: No. 40 WPM is around the 28th percentile of measured typists, and most people reach it within a few weeks of daily practice. The error limit is the part that catches people.

faq.q: How many errors are allowed?
faq.a: Three in a five-minute sample at the 40 WPM standard. That is about 1.5% of the characters, so the practical target is 98.5% accuracy or better.

faq.q: Do I need a proctored certificate?
faq.a: Only if the announcement says so. Many federal postings accept self-certification at application and verify later; some require a dated test result with your name on it.

faq.q: Can I use an online typing test as proof?
faq.a: Sometimes, if the result shows your name, the date and the test length. Check the specific announcement first, because agencies differ on which providers they accept.

pages.tldr: Federal clerk and office-automation postings commonly require 40 WPM from a 5-minute sample with at most 3 errors. That is roughly 200 correct words, or 1,000 correct characters, in five minutes. Accuracy is the gate: four errors fails.

pages.title: Civil Service Typing Test — State and County Rules
pages.metaDesc: State and county clerical jobs usually ask 40 net WPM on a five-minute proctored test, and certificates expire. How the process works and what to practise.
pages.heroP: State and county civil service exams typically require 40 net WPM on a five-minute proctored sample, and they issue a certificate with an expiry date. The rules vary by jurisdiction, so the notice is the authority.

seo.h2: How the process usually runs
p: You apply for a clerical title, the agency tells you whether a typing certificate is required at application or after a conditional offer, and you book a proctored test. The result is filed against your name and often carries an expiry - commonly between one and four years depending on the state.

Some jurisdictions accept a certificate from a commercial testing centre, some run their own at a workforce office, and a few allow remote proctoring. The one constant is that the sample is timed, five minutes in most cases, and scored on net words per minute.

seo.h2: What the scores mean in practice
p:
ScoreWhat it usually clearsWhat it does not
30-35 net WPMSome entry clerk and typist titlesOffice assistant and secretary titles
40 net WPMThe most common civil service floorSenior clerical, legal and medical support
50 net WPMSenior reception, HR support, court clerkTranscription and court reporting
60+ net WPMLegal secretary, word processing operatorStenographic titles, which need machine skills
These are the bands that appear across published county and state postings; a specific notice will name one figure, and that figure is the one that matters.

seo.h2: Net, not gross - and why that changes your strategy
p: Civil service scoring almost always deducts errors before reporting the score. That means a cautious 44 net is worth more than a reckless 55 gross that nets 38 after a dozen mistakes.

Rehearse accordingly: type at the pace where errors stay under about 2%, then check the net figure rather than the raw one. If your net and gross differ by more than 5%, accuracy is the whole project for the next two weeks.

seo.h2: Booking and paperwork
p: Bring photo identification, arrive early, and expect the keyboard to be unfamiliar - usually a basic membrane board rather than the laptop you practise on. Type one warm-up sentence before the clock starts if the proctor allows it.
Keep a copy of the certificate. Replacing a lost one usually means re-testing, and a lapsed certificate takes you off the eligible list until you rebook.

faq.q: What score do I need on a civil service typing test?
faq.a: 40 net WPM is the most common floor for clerical titles, taken from a five-minute sample. Senior clerical, legal and court roles often ask 50 to 60 net WPM.

faq.q: How long is a civil service typing certificate valid?
faq.a: Usually one to four years depending on the jurisdiction. The notice states the validity period; an expired certificate generally takes you off the eligible list until you re-test.

faq.q: Is the test gross or net WPM?
faq.a: Net, in almost all cases - errors are deducted before the score is reported. Practise to a 2% error rate so the deduction cannot change your result.

faq.q: Can I take it online?
faq.a: Some jurisdictions allow remote proctoring and some require an in-person session at a workforce or testing centre. Check the notice for the title you are applying to.

faq.q: Does a higher score improve my ranking?
faq.a: Rarely for typing itself - it is usually a qualifying gate. Your rank on the list comes from the written examination and any experience credits, not from typing faster than the minimum.

pages.tldr: Most state and county clerical postings ask for 40 net WPM on a five-minute test, taken in person or with remote proctoring. Certificates are usually valid for one to four years. Until the certificate is issued you stay off the eligible list.

pages.title: CritiCall Typing Test — What the Dispatcher Battery Measures
pages.metaDesc: CritiCall is a multi-module pre-employment battery for dispatchers, not a typing test. What the keyboarding and data-entry modules check, and how to rehearse.
pages.heroP: CritiCall is not a typing test with extra steps - it is a battery of dispatcher simulations, and keyboarding is one module among many. Here is what the typing modules actually measure and how to prepare for the ones you cannot see on a typing site.

seo.h2: What CritiCall is, and is not
p: CritiCall is a computer-based pre-employment testing battery for public-safety telecommunicators. Agencies configure which modules they use, so two candidates for two different agencies can sit substantially different tests. The keyboarding module is usually a short, time-limited data-entry task rather than a prose passage.

That is why practising prose typing alone does not prepare you. If you have been told your agency uses CritiCall, the typing component is the easiest part; the modules that fail candidates are the ones involving simultaneous listening and recording.

seo.h2: The modules that usually appear
p:
• Keyboarding / data entry: short timed entry of names, addresses and numbers, scored on accuracy and speed.
  • Call summarisation: read or hear a call and produce a short structured summary within a time limit.
  • Memory recall: reproduce details - a plate, a street, a name - after a delay.
  • Cross-referencing and prioritisation: match records, decide which incident outranks which.
  • Map reading and spatial judgement: pick the closest unit or the correct jurisdiction.
  • Basic arithmetic and spelling: small, time-limited question sets.
The exact list is agency-configurable, and the vendor does not publish a universal pass mark. Your agency sets the cut score, and it is not disclosed to candidates in advance.

seo.h2: Rehearsing the keyboarding module
p: Use the Numbers mode for two minutes at a time and grade on errors. The content in the module is alphanumeric - addresses, dates, codes - so digits and capitals matter more than prose rhythm.

Then rehearse the split-attention skill separately: play a recorded voice giving an address and a callback number, type both in one pass, and verify character by character. That is closer to the job than any prose typing test.

seo.h2: What to do on the day
p: Expect to move between modules quickly, with instructions read aloud under time pressure. The common failure is not slowness; it is losing the instruction because you were still finishing the previous screen.

Read the instruction line before touching the keyboard, then work at a pace you can sustain for the whole module. Timed batteries punish the candidate who sprints the first screen and runs out of attention on the fifth.

faq.q: Is CritiCall a typing test?
faq.a: No. It is a multi-module pre-employment battery for dispatchers. Keyboarding and data entry are modules inside it, alongside call summarisation, memory recall, map reading and prioritisation.

faq.q: What WPM does CritiCall require?
faq.a: There is no universal published figure - agencies set their own cut scores. The keyboarding module is typically short and time-limited, in the 35-45 WPM range that dispatch postings quote.

faq.q: How long is the CritiCall test?
faq.a: It varies by agency because each one selects its own module set. Expect a session of roughly one to two hours rather than a five-minute typing sample.

faq.q: Can I practise CritiCall online?
faq.a: You can practise the component skills - timed alphanumeric entry, listening and recording, memory recall - but the actual battery is administered by the agency. Practise the skills, not the interface.

faq.q: What should I practise first?
faq.a: Numbers and addresses, then listening while typing. Those two cover the keyboarding module and the module most candidates find hardest.

pages.tldr: CritiCall is used by many North American public-safety agencies. Its keyboarding and data-entry modules are short and time-limited, typically in the 35-45 WPM range, but the battery also tests call summarisation, memory recall, map reading and prioritisation.

pages.title: Alphanumeric Typing Test — Letters, Digits, Codes
pages.metaDesc: Real data entry is letters and digits mixed: references, postcodes, part numbers. This test type mixes both and scores the characters that matter.
pages.heroP: Most typing tests use prose. Real data entry is alphanumeric: reference codes, postcodes, part numbers, invoice IDs. Mixed content is slower and less forgiving, and it is what employers actually screen.

seo.h2: Why mixed content scores lower
p: On a QWERTY keyboard the letters sit under your fingers and the digits sit on the row above, reached with an extended finger and no tactile landmark. Every transition from a name to a number costs a reach, a visual check and a return.

The result is that someone who types prose at 60 WPM often manages 35-40 WPM on mixed alphanumeric content. That is not a regression; it is a different task, and it is the task data-entry employers test.

seo.h2: What to practise, in order
p:
• Number row reaches - 1 to 0 with the correct finger, without looking down. Two minutes a day.
  • Alternating patterns - strings like AB12CD34, which force a shift between letter and digit clusters.
  • Numeric keypad - if the job is invoice or order entry, the ten-key pad is faster than the number row and worth learning separately.
  • Verification - read your own output against the source, character by character, once per round. This is the step that separates 97% from 99.5%.

seo.h2: How alphanumeric work is scored
p:
UnitFormulaTypical requirement
Keystrokes per hour (KPH)characters per minute × 608,000-12,000
Key depressions per hour (KDPH)all keys pressed, corrections included8,000 (SSC DEO)
Fields per hourcompleted records, not charactersrole-specific
Accuracycorrect fields ÷ total fields97-98%
Field accuracy is the metric that matters in practice. A record with one wrong digit is a failed record regardless of how fast the other nineteen fields were typed.

seo.h2: A two-week drill
p: Week one: two minutes of Numbers mode, twice a day, graded on errors. Add one round of alternating letter-digit strings. Week two: move to five-minute blocks and score fields, not characters - type a real form layout (name, reference, date, amount) repeatedly and count how many records come out clean.
Stop when a five-minute block produces three consecutive clean records. At that point your accuracy is job-ready and further gains come from speed work, which is the easier half.

faq.q: What is an alphanumeric typing test?
faq.a: A typing test using mixed letters and digits rather than prose - reference codes, postcodes, part numbers and IDs. It measures the skill data-entry roles actually use.

faq.q: Why is my alphanumeric speed lower than my WPM?
faq.a: Digits sit on the number row, which needs an extended reach with no tactile landmark. Switching between letters and numbers costs time, so 35-40 WPM on mixed content is normal for a 60 WPM prose typist.

faq.q: What accuracy do employers expect?
faq.a: 97-98% on fields, and often 99% for medical or financial records. One wrong digit makes the whole record invalid, so field accuracy matters more than character speed.

faq.q: Should I use the number row or the keypad?
faq.a: Use the keypad for numeric-heavy work such as invoices and order entry, and the number row when digits are mixed into text. Learning ten-key properly is usually worth a week of practice.

faq.q: How is it scored?
faq.a: Usually in keystrokes per hour or key depressions per hour, sometimes in completed fields per hour. 8,000-12,000 KPH is the common data-entry band.

pages.tldr: Alphanumeric typing mixes letters and digits, which is harder than prose because every digit needs a reach off the home row. Typical data-entry standards are 8,000-12,000 keystrokes per hour with 97-98% accuracy on the fields.

pages.title: Typing Test for Virtual Assistants — What Clients Test
pages.metaDesc: Virtual assistant clients screen at 55-65 WPM with clean accuracy, often with a paid trial task. What to prepare and how to prove your speed remotely.
pages.heroP: Virtual assistant work is mostly written: inboxes, calendars, CRM notes, research summaries. Clients commonly look for 55–65 WPM with clean accuracy, and many screen with a paid trial task rather than a typing test.

seo.h2: Why the bar sits at 55-65 WPM
p: A VA's output is measured in completed tasks, and most tasks are typed: replies, notes, data cleanup, scheduling messages. At 45 WPM a morning of inbox work takes three hours; at 65 WPM it takes two, which is the entire margin a client is paying for.
That is why VA postings cluster at 50-65 WPM rather than the 40 WPM typical of in-office clerical roles. The work is not harder, it is simply a bigger share of the job.

seo.h2: What clients actually check
p:
• Clean written English. Typos in a client-facing email cost more than a slow reply. Accuracy is the first filter.
  • Formatting discipline. Bullets, dates, time zones, signatures - the same output every time.
  • Tool fluency. Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, a CRM, a scheduling tool, and increasingly an AI assistant used to draft rather than to replace judgement.
  • Turnaround. A trial task with a deadline is the most common screen, and it tests all four at once.

seo.h2: How to prove your speed remotely
p: Keep a dated five-minute result with a visible WPM and accuracy, and mention the test length. "62 WPM net, 99% accuracy, five-minute test" is credible; "fast typist" is not.

If a client asks for a trial, deliver it in the format you would actually use - correct file naming, a short cover note, no stray formatting from a copy-paste. Half of VA trials fail on presentation rather than content.

seo.h2: The one skill worth adding
p: Dictation and editing. Drafting by voice and cleaning up by keyboard is how experienced VAs double throughput on long-form work, and it is a different skill from typing tests: you need fast, accurate editing rather than fast transcription.
Practise by dictating a paragraph, then editing it to publishable quality in under two minutes. If the edited version reads better than your typed draft, you have the workflow.

faq.q: What typing speed do virtual assistants need?
faq.a: Most postings ask for 50-65 WPM with high accuracy. The upper end reflects that nearly all VA output is typed, so speed converts directly into completed tasks.

faq.q: Do clients test typing speed?
faq.a: Some ask for a score, but many use a paid trial task instead. A trial tests speed, accuracy, formatting and reliability at the same time, which a typing test cannot.

faq.q: Is 50 WPM enough to start?
faq.a: Yes for general admin support, provided your written accuracy is high. Specialist work such as transcription, bookkeeping support or medical admin usually expects 60 WPM or more.

faq.q: How do I prove my speed without a proctored test?
faq.a: Keep a dated five-minute result showing WPM and accuracy, and offer to re-test live on a call. That is usually accepted because it is verifiable in the moment.

faq.q: Does dictation experience help?
faq.a: Yes. Drafting by voice and editing by keyboard is faster than typing long documents, and it is a selling point for clients with heavy written output.

pages.tldr: Most VA job posts ask for 50-65 WPM and near-perfect written accuracy. Because the work is remote, clients often test with a real task instead of a typing test - so keep a dated score and a sample of clean written work ready.

pages.title: Typing Test for Medical Billing — Codes & Speed
pages.metaDesc: Medical billing and coding asks for 45-55 WPM with near-perfect accuracy on codes, dates and amounts. Why the numeric fields decide it, and how to drill them.
pages.heroP: Billing and coding work is numeric and exact: CPT and ICD codes, dates of service, amounts, member IDs. Employers typically look for 45–55 WPM, but a single transposed digit is a denied claim.

seo.h2: Where the requirement comes from
p: A claim has a fixed shape: patient, payer, codes, dates, amounts. Every field is typed rather than composed, so throughput is a direct function of keyboard accuracy and speed. Postings commonly ask 45-55 WPM, and the accuracy expectation is high because a rejected claim costs the practice money and time.
The number is lower than transcription because the text is short. The consequence of an error is higher, which is why billing tests weight accuracy far more heavily than speed.

seo.h2: Why codes are a different typing problem
p: ICD-10 codes mix letters and digits in patterns like M54.5 or E11.9; CPT codes are five digits, sometimes with modifiers. The digits are frequently the same key reached with the same finger in sequence, which is where transpositions happen.

That is a typing problem, not a knowledge problem: 99213 becoming 99123 is a motor slip. Practise numeric strings and alternating letter-digit patterns until the sequence errors fall, then add the code vocabulary.

seo.h2: A practice set that mirrors the job
p:
• Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, graded on errors rather than speed.
  • One round of alphanumeric entry - the alphanumeric test is closer to claims work than a prose passage.
  • Five-minute blocks scoring clean records: type a mock claim line (code, date, amount) ten times and count how many are perfect.
Target three consecutive clean five-minute blocks before you claim the skill on a CV. That is roughly the accuracy a billing manager is buying.

seo.h2: What to quote on an application
p: Quote net WPM, accuracy and test length, and add the numeric result separately if you have one - for example "52 WPM net, 99% accuracy on alphanumeric entry". Billing managers read the second number first.
If you have coding certification but a modest typing score, say so plainly and offer a timed sample. A 45 WPM coder with clean output is employable; a 65 WPM coder generating denials is not.

faq.q: What typing speed does medical billing require?
faq.a: Usually 45-55 WPM with 98% or better accuracy. Speed matters less than error-free entry of codes, dates and amounts, because a rejected claim costs more than a slow one.

faq.q: Does medical coding need faster typing than billing?
faq.a: No. Both sit in the same band. Coding adds judgement and code lookup rather than more keystrokes, so speed is rarely the limiting factor.

faq.q: How accurate do I need to be?
faq.a: 98% is the usual expectation and 99% is comfortable. Field-level accuracy matters most: one wrong digit in a code or an amount is a denied claim, not a typo.

faq.q: Should I practise numbers or text?
faq.a: Both, but lead with numbers and alphanumeric strings. Claims are mostly codes, dates and amounts, and the number row is where untrained typists lose accuracy.

faq.q: Is 45 WPM enough for a billing job?
faq.a: Often yes, if your accuracy is clean and you know the code sets. Employers will usually prefer a careful 45 over a careless 65 because denials are expensive.

pages.tldr: Medical billing and coding roles usually ask 45-55 WPM with 98%+ accuracy. The speed bar is moderate; the deciding skill is error-free entry of codes, dates and amounts, so practise alphanumeric and numeric content rather than prose.

pages.title: 30 WPM Typing Test — The Beginner Floor, Explained
pages.metaDesc: 30 WPM is the floor most clerical jobs quote and about the 14th percentile. Test it, see what it unlocks, and follow an accuracy-first plan to get past it.
pages.heroP: Thirty words per minute is 150 characters a minute, or 9,000 keystrokes an hour. It is the floor most clerical and dispatch postings quote, and roughly the 14th percentile of measured typists — close enough to reach in weeks, not months.

seo.h2: What 30 WPM is, in every unit
p: 30 WPM is 150 characters per minute, 9,000 keystrokes per hour (KPH), and 9,000 key depressions per hour if you make no corrections. It is 0.5 words per second.
For context: 30 WPM is faster than roughly 86% of people are slower than — that is, about the 14th percentile of the 168,960-person sample behind the CHI 2018 typing study, whose mean was 51.56 WPM.

seo.h2: What it clears, and what it does not
p:
RequirementAt 30 WPM
Some dispatch and call-centre floors (30-35 WPM)Clears
County clerk postings at 35-40 net WPMShort by 5-10
US federal clerical standard (40 WPM)Short by 10
Data entry at 8,000 KPH (26.7 WPM)Clears on speed, accuracy decides
Receptionist at 40-50 WPMShort

So 30 WPM is a starting point rather than a qualification for most office work. The gap to 40 is the single most valuable 10 WPM you will ever add, because it moves you across the most common screening line.

seo.h2: Why people get stuck at 30
p: Almost nobody is stuck at 30 because their fingers are slow. They are stuck because they look at the keyboard, which forces a look-down-look-up cycle on every word, and because they correct with the backspace key instead of slowing down.

The two fixes, in order: cover your hands for one round a day so the looking habit breaks, then set a rule that you do not backspace during a test round. Your raw score will climb by 4-6 WPM within two weeks of holding both rules, before you have practised any speed work at all.

seo.h2: A 14-day plan to leave 30 behind
p: Days 1-7: three one-minute rounds a day, hands covered for one of them, no backspace. Record accuracy only. Days 8-14: switch to two-minute rounds, still no backspace, and add one Numbers round because digits are where beginners lose the most.

At the end, take one five-minute test and record net WPM. If you are above 35, continue with the 40 WPM plan. If you are still at 30, the constraint is the looking habit, not effort — keep the covered round daily for another two weeks.

faq.q: Is 30 WPM good?
faq.a: It is about the 14th percentile, so it is below average but far from hopeless. It clears a few dispatch and data-entry floors; most office postings ask for 40 WPM or more.

faq.q: How long does it take to go from 30 to 40 WPM?
faq.a: Usually two to six weeks of daily ten-minute practice, mostly by fixing the look-at-keyboard habit and cutting corrections. Progress is faster at this level than at 60 WPM.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is 30 WPM?
faq.a: 9,000 KPH. Thirty words per minute is 150 characters per minute, and 150 × 60 = 9,000.

faq.q: Should I focus on speed or accuracy at 30 WPM?
faq.a: Accuracy. At this level most lost time is corrections, so holding 97% accuracy while typing steadily raises the score faster than a deliberate speed push.

faq.q: Can I reach 30 WPM with two fingers?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the trap. Two-finger typing plateaus around 35-40 WPM. Learning the home row costs two uncomfortable weeks and removes that ceiling.

pages.tldr: 30 WPM is about the 14th percentile. It clears some entry clerical and dispatch floors but is below the 40 WPM that most office postings ask. If you are here, the fastest gain is accuracy: most people at 30 WPM lose more time to corrections than to keystrokes.

pages.title: 40 WPM Typing Test — The Standard Employers Ask For
pages.metaDesc: 40 WPM is the line most clerical, receptionist and government jobs draw, and about the 28th percentile. Test it, then use the four-week plan that clears it.
pages.heroP: Forty words per minute is the number that appears in more job postings than any other: 40 WPM, five minutes, few errors. It is roughly the 28th percentile — the threshold that separates 'can type' from 'can be employed to type'.

seo.h2: The number behind the number
p: 40 WPM is 200 characters per minute, 12,000 keystrokes per hour, and 200 words over a five-minute test. On a standard error rule of one error per ten words, you are allowed about twenty errors across the five minutes — which sounds generous until you watch your score after a bad paragraph.

The US federal clerical standard is published as 40 WPM over five minutes with no more than three errors, which is far stricter: 98.5% accuracy. Most private employers quote the speed and leave the accuracy floor at 95%.

seo.h2: Who actually asks for it
p:
RoleStated requirementAt 40 WPM
Receptionist40-50 net WPMBottom of the band
General office / admin40-55 WPMBottom of the band
County clerk-typist35-45 net WPMComfortable
US federal clerk40 WPM, ≤3 errorsExactly at the line
Data entry clerk45-65 WPM or 13,500+ KPHShort
Being exactly at the line is risky on a five-minute test, because one bad sentence can drop you under it. Aim for 44-45 before you apply, which gives you the margin that 40 alone does not.

seo.h2: The four weeks that actually work
p: Week 1 — measure and stop the bleeding. Three five-minute rounds, no backspace rule, accuracy recorded. Most candidates at 40 WPM are correcting 8-12 times a minute; removing that habit alone buys 3-5 WPM.
Week 2 — cover the keyboard. One round a day with hands covered. This is uncomfortable for three days and then stops being an issue, and it is the difference between a ceiling at 45 and no ceiling.

Week 3 — length and mode. Five-minute sentence rounds three times a week, one numbers round a week. Add capitals and punctuation deliberately: real tests include them and untrained typists drop them under time pressure.
Week 4 — simulate. Full-length, time of day matching your interview, unfamiliar keyboard. Then test once and use that number on applications.

seo.h2: What to do if you are already at 55
p: Stop training for 40 and move to the 60 WPM plan; the skill work is the same but the drills change. At 55 you are already above the requirement for almost every clerical role, so further gains are for transcription, legal and medical work rather than for clearing a gate.

faq.q: Is 40 WPM good enough for a job?
faq.a: For most clerical, receptionist and county government roles, yes — 40 WPM is the figure those postings quote. Aim for 44-45 so a bad sentence on a five-minute test cannot drop you below the line.

faq.q: What percentile is 40 WPM?
faq.a: About the 28th percentile of the CHI 2018 sample (mean 51.56 WPM, standard deviation 20.2). Roughly seven in ten measured typists are faster.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is 40 WPM?
faq.a: 12,000 KPH. Forty words per minute is 200 characters per minute, and 200 × 60 = 12,000.

faq.q: How long is the federal 40 WPM test?
faq.a: Five minutes, with no more than three errors in most published announcements. That is 98.5% accuracy, stricter than the 95% floor private employers usually apply.

faq.q: How fast can I go from 30 to 40 WPM?
faq.a: Two to six weeks of daily ten-minute practice for most people, mostly from removing the look-at-keyboard habit and reducing corrections rather than from raw speed drills.

pages.tldr: 40 WPM = 200 CPM = 12,000 KPH, about the 28th percentile. It clears most clerical, receptionist and county government floors, and the US federal standard is exactly this with a three-error limit over five minutes.

pages.title: 50 WPM Typing Test — Beating the Average
pages.metaDesc: 50 WPM is roughly the median adult score and clears most office requirements. Test it, see the 47th percentile, and use the plateau drills that get you to 60.
pages.heroP: Fifty words per minute is the median: half of measured typists are faster, half slower. It clears almost every office requirement and it is where most people plateau — which is why the useful work here is about breaking a ceiling, not clearing a gate.

seo.h2: Where 50 sits
p: Fifty words per minute is 250 characters per minute, 15,000 keystrokes per hour, and about the 47th percentile of the 168,960-person CHI 2018 sample. It is the middle of the distribution, not a fast score — but it is above the 40 WPM line that most clerical postings quote, which is what matters for employment.

It is also the exact point where most self-taught typists stop improving. The reason is not finger speed: it is that they read one word at a time, so their eyes and hands take turns instead of working together.

seo.h2: Why the plateau happens
p: At 50 WPM you are typing roughly four characters per second. That is fast enough that the read-type-read cycle becomes the bottleneck rather than the keystrokes themselves. Fast typists read one to three words ahead and let the hands work on a buffer; plateaued typists read the word they are about to type.

The second cause is uniform speed. Typing every word at the same pace means slowing down for easy words and losing time on hard ones. Skilled typists accelerate through familiar sequences and slow slightly on unfamiliar ones, which averages out higher.

seo.h2: The drills that break 50
p:
• Look-ahead drill: before you start, read the first line aloud in your head. Then type it without re-reading. Do this for five rounds; it feels wrong for three of them.
  • Burst drill: 15-second rounds, maximum speed, twice a day. This trains the top end you cannot reach in a one-minute test.
  • Bigram drill: the twenty most common letter pairs in English (th, he, in, er, an, re, on, at, en, nd...). Practising transitions rather than words is what moves you from 50 to 65.
  • Accuracy floor: never let a session end below 96%. Speed built on errors does not survive a five-minute test.

seo.h2: What 50 unlocks, and what it does not
p: It clears general office, admin, receptionist, county clerk and most customer-service requirements. It does not clear data entry quoted at 13,500+ KPH (45 WPM is 13,500, so you are at the entry edge), legal secretary at 60-75, or medical transcription at 65-80.
If your goal is a specific posting, read the number in the posting and train to that plus five. If your goal is general employability, 50 is enough and the next ten points are optional.

faq.q: Is 50 WPM good?
faq.a: It is about the 47th percentile — essentially the median adult score — and it clears almost every office, admin and receptionist requirement. It is a solid, employable speed rather than a fast one.

faq.q: How do I get from 50 to 60 WPM?
faq.a: Read ahead by one to three words, drill 15-second bursts for top-end speed, and practise common letter pairs rather than whole words. Most people need four to eight weeks of short daily sessions.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is 50 WPM?
faq.a: 15,000 KPH. Fifty words per minute is 250 characters per minute, and 250 × 60 = 15,000.

faq.q: Why am I stuck at 50 WPM?
faq.a: Almost always because you read one word at a time, so your eyes and hands take turns. Look-ahead practice and bigram drills address that directly, where more of the same typing does not.

faq.q: Is 50 WPM enough for data entry?
faq.a: At the entry edge. 50 WPM is 15,000 KPH, above the 8,000-12,000 KPH most postings quote, but below the 13,500-19,500 band used for senior data-entry roles.

pages.tldr: 50 WPM = 250 CPM = 15,000 KPH, about the 47th percentile. It clears office, admin and receptionist bands. The plateau at 50 is usually a rhythm problem: people type word by word instead of reading ahead.

pages.title: 60 WPM Typing Test — The 'Fast Typist' Line
pages.metaDesc: 60 WPM is where employers start calling you fast: the 66th percentile and the floor for legal and transcription work. Test it, train the last stretch.
pages.heroP: Sixty words per minute is the 66th percentile and the point where job descriptions stop saying 'typing required' and start saying 'fast, accurate typing'. It is also the floor for legal, medical and transcription roles.

seo.h2: What 60 WPM represents
p: Sixty words per minute is 300 characters per minute, five characters per second, 18,000 keystrokes per hour, and about the 66th percentile of measured typists. Two thirds of people are slower; one third are faster.

In employment terms it is a threshold: clerical adverts quote 40-50, whereas legal, medical and transcription adverts start at 60 and go up. Crossing 60 changes which jobs are open to you, which is why it is worth more effort than crossing 50.

seo.h2: The accuracy trade at this speed
p: At 60 WPM a 2% error rate means about one error every 8 seconds — roughly seven or eight errors in a five-minute test. On a net-scored test that costs you 5-6 WPM, dropping you back to the mid-50s. That is the arithmetic that keeps people at 55.

So the last stretch is not 'type faster'. It is 'hold 98% while typing at 60', which is a different drill: shorter rounds, stricter error budget, and stopping a round the moment accuracy falls below the floor rather than pushing to the timer.

seo.h2: Drills for the 50-to-60 stretch
p:
• 30-second accuracy sprints: type at 90% of maximum for 30 seconds, stop, check errors. Repeat five times. This builds the accuracy-at-speed habit that longer rounds cannot.
  • Punctuation and capitals: most people lose 3-5 WPM here. Run rounds with quotes and sentence case deliberately until the Shift press stops breaking rhythm.
  • Numbers once a week: the number row is a separate motor skill and it is where a 60 WPM typist becomes a 52 WPM typist on real work.
  • One long round per week: ten minutes, to confirm the speed survives fatigue.

seo.h2: Where 60 is still not enough
p: Medical transcription commonly asks 65-80 WPM with 98-99% accuracy, and it is measured over audio, which is harder than copying visible text. Court reporting is 225 WPM on a stenotype and is a different skill entirely.
For legal secretary work, 60-75 WPM is the advertised band, so 60 is the entry edge — aim for 65 before applying to a firm that tests.

faq.q: Is 60 WPM fast?
faq.a: It is about the 66th percentile and the point where job adverts start calling typing 'fast'. Top 10% is 78 WPM and above, so 60 is comfortably above average but not exceptional.

faq.q: What jobs require 60 WPM?
faq.a: Legal secretary roles (60-75), transcription entry points (65+), medical admin and word-processing operator titles. Most general office roles stop at 50.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is 60 WPM?
faq.a: 18,000 KPH. Sixty words per minute is 300 characters per minute, and 300 × 60 = 18,000.

faq.q: How long does it take to go from 50 to 60 WPM?
faq.a: Four to eight weeks of short daily sessions for most people, provided the practice targets accuracy at speed rather than raw output.

faq.q: Does 60 WPM include errors?
faq.a: Net scores subtract them. A 60 WPM gross score at 94% accuracy nets about 56, which is why the accuracy floor matters as much as the speed target.

pages.tldr: 60 WPM = 300 CPM = 18,000 KPH, about the 66th percentile. It clears legal secretary (60-75), transcription entry (65) and medical admin bands. Getting there from 50 is mostly rhythm and accuracy work, not raw speed.

pages.title: 70 WPM Typing Test — Top 20% and Transcription Entry
pages.metaDesc: 70 WPM is the 82nd percentile and the entry band for transcription work. Test it, see what it unlocks, and learn why rhythm beats force at this level.
pages.heroP: Seventy words per minute is the 82nd percentile — faster than four out of five measured typists, and the entry band for general transcription. At this level the limiting factor stops being your fingers and becomes your rhythm.

seo.h2: Where 70 WPM sits
p: Seventy words per minute is 350 characters per minute, 21,000 keystrokes per hour, and roughly the 82nd percentile of the CHI 2018 sample. It is faster than the top-quintile boundary and still 8 WPM short of the top decile at 78.
That last stretch is the hardest in typing: the 70-to-80 range typically takes months rather than weeks, because the easy inefficiencies are already gone.

seo.h2: What changes at this level
p: Below 60 WPM most gains come from removing bad habits — looking down, backspacing, two-finger reaches. Above 70 there are no bad habits left to remove; the work is consistency. A 70 WPM typist's speed varies by 15-20% between rounds, and the variance itself is what holds the average down.
So the metric to watch changes from peak WPM to the spread between your best and worst round. Narrowing that spread raises the average faster than trying to sprint.

seo.h2: Drills that move the average, not the peak
p:
• Ten consecutive one-minute rounds, once a week. Record all ten. The number that matters is the lowest, not the highest.
  • Hard-text rounds: quotes with punctuation, code, or pangrams. Speed on easy sentences is not transferable; speed on awkward text is.
  • Audio transcription practice: transcribe two minutes of speech and time it. Spoken English runs at 130-160 WPM, so 70 WPM typing leaves you well behind real-time — which is why transcriptionists use foot pedals and text expanders.
  • Text expansion: learn five short forms for phrases you type constantly. At this level, tooling beats training.

seo.h2: Transcription expectations versus typing tests
p: Transcription is advertised at 65-80 WPM, but the measurement is over audio with playback control, not over visible text. The skill gap is short-term memory: you hear a phrase, hold it, and type it, which is harder than copying.
If transcription is the goal, test yourself on audio rather than on this page. If it is not, 70 WPM already clears every clerical requirement and further speed is a hobby.

faq.q: Is 70 WPM fast?
faq.a: Yes — about the 82nd percentile, faster than four in five measured typists. It is the entry band for general transcription and well above every clerical requirement.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is 70 WPM?
faq.a: 21,000 KPH. Seventy words per minute is 350 characters per minute, and 350 × 60 = 21,000.

faq.q: How long does it take to get from 70 to 80 WPM?
faq.a: Usually months, not weeks. The easy inefficiencies are gone by 70; remaining gains come from consistency, hard-text practice and tooling such as text expansion.

faq.q: Is 70 WPM enough for transcription?
faq.a: It is the entry band for general transcription, which advertises 65-80 WPM. Medical and legal transcription often expect the upper end plus domain vocabulary.

faq.q: Why does my score swing 10 WPM between rounds?
faq.a: Variance is normal and grows with speed. Track your lowest of ten rounds rather than your best; narrowing the spread is what raises a 70 WPM average toward 80.

pages.tldr: 70 WPM = 350 CPM = 21,000 KPH, about the 82nd percentile. It reaches the entry band for general transcription (65-80) and clears every clerical requirement. Gains from here come from accuracy and consistency, not force.

pages.title: 100 WPM Typing Test — What the Top 1% Actually Do
pages.metaDesc: 100 WPM is roughly the 99th percentile. What separates it from 70, why most people never get there, and whether it is worth the months it takes.
pages.heroP: One hundred words per minute is roughly the 99th percentile of measured typists. It is not a faster version of 70 WPM — the technique is different, the practice is different, and for most jobs it is not required at all.

seo.h2: What 100 WPM means numerically
p: One hundred words per minute is 500 characters per minute, about 8.3 characters per second, and 30,000 keystrokes per hour. In the CHI 2018 distribution with mean 51.56 and standard deviation 20.2, it sits near the 99th percentile — roughly one typist in a hundred.

For comparison: the fastest decile starts around 78 WPM, so 100 is not the edge of the distribution but well inside its tail. World-record competition typing exceeds 200 WPM on short bursts of known text, which is a different activity again.

seo.h2: The technique difference
p: At 70 WPM you are typing words. At 100 WPM you are typing letter sequences with almost no conscious word recognition — the buffer is two to four words deep and the hands run ahead of attention. Typists at this level typically cannot tell you what they just typed.

That is why deliberate practice at 100 WPM looks strange: it is mostly very short maximum-speed bursts on familiar text, plus accuracy work on unfamiliar text, plus keyboard and layout optimisation. Long slow practice rounds stop helping.

seo.h2: Is it worth it?
p: For employment, no. The highest clerical requirement you will meet is 75-80 WPM (legal, medical transcription) and court reporting uses a stenotype, not a keyboard. Above 80, extra speed adds no job options.

For work where you think in text — programming, live captioning, competitive typing, writing to a deadline — it removes the keyboard as a bottleneck entirely. That is a real but narrow benefit, and it costs months of practice to reach.

seo.h2: If you decide to chase it
p:
• Keyboard: a mechanical board with short-travel switches is measurably faster for most people than a laptop chiclet keyboard. Try before buying.
  • Layout: some typists gain 5-10% from Colemak or Dvorak after a month of pain. Most do not; measure before committing.
  • Bursts: 15-second maximum rounds, ten per session, three sessions a week. Long rounds teach endurance you already have.
  • Accuracy gate: never accept below 97%. A 100 WPM score at 94% nets 94 and fails any real test.

faq.q: Is 100 WPM rare?
faq.a: Yes — roughly the 99th percentile of measured typists. About one in a hundred people in the CHI 2018 sample typed at or above that speed.

faq.q: How many keystrokes per hour is 100 WPM?
faq.a: 30,000 KPH. One hundred words per minute is 500 characters per minute, and 500 × 60 = 30,000.

faq.q: Do any jobs require 100 WPM?
faq.a: No standard clerical role does. Legal and medical transcription top out around 80 WPM, and court reporting uses a stenotype at 225 WPM rather than a keyboard.

faq.q: How long does it take to reach 100 WPM?
faq.a: Usually years from a standing start, and months from 80. The gains come from short maximum-speed bursts, hard-text accuracy work and keyboard optimisation rather than more of the same practice.

faq.q: Is 100 WPM possible with two fingers?
faq.a: Effectively no. Two-finger typing plateaus around 35-40 WPM because each keystroke needs a visual target. Reaching 100 requires all ten fingers and no looking.

pages.tldr: 100 WPM = 500 CPM = 30,000 KPH, about the 99th percentile. No clerical job requires it. It matters for competitive typing, live captioning and heavy code work, where the bottleneck otherwise becomes the keyboard.

pages.heroP: Find your score in the table, read the verdict. Percentiles come from the 168,960-person sample behind the CHI 2018 typing study (mean 51.56 WPM, SD 20.2), and the job bands come from advertised requirements.

seo.h2: The chart
