seo.h2: How to read the verdict column
p: The verdict is relative to the measured population, not to a job you want. A 45 WPM score is genuinely average and genuinely enough for a receptionist posting; both statements are true at once. Employers do not rank candidates by percentile, they compare against a fixed number in the advert.
So use the percentile to know where you stand and the job column to know what to aim at. If the posting says 50 and you are at 44, the gap is a fortnight of accuracy work, not a personality problem.

seo.h2: The score you should be quoting
p: Five-minute net WPM with the accuracy beside it. A 15-second run reads 5-10 WPM higher, random word lists read lower than sentences, and gross reads higher than net. Any of those will flatter or penalise you relative to this chart.
If you only have a one-minute score, subtract 5 before reading the table. It is a rough correction, but it is closer than treating a burst as your real speed.

seo.h2: Moving up one band
p:
• 20 to 30: stop looking at the keyboard. One covered round a day for two weeks. This is the largest single gain available to anyone.
  • 30 to 40: stop backspacing during tests. Most people at 30 lose 5-6 WPM to corrections.
  • 40 to 50: accuracy at speed. Thirty-second sprints at 90% of maximum, checked every round.
  • 50 to 60: read ahead. The bottleneck moves from the fingers to the eyes, and look-ahead practice fixes it.
  • 60 to 80: consistency. Type ten one-minute rounds and track your worst, not your best.
Each band has a different cause, which is why generic advice stops working after the first twenty points.
The underlying study figures, the phone-versus-keyboard comparison and a CSV of this curve are on the benchmarks page.
How the count is made - five characters per word, errors subtracted - is set out on the words per minute test page, which reports both raw and net.
If you have characters and time rather than a test score, the typing speed calculator converts them into gross WPM, net WPM, CPM, KPH and a percentile.

faq.q: Is 60 WPM good?
faq.a: Yes — about the 66th percentile, faster than two thirds of measured typists, and the point where job adverts start calling typing fast. It is the entry band for legal secretary and transcription work.

faq.q: Is 40 WPM good?
faq.a: It is the standard floor: around the 28th percentile and the number most clerical, receptionist and county government postings quote. Aim for 44-45 so a bad sentence cannot drop you under it.

faq.q: What is the average typing speed?
faq.a: 51.56 WPM from the CHI 2018 study of 168,960 volunteers, with a standard deviation of 20.2. Older sources quoting 40 WPM describe office-worker samples instead.

faq.q: Is 100 WPM rare?
faq.a: Yes, about the 99th percentile. No standard clerical job requires it; it matters for competitive typing, live captioning and heavy code work.

faq.q: Why does my WPM change between tests?
faq.a: Test length, text type and scoring method all move the number by 5-10 WPM. A five-minute net score on sentences is the figure this chart refers to; a 15-second gross score is not comparable.

pages.webAppName: WPM Chart: Is Your Typing Speed Good?
pages.tldr: Under 26 WPM is the bottom decile. 40 is the most common job floor. 52 is the median measured typist. 78 starts the top 10%. 100 is roughly the top 1%. Most clerical jobs stop asking at 50.

pages.title: Typing Speed: Phone vs Keyboard (Measured Study Data)
pages.metaDesc: Phone typing averages 36.2 WPM, desktop keyboards 51.6 WPM - from two studies with 37,370 and 168,960 volunteers. Why the gap exists and what it means.
pages.heroP: Two large studies measured the same task on different devices: 36.2 WPM on a phone (37,370 volunteers) and 51.6 WPM on a desktop keyboard (168,960 volunteers). The 15 WPM gap is real, measured, and mostly mechanical.

seo.h2: The two measurements, side by side
p:
MeasurePhone (touchscreen)Desktop keyboard
Average speed36.17 WPM (SD 13.22)51.56 WPM (SD 20.2)
Uncorrected error rate2.34%1.17%
Keystrokes per character1.181.173
Volunteers37,370168,960
SourcePalin, Feit, Kim, Kristensson & Oulasvirta, MobileHCI 2019, doi.org/10.1145/3338286.3340120Dhakal, Feit, Kristensson & Oulasvirta, CHI 2018, doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220

Both studies used the same method - transcribe a displayed English sentence - so the comparison is unusually clean. The mobile study explicitly compares itself to the desktop one and reports that average performance is about 15 WPM slower on a phone.

seo.h2: Where the gap comes from
p:
• Fewer fingers. Over 74% of phone typists use both thumbs, and two thumbs are faster than one thumb or one index finger - but still nowhere near ten fingers on a physical keyboard.
  • No tactile feedback. You cannot feel the key boundary, so every press carries a small positional uncertainty that a keyboard removes.
  • Correction cost. Fixing a mistake on glass takes more gestures, which is why phone typists leave more errors uncorrected (2.34% versus 1.17%) rather than fixing them.
  • Layout. A QWERTY touchscreen is a compromise; physical keyboards can be swapped for whatever suits your hands.

seo.h2: Phone typing percentiles
p: Using the mobile distribution (mean 36.2, SD 13.2), a normal approximation gives a rough position:

Phone WPMApprox. percentileReading
2011thSlow thumb typing
3032ndBelow the phone average
3650thExactly average for phone users
4575thFast for a phone
6097thExceptional on glass
The approximation is labelled as such: the mobile distribution is right-skewed, so the far tail is less reliable than the middle.

seo.h2: What this means for a typing test
p: Most online typing tests and every job screening test assume a physical keyboard. A 36 WPM phone score is not evidence that you would score 36 WPM at a desk - the desk number is usually higher, often by 10-15 WPM if you touch type.

The reverse is also true and less convenient: a good desktop score does not transfer to mobile work. If your job involves replying from a phone, practise separately, because the two skills share vocabulary but not motor memory.

seo.h2: Should you practise typing on a phone?
p: Only if the work happens on a phone. Practising phone typing to raise a desktop score is wasted effort; the mechanics do not transfer. If you want the desktop number to rise, use a keyboard and work on accuracy and look-ahead.

Where phone practice does pay: switching to two thumbs if you currently use one finger, and enabling autocorrect, which the mobile study found correlates with faster entry. Word prediction, by contrast, correlated with slower entry in that dataset.

faq.q: How fast does the average person type on a phone?
faq.a: 36.17 words per minute, from a study of 37,370 volunteers (Palin et al., MobileHCI 2019), with 2.34% of errors left uncorrected. The fastest participants exceeded 80 WPM.

faq.q: How much slower is phone typing than a keyboard?
faq.a: About 15 WPM on average: 36.2 on a phone versus 51.6 on a desktop keyboard, measured with the same transcription task in two large studies.

faq.q: Does two-thumb typing help?
faq.a: Yes. Over 74% of participants used both thumbs, and that was significantly faster than one thumb or a single index finger, though still about 70% of desktop speed.

faq.q: Why do people leave more errors on a phone?
faq.a: Correcting on a touchscreen costs more gestures than pressing backspace on a keyboard, so phone typists accept more errors instead of fixing them - 2.34% uncorrected versus 1.17% on desktop.

faq.q: Can I take a job typing test on my phone?
faq.a: You can, but do not. Screening tests assume a physical keyboard and the same skill typically scores 10-15 WPM higher on one. Use a desktop or laptop for any test that counts.

pages.tldr: Phone: 36.2 WPM average, 2.3% uncorrected errors (Palin et al., MobileHCI 2019, n=37,370). Desktop: 51.6 WPM, 1.17% errors (Dhakal et al., CHI 2018, n=168,960). Touchscreens run about 70% of keyboard speed, even with two thumbs.

pages.title: Typing Speed by Grade — What to Expect, 1st to 8th
pages.metaDesc: Typical typing speed for each school grade, from 1st to 8th, with what to teach at each stage and why accuracy matters more than speed before grade 6.
pages.heroP: Grade-level typing expectations are bands, not standards: schools differ enormously in how much keyboarding time they provide. Here is what the published classroom ranges look like, and what to actually teach at each stage.

seo.h2: The bands
p:
GradeTypical WPM bandPriority
1st-2nd5-11 WPMFinding letters; keyboard familiarity, not speed
3rd10-20 WPMHome row and correct fingers
4th15-25 WPMAll letters without looking down
5th25-35 WPMAccuracy above 90%, capitals with Shift
6th30-40 WPMPunctuation, sustained paragraphs
7th-8th35-45 WPMEditing, formatting, real documents

These are the ranges that appear across classroom keyboarding curricula and district technology plans; treat them as a guide to whether a child is roughly on track, never as a pass or fail line. A child who has had no formal instruction can be two grades behind the band and still catch up in a term.

seo.h2: Why younger children score lower - and should
p: Two things are still developing before about age ten: hand size relative to the keyboard, and the fine motor control needed for independent finger movement. A seven-year-old reaching across a full-size keyboard is doing a different physical task from a twelve-year-old.

That is why early keyboarding instruction focuses on letter location and posture rather than words per minute. Pushing speed before the hands are ready produces the two-finger hunt-and-peck style that later caps out around 35-40 WPM.
For the adult benchmarks those grade bands are heading towards, see average typing speed.

seo.h2: What to do at each stage
p:
• Grades 1-2: letter games, five minutes at a time, no timer. The goal is knowing where the keys are.
  • Grades 3-4: home row drills and short un-timed copying. Cover the hands for one round a week once the home row is secure.
  • Grade 5: timed one-minute tests, but score accuracy first. A child at 90% accuracy will overtake a faster child who types sloppily.
  • Grades 6-8: full-length tests, real documents, editing practice. This is when speed starts to matter for schoolwork volume.

seo.h2: How to measure without stressing a child
p: One test a week, one minute long, and read out the accuracy before the speed. Children optimise for whatever the adult reacts to - if the number that gets attention is WPM, they will type faster and sloppier within a fortnight.
Keep a simple record of the weekly score so progress is visible when it feels slow. Children improve in steps: three flat weeks and then five WPM in one.

seo.h2: When a child is behind the band
p: First check the physical setup: feet supported, elbows near 90 degrees, screen at eye level, a keyboard that is not oversized. A child typing on an adult keyboard at the wrong height will underperform regardless of practice.

Then check the method: are they using all fingers and not looking? If not, that is the whole project for the next month, and grade-level speed will follow. If both are fine and the score is flat, the issue is usually practice frequency, not ability - five minutes four times a week beats thirty minutes once.

faq.q: How fast should a 5th grader type?
faq.a: Roughly 25-35 WPM with 90%+ accuracy if they have had regular keyboarding practice. Bands vary widely by school and by how much instruction the child has actually received.

faq.q: How fast should a 3rd grader type?
faq.a: Usually 10-20 WPM. At this age letter location and home-row habit matter far more than speed, and timed tests should not be the main activity.

faq.q: What is a good typing speed for an 8th grader?
faq.a: 35-45 WPM is a reasonable band by the end of middle school, with accuracy above 95%. Students who reach it usually had formal instruction around grade 4 or 5.

faq.q: Is 20 WPM bad for a 10-year-old?
faq.a: No. It is normal for a child without formal keyboarding instruction, and it is well within the grade 4-5 band. What matters is whether the fingers are on the home row.

faq.q: How often should children practise?
faq.a: Ten minutes, three to four times a week. Short frequent sessions build the motor pattern; a long weekly session mostly builds frustration.

pages.tldr: Rough bands: grade 1-2, 5-11 WPM; grade 3, 10-20; grade 4, 15-25; grade 5, 25-35; grade 6, 30-40; grade 7-8, 35-45. Below grade 6 the goal is home-row habit and accuracy, not speed.

pages.title: How to Put WPM on a Résumé (With Real Examples)
pages.metaDesc: Exact lines to use, when a typing speed helps an application and when it hurts, and what a recruiter will ask you to prove. Includes net vs gross wording.
crumbs: How to Put WPM on a Résumé
pages.h1: How to Put WPM on a Résumé
pages.heroP: A typing speed belongs on a résumé only when the job screens for it, and it should be written so it can be verified: method, length and accuracy, not a bare number.

seo.h2: Where it goes
p: Put it in the skills section, not the summary. A recruiter scanning for a 50 WPM requirement looks at skills, certifications and the line under the job title - not at a paragraph about your professional philosophy.

• Skills line: Typing: 62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy (5-minute test)
  • Within a role bullet: "Typed 60+ WPM net while handling 40+ client records daily" - only when the job actually required it.
  • Certification line: Typing certificate, 55 WPM, proctored at [testing centre], [date] - when a formal certificate is required.

seo.h2: Why net, with the length
p: Net WPM subtracts errors, so it is the number a screening test will reproduce. Gross WPM without a length is unverifiable and reads as the flattering version - recruiters who hire typists know the difference.

Adding the test length does two things: it signals that you know a 15-second burst is not a working speed, and it pre-answers the follow-up question. "62 WPM net (5-minute)" is more credible than "70 WPM" even though the number is lower.

seo.h2: When to leave it off
p: Leave it off when the role does not screen for typing: management, sales, design, engineering, research. A speed listed against a job that never asked for it looks like filler, and an average number can create a doubt that would not otherwise exist.
The exception is when typing is an explicit part of the posting - a project manager who writes documentation all day can reasonably list 60 WPM if the advert mentions documentation volume.

seo.h2: What happens in the interview
p: If you list a number, expect to be tested. Most employers use a short online test, and a handful ask for a certificate. If your listed score came from a one-minute burst on a good day, the live test will read 5-8 WPM lower and the discrepancy is what they will notice.
So list the score you can reproduce on a bad day, at the test length the employer uses. If you do not know the length, assume five minutes and quote that.

seo.h2: If you have no recent score
p: Take a five-minute test now, screenshot the result, and use that number - it is current and reproducible. Re-test every six months or after a role change, because typing speed drifts with how much you type.
Keep the screenshot. It costs nothing and it settles the occasional "can you prove that" question without a re-test.

faq.q: Should I put my WPM on a résumé?
faq.a: Yes for clerical, data entry, transcription, dispatch, legal support and customer service roles that screen for typing. No for roles where typing is not part of the job description.

faq.q: How do I write WPM on a résumé?
faq.a: "Typing: 62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy (5-minute test)". Net, with accuracy and test length, so the number is reproducible rather than flattering.

faq.q: Is 60 WPM good enough to list?
faq.a: Yes. 60 WPM net is about the 66th percentile and above almost every clerical requirement. Below 40 WPM, only list the number if the posting explicitly asks for a lower threshold.

faq.q: Should I list gross or net WPM?
faq.a: Net. Screening tests deduct errors, so a net figure is what they will measure. Gross WPM without a stated method reads as inflated.

faq.q: Will an employer verify my typing speed?
faq.a: Often yes, with a short online test or a certificate. List a score you can reproduce at the same test length, because a live test that reads lower than your résumé is a credibility problem.

pages.webAppName: How to Put WPM on a Résumé

pages.tldr: Write it as: "Typing: 62 WPM net, 98.5% accuracy (5-minute test)". Include it for clerical, data entry, transcription, dispatch and legal support roles. Leave it off creative, management and engineering applications unless typing is the job.

pages.title: Will Employers Accept a Free Typing Certificate?
pages.metaDesc: Self-issued certificates are not credentials. Which employers accept them, when a proctored test is required, and how to tell the difference before you pay.
pages.h1: Will Employers Accept a Free Typing Certificate?
pages.heroP: A free certificate printed from a website is self-reported evidence, not a credential. Some employers accept it, some require a proctored test, and knowing which is which saves you a wasted application - or a wasted fee.

seo.h2: Three kinds of typing evidence
p:
TypeWhat it provesWho accepts it
Self-issued certificate (printed from a website)That you used the site and got a scoreSome private employers, as a screening signal
Third-party timed result (dated, named, unproctored)A specific score on a specific dateMany private employers; occasionally agencies
Proctored certificate (testing centre or remote proctor)That someone observed the testGovernment, courts, staffing agencies, some hospitals
The difference that matters is observation. A certificate nobody watched you earn establishes intent and baseline skill; it does not establish that the score is yours.

seo.h2: Where a free certificate is genuinely useful
p:
• Private-sector applications where the recruiter just wants a rough number before scheduling an interview.
  • Freelance profiles - showing a dated result is better than claiming "fast typist".
  • Your own tracking - a monthly certificate is a simple progress record.
In all three cases the certificate is a convenience, not proof. Do not pay for one believing it changes the category.

seo.h2: Where it will be rejected
p: Public-sector postings frequently state the requirement in a way that excludes self-issued documents: "must submit a typing test with your name and date", "proctored within the last twelve months", "issued by an approved testing centre". If the wording includes any of those, a website certificate is not the document they want.

Court and legal roles, dispatch centres and hospital transcription departments are the most consistent about requiring a proctored result. The cost is usually modest; the inconvenience is the appointment.

seo.h2: Red flags in paid certificate services
p:
• No stated proctoring. If nobody observes the test, you are buying a PDF.
  • No verification ID or lookup page. An employer cannot check it, so it carries no more weight than your own screenshot.
  • No expiry stated. Real credentials state validity; typing certificates typically run one to four years.
  • Scores that cannot be this high. A service guaranteeing 90+ WPM to anyone is selling paper.

seo.h2: What to do instead
p: Keep a dated, named screenshot of a five-minute result and put the number on your résumé with the test length and accuracy. Then let the employer test you - which most will, and which you will pass if the listed number is honest.

If a posting demands a proctored certificate, book one at a local testing centre or workforce office and treat the fee as part of the application cost. It is the only version that satisfies that wording.

faq.q: Do employers accept free online typing certificates?
faq.a: Some private employers accept them as a screening signal, but they are self-reported. Government, court, dispatch and hospital roles usually require a proctored or employer-administered test instead.

faq.q: Is a typing certificate a real credential?
faq.a: Only a proctored one. A certificate printed from a website shows that you took a test, not that anyone verified the result.

faq.q: How long is a typing certificate valid?
faq.a: Typically one to four years depending on the issuer or agency. Postings often refuse results older than twelve months, so check the wording before reusing an old certificate.

faq.q: Can I put a certificate score on my résumé?
faq.a: Yes, with the test length and accuracy, for example "55 WPM net, 98% accuracy, five-minute test". Expect to be re-tested, and list a score you can reproduce.

faq.q: Should I pay for a certificate?
faq.a: Only when a posting asks for a proctored result or a specific issuer. For private-sector applications, a dated screenshot and an honest résumé line do the same job for free.

pages.webAppName: Will Employers Accept a Free Typing Certificate?
pages.tldr: Self-issued certificates show effort, not verification. Government, court and staffing-agency roles usually require a proctored or employer-administered test. Private employers commonly accept a screenshot of a dated result and re-test you themselves.

pages.title: All Typing Tests — Every Mode, Length and Language

pages.heroP: Every test on the site in one directory: duration variants, languages, skill drills, exam and job pages, metrics and guides. Each link says what the page measures rather than repeating a keyword.

seo.h2: Find the test you need
p: 184 tests
Type a word above to filter the list below - a job title, a language, a unit, a length, a format. The directory is generated from the site's own page configuration, so it always matches what exists.

seo.h2: How to use this directory
p: Three questions decide which page you want. First: are you measuring or improving? A timed test on the home page measures; a practice page with drills improves.
Second: what length? Fifteen and thirty seconds measure a burst, one to three minutes matches most screening tests, and five to ten minutes measures the pace you can hold through a working session.

Third: what content? Sentences are the default, quotes add punctuation and capitals, numbers train the row that data entry actually uses, and code tests are for programmers. Languages switch the practice pool without changing the timer.

seo.h2: Choosing by goal
p:
• I have an interview or screening test — start with the five-minute test, then the role page for your job, which lists the threshold the employer is likely to use.
  • I want a number to quote — a five-minute net score with accuracy is the reproducible one. The certificate page explains what a self-issued certificate does and does not prove.
  • I am learning from scratch — home row, then beginner, then one-minute rounds. Ten minutes a day beats a weekly marathon.
  • I am stuck at a speed — the WPM chart names the cause for each band, from looking at the keyboard at 20 WPM to inconsistency above 70.

seo.h2: Why this page exists
p: The footer already links every page, but a flat list of 160 links tells a reader nothing about which one to open. This directory groups them by the question they answer, and it is generated from the same configuration that builds the pages, so it cannot drift out of date or link to something that no longer exists.
New to this? The free typing test gives you a sixty-second baseline before you choose a longer test; come back here once you know roughly where you stand.
Choosing between sites rather than tests? The comparison of six free typing tests covers sign-up, ads, languages and certificates.
For the length most screening tools use, start with the three-minute test.
The timed typing test page explains what each countdown length actually measures, if you are unsure which to pick.

faq.q: How many typing tests are on this site?
faq.a: 160 pages, covering nine timed lengths, twelve language pools, skill drills, exam and job pages, metrics explainers and guides. Every one is free and needs no account.

faq.q: Which test should I take first?
faq.a: The five-minute sentence test on the home page. It is the length most screening tests use, and it produces the net score you can quote elsewhere. Use shorter rounds only for warm-ups.

faq.q: Do I need an account?

faq.q: Which test is best for a job application?
faq.a: The role page for that job, plus a five-minute test to get the number. Roles differ: reception is 40-50 WPM, data entry is quoted in keystrokes per hour, legal and transcription start at 60.

faq.q: Are the tests the same engine?
faq.a: Yes. Every page runs the same typing engine with a different duration, text mode, language pool or layout, so scores are comparable across pages and over time.

pages.title: SQL Typing Practice — Real Queries, Symbols and Speed
pages.metaDesc: Type real SQL: SELECT, JOIN, CTEs, window functions. Trains the symbols that slow analysts down - quotes, semicolons, parentheses, pipes.
pages.heroP: SQL is punctuation with words attached. Every query needs quotes, semicolons, parentheses and usually a pipe, and those keys are where analysts lose their speed. This drill types 36 real queries, not prose.

seo.h2: What makes SQL slow to type
p: Plain English uses 26 letters and a space. A single SELECT statement uses quotes, a semicolon, parentheses, an underscore, a dot and often a pipe or a cast operator. None of those sit under the home row, so a typist who is comfortable at 70 WPM on prose will typically drop to 40-50 WPM here.

The second factor is structure. You are not copying a sentence, you are reproducing a syntax tree, and the eye has to jump between keywords and symbols instead of flowing left to right. That is a trainable skill and it is separate from general typing speed.

seo.h2: The characters that dominate
p:
• Single quotes on the pinky, doubled in SQL because strings are delimited - the most common source of a broken query.
  • Parentheses and underscores on the right pinky, which is already the weakest finger for most typists.
  • Semicolons and colons, one key apart, typed in sequence in casts and labels.
  • Pipes and arrows for concatenation and JSON access, which pull the right hand off the home row entirely.
If your error log concentrates on the pinky keys, that is not a knowledge gap - it is a reach problem, and it responds to a few minutes of deliberate symbol drill per day.

seo.h2: How to practise without writing nonsense
p: The pool on this page is 36 real statements: a projection, a join with an alias, a grouped aggregate, a CTE, a window function, an index creation, an UPDATE with a timestamp. They are the shapes you actually type in a working day, not keyword soup.

Run one-minute rounds until the syntax stops needing thought, then move to three-minute rounds. Analysts rarely type one query at a time; they type twelve in a row while reading output, and the stamina matters more than the peak.

seo.h2: Where to go next
p: If you write Python or JavaScript, the Python code typing and JavaScript code typing pools use the same engine with different syntax. For spreadsheet work, the Excel formula practice page trains the same bracket-and-comma vocabulary in a different grammar.
For a general benchmark rather than a drill, take the WPM test - code typing and prose typing are not comparable numbers, so keep the two scores separate.

faq.q: What is a good typing speed for SQL?
faq.a: 40-60 WPM on real queries is comfortable for most analysts. Prose speed is not comparable because SQL has roughly one symbol every five characters, and symbols need extended reaches.

faq.q: Why is my code typing slower than my normal WPM?
faq.a: Symbols do not sit under the home row. Quotes, parentheses, underscores, pipes and semicolons all need an extended finger, and alternating between words and symbols breaks the rhythm that prose typing relies on.

faq.q: Is this real SQL?
faq.a: Yes - 36 statements covering SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, CTEs, window functions, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL and JSON access, written in ordinary PostgreSQL-flavoured syntax.

faq.q: Does code typing speed matter for a job?
faq.a: Indirectly. No one screens analysts on typing speed, but at 30 WPM the keyboard becomes the bottleneck when you are writing long ETL scripts or documentation.

faq.q: How often should I practise?
faq.a: Five to ten minutes a day, one-minute rounds, scored on errors. Symbol accuracy improves faster than raw speed, and it is the part that actually costs you time in a query.

pages.tldr: SQL typing is bracket-and-quote work: roughly one symbol every five characters. Practise at 40-60 WPM on queries you would actually write, and watch accuracy rather than speed - a misplaced semicolon is a failed query, not a typo.

pages.title: TypeScript Typing Practice — Generics and Symbols
pages.metaDesc: Type real TypeScript: generics, type guards, optional chaining, JSX-adjacent syntax. Trains angle brackets, colons and arrows where TS typists slip.
pages.heroP: TypeScript adds a second layer of punctuation to JavaScript: angle brackets, colons, question marks and arrows in every signature. This drill types 36 real lines from application code, not toy examples.

seo.h2: The symbols that cost you time
p:
• Angle brackets for generics, typed with Shift plus comma and Shift plus full stop - two reaches that pull both hands off the home row.
  • Colons and question marks in type annotations and optional properties, frequently adjacent.
  • Arrow operators in callbacks, which need the hyphen and the greater-than key in sequence.
  • Braces and parentheses in destructuring and object literals, often nested three deep.
A JavaScript typist at 65 WPM typically measures 50-58 WPM on the same content once types are added. That is not a regression in skill; it is more symbol work per line.

seo.h2: What is in the pool
p: Thirty-six lines taken from ordinary application code: an interface with optional fields, a discriminated union result type, a typed reducer, a generic type guard, an error class with a constructor parameter property, a debounce hook, a fetch with an abort signal, and a schema `.safeParse` branch.

They are deliberately not one-liners from tutorials. Real files mix declarations, expressions and early returns, and switching between those shapes is what makes editor typing feel different from typing a passage.

seo.h2: Practising for real work
p: Type the lines as written, including semicolons and trailing commas. Autocomplete does not type for you during the drill, which is the point: you are rebuilding the muscle memory that autocomplete usually hides.

Then run one round with the on-screen keyboard visible and watch which key your eye goes to before the miss. It is usually the bracket cluster on the right, and it is fixable in a week of two-minute drills.

seo.h2: Related practice
p: For plain JavaScript, the JavaScript code typing page uses the same engine without the type layer. For Python, Python code typing. Spreadsheet work is on the Excel formula page.

faq.q: Is TypeScript typing slower than JavaScript?
faq.a: Yes, typically 10-20% slower at the same accuracy, because types add angle brackets, colons, question marks and arrow operators that JavaScript does not require.

faq.q: What speed should a developer type at?
faq.a: Most developers sit above 60 WPM on prose and 45-55 WPM on code. No employer screens for it, but below 40 WPM the keyboard starts to limit how much code and documentation you produce.

faq.q: Does autocomplete make this pointless?
faq.a: No. Autocomplete hides the symbol reaches, so they stay weak. Typing full lines rebuilds them, which is what you need when you write something autocomplete does not know.

faq.q: Is this real TypeScript?
faq.a: Yes, 36 lines of ordinary application TypeScript: interfaces, unions, generics, hooks, async/await, error classes and schema validation branches.

faq.q: How long until I see improvement?
faq.a: Two weeks of five-minute daily drills usually shows 5-8 WPM on this content, mostly from the bracket cluster ceasing to need a visual check.

pages.tldr: TypeScript is symbol-dense: generics add <>, types add :, optional fields add ?, and arrow functions add =>. Expect 10-20% lower speed than plain JavaScript at the same accuracy until the symbol reaches become automatic.

pages.title: Rust Typing Practice — Lifetimes, Matches, Arrows
pages.metaDesc: Type real Rust: fn signatures, lifetimes, match arms, iterator chains, Result handling. A drill for the punctuation-heavy syntax Rust actually uses.
pages.heroP: Rust is the most punctuation-dense mainstream language: lifetimes, turbofish-free generics, match arms, ? and => on nearly every line. This drill types 36 real lines from ordinary Rust code.

seo.h2: Why Rust is harder to type than it looks
p: Three characters dominate: & for borrows, ' for lifetimes and char literals, and < > for generics. Each sits on the top row or the right pinky, and lifetimes put the apostrophe immediately after an ampersand - a two-key sequence that prose never asks for.

Then there is the shape of idiomatic Rust: `match` arms with indentation, iterator chains broken across lines, and `?` at the end of expressions. The line breaks are part of the syntax you are training, not formatting noise.

seo.h2: What is in the pool
p: Thirty-six lines covering the constructs that appear in real files: a struct with a generic parameter, a lifetime-annotated function, a `match` with an error branch, a `HashMap` build, an iterator chain with `filter_map`, a trait implementation, a `#[derive]` attribute, an async function signature with `anyhow::Result`, and a test module.
The lines are short enough to finish inside a minute round and varied enough that you cannot memorise the sequence.

seo.h2: How to drill symbols without boredom
p: Alternate two rounds per session: one straight accuracy round at your normal pace, one where you deliberately slow to 80% and watch the right hand. The second round is where the improvement happens; the first is where you measure it.
Track the errors rather than the WPM for the first week. In symbol-dense code, error count is the leading indicator and speed follows it, not the other way round.

seo.h2: Related practice
p: Same engine, different grammar: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, SQL. If you want the general number, use the programmer typing benchmarks page.

faq.q: What typing speed do Rust developers have?
faq.a: No one measures this formally. In practice most developers type prose at 60-90 WPM and real Rust at 40-55 WPM because of symbol density and line breaks.

faq.q: Why do lifetimes slow typing down?
faq.a: A lifetime needs an apostrophe immediately followed by a letter, and borrows need ampersands. Both sit on the top row and the right pinky, so the sequence interrupts the home-row rhythm.

faq.q: Is this real Rust?
faq.a: Yes, 36 lines of ordinary Rust: generics, lifetimes, match arms, iterator chains, trait impls, async signatures and a test module.

faq.q: Does typing speed matter for a Rust job?
faq.a: Not directly. It matters only when the keyboard becomes the bottleneck for long files, documentation or review comments - below about 40 WPM on code, that happens regularly.

faq.q: How much practice is enough?
faq.a: Five minutes a day for two to three weeks. Symbol accuracy responds quickly; after that, speed follows without extra drills.

pages.tldr: Rust needs ampersands, apostrophes, angle brackets, question marks and double colons, often in the same expression. Expect 40-55 WPM on real code even if you type prose at 75; accuracy on brackets and apostrophes is the limiting factor.

pages.title: Excel Formula Typing Practice — Brackets & Commas
pages.metaDesc: Type real Excel formulas: XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, FILTER, LET, LAMBDA. Trains the bracket, comma and dollar-sign reaches that slow spreadsheet work down.
pages.heroP: A formula is a chain of brackets, commas and dollar signs wrapped around a function name. XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, FILTER and LET all punish the keys you never practise. This drill types 36 real formulas.

seo.h2: The four characters that decide a formula
p:
• Parentheses - every function opens one and most nest two deep; an unbalanced bracket stops Excel accepting the entry at all.
  • Commas - the argument separator in en-US locales, and a semicolon in many European ones. Typing a full stop instead is the single most common formula error.
  • Dollar signs - absolute references need Shift+4, a reach that pulls the left hand off the home row.
  • Double quotes - required around text criteria, and doubled inside strings.
None of these appear often in prose, which is why people who type quickly in Word still fumble a nested IF.

seo.h2: What is in the pool
p: Thirty-six formulas at the level a real spreadsheet uses: a basic SUM range, IFERROR-wrapped VLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH, SUMIFS with two criteria, TEXTJOIN, XLOOKUP with a fallback, SUMPRODUCT, LET, FILTER, SORT(UNIQUE()), MAP with LAMBDA, CHOOSECOLS, VSTACK and a SEQUENCE date series.
They are written the way they appear in a cell, including the leading equals sign, because that keystroke is part of the habit.

seo.h2: Practising so it transfers
p: Type into a plain text field first, then reproduce the best lines in a real workbook. The drill builds the keystroke sequence; the workbook confirms that the brackets balance and the separators are the ones your locale expects.
If your locale uses semicolons as argument separators, type the formulas with semicolons after the drill. Muscle memory for the wrong separator is worse than no practice.

seo.h2: Related practice
p: Numeric work benefits from the 10-key typing test, and data-entry roles are covered by the keystrokes per hour test. For database syntax rather than spreadsheet syntax, see SQL typing practice.

faq.q: Does typing speed matter in Excel?
faq.a: For formula-heavy work, yes. Analysts who can type a nested function without looking at the keyboard build models noticeably faster, and they make fewer bracket-balance errors.

faq.q: What is the most common formula typing mistake?
faq.a: An unbalanced parenthesis, followed by a full stop typed where a comma separator belongs. Both are stopped by Excel and both cost a re-type of the whole argument list.

faq.q: Should I use semicolons or commas?
faq.a: Whichever your locale uses. En-US uses commas; many European locales use semicolons. Practise the one your workbook expects, because the habit is hard to unlearn.

faq.q: Are these real Excel formulas?
faq.a: Yes, 36 formulas using current functions including XLOOKUP, XMATCH, FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE, LET, LAMBDA, MAP, CHOOSECOLS and VSTACK.

faq.q: How long should I practise?
faq.a: Five minutes a day for a week is enough to stop fumbling the bracket and dollar reaches; after that, use it as a warm-up before model-building sessions.

pages.tldr: Excel formulas are 30-40% punctuation by character count. The frequent failures are unbalanced brackets, a comma typed as a full stop, and a missing $ in an absolute reference. Practise with the formula bar visible and check balance after each line.

pages.title: Typing Test for Accountants — 10-Key and Numeric Speed
pages.metaDesc: Accounting work is numbers first: 10-key speed, decimal accuracy and spreadsheet entry. What firms screen for and how to build numeric speed that transfers.
pages.heroP: Accountants do not need prose speed. They need numeric accuracy at pace: 10-key entry, decimals in the right place, and the ability to type a figure once and have it be right.

seo.h2: What the job actually requires
p: A ledger entry is a date, an account code, a description and an amount. Three of those four are numeric or alphanumeric, and the amount has a decimal point in a position that matters more than any word you will type all day.
Firms rarely quote a words-per-minute figure in accounting adverts because prose speed is not the constraint. If they test at all, it is a numeric or 10-key exercise, or an Excel-based work sample.

seo.h2: The numbers to aim at
p:
TaskTargetWhy
10-key numeric entry8,000-12,000 KPHThe band employers quote for numeric data entry
Accuracy on amounts99%+A transposed digit is a reconciliation problem
Alphanumeric codes97-98%Account and tax codes mix letters and digits
Prose notes40-50 WPMEnough for memos and client correspondence
In practice the accuracy column decides whether you are useful. A 12,000 KPH entry rate with 96% accuracy creates more work than it saves, because every error has to be found later.

seo.h2: Building 10-key speed that transfers
p: Learn the keypad as a separate instrument: 4-5-6 on the home row, index on 4, middle on 5, ring on 6, thumb on 0. Type without looking, entering a figure and pressing Enter after each, which is how accounting software behaves.
Then add the parts that break in real work: negative signs, decimal points, and the Tab key between fields. A drill that only types clean integers trains a skill you will never use.

seo.h2: Where the test fits
p: Use the 10-key typing test for keypad speed, the Numbers mode on this page for mixed numeric content, and the Excel formula practice page for spreadsheet syntax. Then measure prose separately with the WPM test if a posting asks for it.
Keep the three numbers distinct on a CV. "12,000 KPH 10-key, 99.2% accuracy; 48 WPM prose" tells an accounting manager far more than a single WPM figure.

faq.q: What typing speed do accountants need?
faq.a: Postings rarely quote one. Numeric entry at 8,000-12,000 keystrokes per hour with 99% accuracy on amounts matters more than prose speed, which is usually fine at 40-50 WPM.

faq.q: Is 10-key speed tested for accounting jobs?
faq.a: Sometimes, especially for accounts payable, payroll and bookkeeping roles. Larger firms more often use an Excel work sample, which tests the same accuracy under realistic conditions.

faq.q: How fast is 10,000 keystrokes per hour?
faq.a: About 33 words per minute equivalent, or 167 characters per minute. On a numeric keypad that is a comfortable working pace rather than a sprint.

faq.q: Why does accuracy matter more than speed here?
faq.a: A transposed digit in an amount becomes a reconciliation break, which takes longer to find and fix than the entry saved. Accounting work is judged on the ledger balancing, not on entry rate.

faq.q: Should I practise on the number row or the keypad?
faq.a: The keypad, for amounts. Use the number row only for alphanumeric strings such as account codes where your hand is already on the main keyboard.

pages.tldr: Accounting roles rarely advertise a WPM figure. What matters is numeric entry: 8,000-12,000 keystrokes per hour on the keypad, 99%+ accuracy on amounts, and comfort with decimals and negative signs. Practise Numbers mode and the 10-key drill.

pages.title: Typing Test for Paralegals — 50-65 WPM and Formatting
pages.metaDesc: Paralegal work screens around 50-65 WPM with clean formatting: exhibit lists, citations and numbered paragraphs. What to rehearse beyond raw speed.
pages.heroP: Paralegal typing is document work: exhibit lists, citations, numbered paragraphs and defined terms. Firms look for 50–65 WPM, but the errors that matter are formatting errors, not slow words.

seo.h2: The requirement, and what sits behind it
p: Paralegal and legal assistant adverts commonly quote 50-65 WPM, below the 60-75 band for legal secretaries because the role includes more research and drafting than pure transcription. Accuracy expectations are high in both, because a document that misnames a party is a real problem.

That is why the useful practice is not speed drills on random sentences but repeated typing of the structures you will actually produce: a caption block, a numbered list with consistent indentation, a citation with the right punctuation, a table of exhibits.

seo.h2: Formatting is the skill being tested
p:
• Numbering. Auto-numbering that renumbers when you paste is the most common way a filing goes out wrong.
  • Defined terms. "the Company" keeps its capital; the rest of the document depends on it.
  • Citations. Italics, full stops and abbreviations follow a house style, and consistency is the whole point.
  • Track changes. Typing inside a tracked document is slower and less forgiving than typing a blank page.

seo.h2: A rehearsal that matches the work
p: Take one real clause with three sub-paragraphs and a defined term, and type it three times: once for accuracy, once at pace, once with track changes on. Compare the three outputs against the source line by line. That exercise finds more problems than any typing test.

Then run five-minute rounds on dense text with punctuation, targeting 98% accuracy. If accuracy falls below that at 65 WPM, work at 58 until it holds - a legal document with two errors a page costs more to check than it saved to type.

seo.h2: Related pages
p: For the transcription-heavy version of the role, see legal secretary. For dictation and audio work, audio typing. For the general benchmark that most postings quote, the WPM chart shows where 50-65 sits.

faq.q: What typing speed do paralegals need?
faq.a: Usually 50-65 WPM with high accuracy. Legal secretary roles sit slightly higher at 60-75 because transcription is a larger part of the job.

faq.q: Is 50 WPM enough for a paralegal job?
faq.a: For many roles, yes, provided formatting and accuracy are clean. Firms that test usually care more about whether a citation and a numbered list come out identical every time.

faq.q: Do paralegal tests include legal terminology?
faq.a: Sometimes. Work-sample tests use real clauses with defined terms and citations, which is why practising on legal text beats practising on random sentences.

faq.q: How do I improve accuracy on citations?
faq.a: Type the same citation ten times from the source, checking character by character, rather than typing ten different citations once. Pattern repetition is what makes punctuation automatic.

faq.q: Does typing speed matter more than research skill?
faq.a: No. Typing is a threshold you clear; the role is judged on document accuracy and research quality. That is why the bar sits at 50-65 rather than 75+.

pages.tldr: Paralegal postings typically ask 50-65 WPM with high accuracy. The differentiator is consistency: party names, case citations and paragraph numbering must be identical every time, which is a different skill from fast prose.

pages.title: USPS Postal Exam Typing Test — What Is Actually Tested
pages.metaDesc: The USPS virtual entry assessments do not include a typing test. What 474-477 actually measure, where keyboard speed matters, and what to practise.
pages.heroP: The honest answer first: the USPS virtual entry assessments do not contain a typing test. They measure work simulation, memory and customer service judgement. Keyboard speed still matters on the job, and some roles test it locally.

seo.h2: What the postal assessments actually contain
p: USPS replaced its older paper exams with virtual entry assessments tailored to job families: 474 for mail handler, 475 for mail processing, 476 for customer service and 477 for maintenance. They present work-sample scenarios - sorting decisions, address matching, register and money-order arithmetic, customer interactions - and score judgement and speed of decision rather than keystrokes.

That is why a candidate searching for a postal typing test usually finds practice sites selling a typing drill that does not match the exam. Practising WPM will not raise a 476 score; practising the scenario format will.

seo.h2: Where keyboard speed does matter
p:
• Data-entry-adjacent roles - address updates, redirects and claims work move faster with clean numeric typing.
  • Facility-level checks - some offices still administer a basic keyboarding or data-entry exercise during onboarding.
  • The job itself - retail counter and processing roles type addresses, tracking numbers and short notes all day, and an unfamiliar keyboard slows that down.
The figure that appears in comparable clerical settings is 30-40 WPM with accuracy above 95%. Treat it as a sensible personal target, not a published USPS requirement.

seo.h2: What to practise instead, if the exam is your goal
p: Work on the scenario skills: reading an address quickly and spotting the mismatch, doing change-making arithmetic without a calculator, remembering a short instruction sequence, and choosing the answer that follows procedure rather than the one that feels kindest.
Then use typing practice as a background habit - five minutes a day for the job, not for the exam. The two goals are different and mixing them wastes the preparation window.

seo.h2: If you do want a keyboard number
p: Take a five-minute sentence test and a two-minute numbers test, record net WPM and accuracy for both, and keep the screenshot. It is useful for the interview conversation and for any local keyboarding check, and it costs five minutes.
For address-style content specifically, the alphanumeric typing test is closer to the work than a prose passage, because postcodes and route numbers are mixed letter-digit strings.

faq.q: Does the USPS exam include a typing test?
faq.a: No. The virtual entry assessments (474, 475, 476, 477) are scenario-based work simulations. They do not report a words-per-minute score.

faq.q: What typing speed does USPS require?
faq.a: There is no published universal WPM requirement for the entry assessments. Comparable clerical roles quote 30-40 WPM with 95% accuracy, which is a sensible target for the job rather than an exam rule.

faq.q: Why do websites sell postal typing practice?
faq.a: Because people search for it. The practice is usually generic typing drill content that does not match the assessment format, so it will not raise a 474-477 score.

faq.q: What should I practise for the postal exam?
faq.a: Address comparison, money and change arithmetic, short instruction memory, and procedure-following judgement. Those are the four skills the scenarios actually test.

faq.q: Is keyboarding tested at the facility?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some offices run a basic keyboarding or data-entry exercise during onboarding. It is usually a low bar, but a clean 40 WPM with accurate digits removes the risk.

pages.tldr: USPS 474/475/476/477 are scenario-based virtual assessments, not typing exams. No WPM score is reported. Keyboarding speed matters for data-entry-heavy roles and some facility tests, and the commonly cited clerical target is 30-40 WPM.

pages.title: Typing Test for Seniors — Speed After 60, Done Right
pages.metaDesc: A typing test for older adults: larger text, two-to-three minute rounds, no leaderboard. What changes with age, what does not, and a realistic target.
pages.heroP: Typing speed settles with age, but accuracy and comfort do not have to. This page is about testing without strain: longer rounds, bigger text, and a realistic target instead of a leaderboard.

seo.h2: What actually changes with age
p: Two things slow down measurably: reaction time and fine motor steadiness. Both show up as more mistyped adjacent keys rather than as slower thinking, which is why older typists often report knowing the word but hitting the wrong key.

What does not change is vocabulary, sentence planning or the knowledge of where the keys are. That is why accuracy-focused practice still pays: the skill you already have is the part that carries over, and the reach is the part that needs the work.

seo.h2: Set the test up so it measures the right thing
p:
• Length: two to three minutes. A 15-second sprint measures reaction time, which is exactly what declines; a longer round measures sustainable pace.
  • Text: sentences rather than random words. Familiar sentence structure lets you use knowledge instead of reaction.
  • Display: browser zoom at 125-150% and the widened keyboard view. Reading strain produces more errors than typing strain.
  • Posture: feet flat, elbows near 90 degrees, screen at eye level. A laptop on a coffee table is the most common cause of shoulder fatigue in an hour of practice.

seo.h2: A target that is worth having
p: Thirty to forty words per minute with 97% accuracy covers email, forms, banking, messaging and almost every personal computing task. It is also inside the band that part-time and volunteer clerical roles quote.
Chasing 70 WPM is not useful unless you are going back into transcription or legal support. Chasing 97% accuracy is useful at any age, because it removes the corrections that make typing feel tiring.

seo.h2: When to stop, and what to watch
p: Stop a session at the first sign of tingling or numbness in the fingers, or aching in the forearm. Those are early signs of strain and they respond to rest, not to more practice. Persistent numbness is worth a doctor's opinion rather than a typing drill.
Ten minutes, three times a week is a good ceiling to start with. If that feels easy after two weeks, extend the rounds rather than the frequency - shorter sessions recover better.

faq.q: How fast do people over 60 type?
faq.a: Most sit between 25 and 45 WPM, and the variation within the group is much larger than the average difference from younger typists. Accuracy is usually maintained even when speed settles.

faq.q: Is it too late to learn touch typing after 60?
faq.a: No. Adults learn the key map quickly because they already read and write fluently; the slower part is building new finger habits, which takes a few weeks of short daily practice.

faq.q: How long should a test be?
faq.a: Two to three minutes. Short sprints measure reaction time, which declines with age, so they understate what you can actually sustain.

faq.q: Should I use a bigger font?
faq.a: Yes. Reading strain causes more errors than typing strain at any age. Zoom the browser to 125-150% and use the widened keyboard view.

faq.q: What should I do about aching hands?
faq.a: Stop the session, rest, and check posture and keyboard height before resuming. Persistent numbness or tingling should be reviewed by a doctor rather than worked through.

pages.tldr: Most people over 60 type somewhere between 25 and 45 WPM, and the spread within the group is far wider than the difference from younger typists. Use a 2-3 minute round, favour accuracy, and stop at the first sign of hand or wrist discomfort.

pages.title: Typing Test for Customer Service — Chat and Email Speed
pages.metaDesc: Customer service screens at 35-50 WPM, more for live chat. What each channel demands, why accuracy beats speed in written support, and how to rehearse.
pages.heroP: Written support is a typing job with a customer attached. Chat and email roles usually ask 35–50 WPM, and the thing that gets measured in probation is not speed but whether your replies are clear and typo-free.

seo.h2: Speed by channel
p:
ChannelTypical WPMWhat the job really tests
Phone support with notes30-40Capturing names, references and next steps while listening
Email support40-50Clear, correct written English; template editing under time pressure
Live chat45-60Typing the conversation itself, often with two or three chats open
Social media support40-55Public tone, short replies, high visibility of mistakes
The bands come from advertised requirements and from what contact-centre training programmes assume. A posting that quotes 35 WPM for email is unusual; 45 is the common floor for written channels.

seo.h2: Why accuracy outranks speed here
p: A typo in a reply is read by a customer who is already frustrated. It costs trust in a way that a slow reply does not. Support teams therefore judge written output on clarity and correctness, and they will happily keep a 45 WPM agent who writes cleanly over a 65 WPM agent who needs every message checked.
Practise accordingly: type a short reply, then proofread it. Two-thirds of the improvement in the first month comes from the proofreading habit, not from the keyboard.

seo.h2: Drills that match the work
p:
• Two-minute sentence rounds for the base pace, one a day.
  • Template editing - take a canned reply and rewrite the middle sentence for a specific customer in under 30 seconds. That is the actual task.
  • Numbers mode once a week for order and reference numbers, which is where written support makes its costly mistakes.
  • Two conversations at once - type alternate replies to two prompts without mixing them up. Chat roles test this informally within the first week.

seo.h2: Related pages
p: Voice-first roles are covered on the call centre page, which includes the listening-while-typing drill. For the numeric side, see alphanumeric typing. For a general number to quote, the WPM chart shows where 45 sits.

faq.q: What WPM do customer service jobs require?
faq.a: Usually 35-50 WPM depending on channel: 30-40 for phone support notes, 40-50 for email, and 45-60 for live chat where you type the conversation itself.

faq.q: Is 40 WPM enough for live chat?
faq.a: It is marginal. Chat roles usually ask 45-60 because you type the entire interaction, often across two or three concurrent conversations.

faq.q: Does accuracy matter more than speed?
faq.a: Yes in written support. A typo in a reply reaches a frustrated customer and costs trust; a slightly slower correct reply does not. Teams keep clean 45 WPM agents over sloppy 65 WPM ones.

faq.q: How do I practise typing while handling a customer?
faq.a: Practise template editing: rewrite the middle sentence of a canned reply for a specific customer in under 30 seconds, then check it for typos. That is the real task.

faq.q: Are there tests for chat support roles?
faq.a: Often yes, usually a short typing test plus a written role-play. The role-play is the deciding part, which is why tone and clarity practice matters as much as WPM.

pages.tldr: Voice support: 30-40 WPM for notes. Email support: 40-50 WPM. Live chat: 45-60 WPM because you type the conversation, often two at once. Accuracy and tone matter more than raw speed in every channel.

pages.title: 30-Day Typing Plan — Day by Day, 15 Minutes a Day
pages.metaDesc: A 30-day typing plan with a daily drill, a weekly checkpoint and honest expected gains: 5-15 WPM for beginners, 3-6 for anyone already past 60.
pages.heroP: Fifteen minutes a day for thirty days, with a checkpoint every Sunday. The plan changes what you practise each week because the cause of slow typing changes as you get faster.

seo.h2: The daily block (15 minutes)
p:
• 2 min warm-up - one 60-second round at a comfortable pace, no target.
  • 8 min drill - whatever the week prescribes, in 60- or 120-second rounds.
  • 3 min accuracy round - slow to 85% of your pace and aim for zero errors.
  • 2 min log - net WPM, accuracy, and one sentence on what felt wrong.
The log is not bureaucracy. Fifteen minutes of daily data tells you whether the plan is working in week two, instead of leaving you guessing at day thirty.

seo.h2: Week 1 — remove the two habits that cap speed
p: Drill: covered-keyboard rounds and no-backspace rounds, alternating. One round with your hands covered, one round where a mistake is not corrected - just keep going. Both feel wrong for three days.

Checkpoint: accuracy should be above 92% by day seven, and your no-backspace score should be within 3 WPM of your normal score. If it is not, the corrections are costing you more than they are worth, which is the whole point of the week.

seo.h2: Week 2 — make the home row automatic
p: Drill: home-row and top-row drills, plus one round of pangrams a day (they touch every letter). Type slowly enough that you never look down - slow and correct beats fast and corrected.
Checkpoint: by day fourteen you should be able to type a full sentence without glancing at the keyboard. Speed usually rises 3-8 WPM in this week without any deliberate speed work.

seo.h2: Week 3 — accuracy at speed, punctuation and digits
p: Drill: 30-second sprints at maximum speed followed by a slow accuracy round, three pairs per session. Add one Numbers round and one punctuation-heavy round (quotes) every other day.
Checkpoint: your sprint peak should be 10-15 WPM above your sustainable pace. If the two are equal, you are not pushing; if accuracy collapses in the sprint, you are pushing past control.

seo.h2: Week 4 — full length and consistency
p: Drill: five-minute rounds, three per session, no pause. Then one ten-minute round on the final two days. Score the lowest round of the three, not the highest - that is the number an employer would see on a bad day.
Checkpoint: compare day 30 against day 1 on the same test length. Beginners typically gain 5-15 WPM, people already above 60 typically gain 3-6. Both are real; neither is a guarantee.

seo.h2: What to do on day 31
p: Drop to maintenance: five minutes, four days a week, one full test a month. Most of what you gained stays if you keep typing daily at work or in messages; the part that fades is the deliberate accuracy habit.
If you want to keep climbing, the next project is look-ahead reading - see the 50 WPM plan for the drills that break a plateau, and the WPM chart to see which cause applies at your band.

faq.q: Can you really improve typing in 30 days?
faq.a: Yes, by 5-15 WPM if you are starting below 50, and 3-6 WPM if you are already over 60. The gains come from removing habits, not from talent.

faq.q: How long should each session be?
faq.a: Fifteen minutes a day. The plan is built around 2 minutes warm-up, 8 minutes drill, 3 minutes accuracy and 2 minutes logging.

faq.q: What if I miss a day?
faq.a: Continue where you left off rather than restarting. The weeks are ordered by cause, not by calendar; a missed day costs nothing, a missed week means repeating that week's checkpoint.

faq.q: Do I need special software?
faq.a: No. Timed rounds, a covered keyboard (a cloth works), and a note of your scores are enough. The drill content matters more than the tool.

faq.q: When should I stop the plan?
faq.a: At day 30, then switch to maintenance: five minutes, four days a week. Deliberate practice has diminishing returns once your habits are clean.

pages.tldr: Weeks 1-2: stop looking down and stop backspacing. Week 3: accuracy at speed, punctuation and digits. Week 4: full-length tests and consistency. Expected: 5-15 WPM if you are new, 3-6 if you are already over 60.

howto.description: A 15-minutes-a-day plan that changes what you practise each week because the cause of slow typing changes as you get faster.

steps.name: Week 1: remove the two habits that cap speed
steps.text: Alternate covered-keyboard rounds with no-backspace rounds for 15 minutes a day. Accuracy targets: above 92% by day seven.

steps.name: Week 2: make the home row automatic
steps.text: Home-row and top-row drills plus one pangram round daily, typed slowly enough that you never look down.

steps.name: Week 3: accuracy at speed
steps.text: Three pairs of 30-second maximum-speed sprints followed by a slow accuracy round, plus one numbers and one punctuation round every other day.

steps.name: Week 4: full length and consistency

pages.title: Typing Test for Court Clerks — Case Numbers & Filings
pages.metaDesc: Court clerk work is docket entry: case numbers, filing codes, party names. Usually 45-55 WPM with near-perfect accuracy on identifiers and dates.
pages.heroP: A court clerk types case numbers, filing codes, party names and dates into a docket system all day. The speed bar is moderate — 45 to 55 WPM — but an identifier typed wrong creates a filing that cannot be found.

seo.h2: What the job types
p: A docket entry looks like this: a case number with a year and a court code, a filing type from a fixed list, the filing party, a date, and a short description. Almost every field is either a code or a proper noun, and several are checked against an existing record.

That shape matters for practice. Copying prose trains sentence rhythm; docket entry trains short alphanumeric bursts with a verification step after each field. The second is what the job actually rewards.

seo.h2: Why identifiers dominate the error budget
p: A misspelt word in a note is readable. A case number with a transposed digit is a filing that cannot be retrieved by the parties who need it, and fixing it usually requires a correction entry and a supervisor.

• Case numbers - alphanumeric with a year and a court or division code.
  • Dates - filing date, hearing date, deadline; format depends on the court.
  • Party names - often unusual spellings, and never autocorrected.
  • Filing codes - short, similar-looking, and chosen from a list rather than typed freehand.

seo.h2: The drill that transfers
p: Type a case number, check it character by character, then type the next one. Ten repetitions of the same number beat one pass through ten different numbers, because the goal is a verification habit rather than exposure to variety.

Then add the field-switching behaviour: case number, Tab, filing type, Tab, date, Enter. Real docket systems move between fields, and typing a clean number followed by a wrong Tab is a lost record just the same.

seo.h2: Speed bands and what they clear
p:
BandClearsNotes
35-45 WPMEntry-level clerk-typist titlesUsually paired with a data-entry exercise
45-55 WPMMost court clerk and deputy clerk postingsThe common advertised band
55+ WPMHigh-volume filing desksAccuracy floor matters more than the extra speed

Public-sector postings often state the requirement in net WPM on a five-minute sample, and some require a proctored certificate. Check the notice: the wording tells you which document they will accept.

faq.q: What typing speed do court clerks need?
faq.a: Usually 45-55 WPM with high accuracy, and often on a five-minute proctored sample. The accuracy requirement is strict because a wrong case number creates an unretrievable filing.

faq.q: Is court clerk work mostly typing?
faq.a: A large part of it is docket entry and filing, which is typing in short alphanumeric bursts. The rest is checking documents, answering counter enquiries and managing records.

faq.q: Do I need a certificate to apply?
faq.a: Some jurisdictions require a proctored typing certificate with a stated speed and date; others accept self-certification and test later. The posting states which, and the wording is usually explicit.

faq.q: How do I practise case-number accuracy?
faq.a: Type the same number ten times, checking character by character after each attempt, then move to a new one. Repetition builds the verification habit that prevents transposition errors.

faq.q: Does legal terminology matter?
faq.a: Somewhat. You need to recognise filing types and party designations, but you select codes rather than compose text, so accuracy matters more than vocabulary.

pages.tldr: Court clerk postings commonly ask 45-55 WPM with high accuracy. The critical skill is error-free entry of case numbers, dates and party names, not prose speed. Practise alphanumeric strings and verify every entry against the source.

pages.title: Typing Test for Medical Receptionists — Speed & IDs
pages.metaDesc: Front-desk clinic roles usually ask 40-50 WPM while handling patient IDs, insurance numbers and appointment slots. What to rehearse and why digits decide it.
pages.heroP: Medical reception is typing with a queue: patient names, dates of birth, insurance IDs and appointment slots, entered while someone waits. Clinics commonly ask 40–50 WPM, and the failure mode is always a digit.

seo.h2: What the front desk actually enters
p: A registration is a form: name, date of birth, address, phone, insurance carrier, member ID, group number, reason for visit. Between six and eight of those fields are numeric or alphanumeric, and two of them (date of birth and member ID) are the ones that cause billing rejections when mistyped.
The typing is short and interrupted. That combination — many short entries, frequent interruptions — is why front-desk staff who type 50 WPM in a test can still feel slow on a Monday morning.

seo.h2: Why digits decide the outcome
p: Letters can be inferred from context; digits cannot. A member ID with two digits swapped is rejected by the clearing house weeks later, and the correction costs the practice more than the registration did.

• Dates of birth - format-sensitive, and a common source of duplicate patient records.
  • Insurance member IDs - alphanumeric, often 10-15 characters with no internal logic to catch an error.
  • Phone numbers - ten digits, typed while the patient is still talking.
  • Appointment times - a single digit decides whether someone arrives at 9 or 19 past the hour.

seo.h2: A rehearsal that matches the desk
p: Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, graded on errors. Then a form drill: type a mock registration (name, DOB, phone, member ID) ten times and count how many are completely clean. Three clean records in a row is the realistic readiness bar.
Add the interruption: type half a record, look away for five seconds, then finish it. That is the actual working condition, and it is where the errors appear in practice rather than in a quiet test.

seo.h2: Practical notes for the interview
p: If asked for a speed, quote net WPM with accuracy and test length, and mention numeric entry separately if you have a figure. A clinic manager reads the accuracy number first, because they have seen what a mistyped member ID costs.
Ask which practice-management system they use. The typing skill transfers; the keyboard shortcuts do not, and knowing the system name tells you what the first week will feel like.

faq.q: What typing speed do medical receptionists need?
faq.a: Most clinic postings ask 40-50 WPM with accuracy above 97%. Medical and dental front desks sit at the top of that band because patient identifiers must be exact.

faq.q: Is medical terminology required?
faq.a: Basic familiarity helps for reason-for-visit fields, but you select from lists more often than you compose. Accuracy on names, dates and insurance numbers matters more.

faq.q: How can I improve accuracy on numbers?
faq.a: Two minutes of numeric practice daily, graded on errors rather than speed, plus a form drill where you type the same mock registration ten times and count clean records.

faq.q: Will they test my typing in the interview?
faq.a: Sometimes, usually a short online test or a timed registration exercise. Larger practices and hospital groups are more likely to test formally.

faq.q: Does speed matter more than system knowledge?
faq.a: No. Speed is a floor; knowing the practice-management system and the registration workflow is what makes someone fast in the first month.

pages.tldr: Most clinic front-desk postings ask 40-50 WPM with 97%+ accuracy. Patient identifiers and insurance numbers are numeric-heavy, so practise the Numbers mode and alphanumeric strings rather than prose.

pages.title: Typing Test for Insurance Claims — Codes & Accuracy
pages.metaDesc: Claims processing is code entry: policy numbers, loss codes, amounts. Usually 45-55 WPM with 98%+ accuracy on identifiers and figures, not prose speed.
pages.heroP: Claims work is code entry under a queue: policy numbers, claim references, loss codes, reserve amounts. The advertised speed is modest — 45 to 55 WPM — and the accuracy expectation is the strictest in clerical work.

seo.h2: The shape of a claim entry
p: A first-notice-of-loss record is a fixed form: policy number, insured name, date of loss, loss type code, description, estimated reserve, adjuster assignment. Two of those fields are money, three are codes, one is narrative. The narrative is the only part where prose typing helps.
That ratio is why claims processors who type 50 WPM with clean digits outperform colleagues at 65 WPM who need corrections. The queue measures completed, correct records.

seo.h2: Where errors actually cost money
p:
• Reserve amounts - a misplaced decimal changes a reserve by a factor of ten.
  • Policy numbers - alphanumeric, no checksum you can rely on, and a wrong digit attaches the claim to the wrong policyholder.
  • Loss codes - similar-looking categories where a mis-selection routes the claim to the wrong team.
  • Dates of loss - coverage windows depend on them, so a wrong year can void a valid claim.

seo.h2: How to train for it
p: Two minutes of Numbers mode daily, then a record drill: type a mock claim (policy, date, code, amount) ten times, verify against the source each time, and count clean records. Target three consecutive clean records before you claim the skill.

Practise decimal placement deliberately. Type amounts with two decimal places and a thousands separator until the pattern is automatic, because that is the field where a single keystroke has the largest consequence.

seo.h2: Bands and adjacent roles
p: Claims processing usually advertises 45-55 WPM with 98% accuracy. Related roles differ: medical billing sits at 45-55 with 98%, data entry is quoted in keystrokes per hour at 8,000-12,000, and customer service claims handling drops to 35-45 because the work is more conversation than entry.
If a posting quotes keystrokes per hour instead of WPM, convert before deciding whether you qualify — 10,000 KPH is about 33 WPM, which is a different test from a 50 WPM prose reading.

faq.q: What typing speed do insurance claims jobs need?
faq.a: Usually 45-55 WPM with accuracy of 98% or better. Codes, amounts and policy numbers dominate the work, so numeric accuracy is the deciding factor.

faq.q: Is claims processing a typing job?
faq.a: A large part of it is data entry into a claims system, alongside document review and correspondence. The entry is short, coded and repeated, rather than long-form typing.

faq.q: Why is 98% accuracy required?
faq.a: A wrong reserve amount, policy number or loss date can misroute a claim, delay payment or change a reserve by a factor of ten. Corrections are expensive and sometimes regulated.

faq.q: How do I practise decimal amounts?
faq.a: Type amounts with two decimals and a thousands separator until the pattern is automatic, then add the surrounding fields (policy number, date, code) so you practise the field-switching as well.

faq.q: Does claims experience matter more than typing speed?
faq.a: Yes for the role, no for the screening test. Employers test the typing floor because it is cheap to measure; the job itself is judged on accuracy and turnaround.

pages.tldr: Claims processor postings typically ask 45-55 WPM with 98%+ accuracy. Almost every field is a code, an amount or an identifier, so numeric and alphanumeric accuracy decides performance, not prose speed.

pages.title: Typing Test for Warehouse Admin — SKUs & Labels
pages.metaDesc: Warehouse admin types SKUs, quantities, carrier references and addresses. Usually 35-45 WPM, but speed matters less than not mistyping a SKU or a postcode.
pages.heroP: Warehouse administration is SKUs, quantities, carrier references and addresses. The speed bar is low — 35 to 45 WPM — but a mistyped SKU or postcode sends the wrong item to the wrong place.

seo.h2: What the work looks like
p: A goods-in entry is a purchase order reference, a SKU list with quantities, a supplier and a date. A dispatch entry is an order reference, a carrier, a tracking number, a postcode and a weight. Both are short fields typed at speed while a vehicle waits.

Because the rhythm is driven by the dock rather than the screen, the typical failure is not slow typing but a skipped field or a transposed digit in a postcode. Speed matters mainly so the queue does not build.

seo.h2: Codes and postcodes are the risk
p:
• SKUs - often alphanumeric with similar-looking variants (0/O, 1/I, 5/S).
  • Postcodes - a single wrong character changes the delivery area.
  • Quantities - digits only, and an extra zero is a real cost.
  • Tracking references - long, no internal logic, and copied from a label.
Where barcode scanning exists, typing is the fallback and the audit path; where it does not, typing is the only record. Both need the same accuracy habit.

seo.h2: Practising without a warehouse
p: Two minutes of Numbers mode a day, plus an address drill: type ten postcodes and street lines, then check them character by character. Add a SKU drill with confusable characters (0/O, 1/I, 5/S) because that is where picking errors originate.
If you already work in a warehouse, copy real SKUs from a pick list rather than random strings. Familiarity with the format is what makes the practice transfer.

seo.h2: Realistic expectations
p: 35-45 WPM clears most warehouse admin postings, and many roles never test it formally — they check whether you can use the warehouse management system without errors. If a test exists, it is usually a short alphanumeric exercise.
For adjacent roles, see data entry if the work is volume entry, or alphanumeric typing for the drill that matches SKU and postcode content.

faq.q: What typing speed do warehouse admin jobs need?
faq.a: Usually 35-45 WPM. Many roles do not test formally; they check whether you can enter codes and quantities into the warehouse system without errors.

faq.q: Is typing or scanning more important?
faq.a: Both matter. Scanning is faster where barcodes exist, but typing is the fallback and the audit path, and quantities and exceptions are usually keyed by hand.

faq.q: How do I avoid SKU errors?
faq.a: Practise confusable characters (0/O, 1/I, 5/S) deliberately, and verify each SKU against the pick list character by character for the first weeks on the job.

faq.q: Do I need to type fast to work in logistics?
faq.a: No. The dock sets the pace, and accuracy determines whether the queue clears. 35-45 WPM with clean codes is enough for most admin roles.

faq.q: What should I practise first?
faq.a: Numbers and postcodes. They are the fields with real-world consequences, and they are where untrained typists lose accuracy first.

pages.tldr: Warehouse and logistics admin roles usually ask 35-45 WPM with strong accuracy on codes and postcodes. Practise alphanumeric strings and addresses rather than prose; scanning workflows mean the typing is short and repetitive.
