These are not measurements of a population; they are what employers and certifying bodies publish. Two employers in the same sector commonly differ by ten WPM, so read the posting rather than the table. Detail per role: typing speed requirements by job.

seo.h2: What is not on this page, and why
p: There is no average speed by country, no average by gender, and no "average for a 12-year-old" figure here, because we could not find a primary measurement for them that we were willing to cite. Sites that publish those numbers rarely link a study.
There is also no traffic or leaderboard statistic: this site stores results in the visitor's browser, so it has no server-side dataset to aggregate and will not pretend to have one.

seo.h2: How to cite this page
p: Preferred form: "Typing.Rerivo, Typing Speed Benchmarks, https://typing.rerivo.com/typing-speed-benchmarks.html (accessed DATE)". The underlying numbers should be cited to the papers above, not to this page - the page is a convenient summary, not the source.
If you reuse the CSV, keep the column names and note that the percentile column is a normal approximation of the CHI 2018 distribution.

faq.q: What is the average typing speed in 2026?
faq.a: 51.56 WPM on a desktop keyboard, from the CHI 2018 study of 168,960 volunteers. On a phone the measured average is 36.17 WPM from a 37,370-person study.

faq.q: What percentile is 60 WPM?
faq.a: About the 66th on desktop. The percentile curve here is a normal approximation of the CHI 2018 distribution (mean 51.56, SD 20.2), validated against the study's reported deciles.

faq.q: Can I download the data?
faq.a: Yes - typing-speed-benchmarks.csv has 25 rows at 5 WPM steps with percentile, CPM and keystrokes per hour. Reuse it with attribution to Typing.Rerivo and the original papers.

faq.q: Why are there two different averages on different sites?
faq.a: Older sources quote about 40 WPM from small office-worker samples; the 51.56 WPM figure comes from a 168,960-person online sample. Both describe real populations but not the same one.

faq.q: Is the phone number comparable to the desktop number?
faq.a: Yes, unusually so: both studies used the same transcription task and the mobile paper compares itself to the desktop one directly, reporting about 15 WPM difference.

pages.title: German Typing Test — Umlaute, ß und QWERTZ
pages.metaDesc: German typing test with real sentences: ä ö ü ß, QWERTZ layout, comma rules. Measures Wörter pro Minute and Anschläge pro Minute. No sign up.
pages.heroP: Real German sentences with the characters that actually slow typists down: ä, ö, ü, ß and the comma-heavy clause structure. Works on a QWERTZ keyboard, no sign up, results stay in your browser.

seo.h2: What makes German different to type
p: German adds four characters that English does not use: ä, ö, ü and ß. On a QWERTZ keyboard they sit on dedicated keys to the right of P and L, so they need a reach rather than a modifier - which means they interrupt the hand position less than a Shift combination, but they are pressed less often and therefore practised less.

The second difference is length. German compounds produce long words (Geschwindigkeitsmessung, Tastaturbelegung), and long words mean more consecutive keystrokes per word with no space to reset the hand. Typists who are comfortable at 60 WPM on English often measure 50-55 on German text at the same accuracy.

seo.h2: Wörter pro Minute und Anschläge pro Minute
p: German-language typing tests usually report two figures. Wörter pro Minute (WPM) counts five characters as one word, the same convention used in English. Anschläge pro Minute (CPM, sometimes Zeichen pro Minute) counts every character, which is what German office job adverts often quote.

Anschläge/MinWörter/MinEinordnung
15030Anfangsniveau, Übung nötig
20040Solide für Büroarbeit
25050Gut, über dem Durchschnitt
30060Schnell, für Sekretariat und Datenerfassung
40080Sehr schnell, obere 10%
The conversion is arithmetic: WPM = Anschläge ÷ 5. Nothing about German text changes the formula, only the character mix.

seo.h2: QWERTZ, and why your layout matters
p: German-speaking countries use QWERTZ: Y and Z are swapped relative to QWERTY, and the umlauts sit on their own keys. If you type on a QWERTZ keyboard, this test works as-is, because the browser reports the character your operating system produces, not the physical key.

If you are learning German on a QWERTY keyboard, enable the German layout in your operating system before practising. Typing German text on an English layout means hunting for the umlauts, which trains the wrong habit and produces a score that does not transfer.

seo.h2: How to practise
p: Start with one-minute rounds on sentences, then move to five minutes once accuracy holds above 97%. German rewards rhythm more than speed: the comma clauses give you natural places to breathe, and typists who rush through them accumulate errors on the endings.

If your goal is a specific job, check what the advert quotes. Office and Verwaltung roles typically ask 200-300 Anschläge pro Minute; Datenerfassung is quoted in keystrokes per hour, which you can convert on the WPM to KPH converter.
For the general benchmarks behind these bands, see the average typing speed page; for the English version of this test, English typing test.

faq.q: What is a good German typing speed?
faq.a: 200-250 Anschläge pro Minute (40-50 Wörter pro Minute) is solid for office work. Office and administrative roles commonly ask 200-300, and data entry is quoted in keystrokes per hour.

faq.q: Does this test work on a QWERTZ keyboard?
faq.a: Yes. The test compares the characters your operating system produces, so a German layout with umlauts and ß on their own keys works without configuration.

faq.q: Why is my German speed lower than my English speed?
faq.a: German compounds produce longer words with more consecutive keystrokes, and the umlauts are pressed less often than letters, so they stay less practised. A 10% drop at equal accuracy is normal.

faq.q: How do I type ä ö ü ß?
faq.a: On a QWERTZ keyboard they have their own keys to the right of P and L. On a QWERTY keyboard, add the German layout in your OS settings rather than using Alt codes, which do not train the correct motion.

faq.q: How many WPM is 200 Anschläge pro Minute?
faq.a: Forty words per minute. Anschläge ÷ 5 = Wörter pro Minute, the same five-characters-per-word convention used by English typing tests.

pages.tldr: Type real German text and get Wörter pro Minute (WPM) plus Anschläge pro Minute (CPM). Umlauts and ß are separate keys on QWERTZ, and they are where most errors appear. 200-250 Anschläge pro Minute is a solid office speed.

pages.title: French Typing Test — Accents, ç and AZERTY
pages.metaDesc: French typing test with real sentences: é è ê à ç ù œ and French punctuation spacing. Measures mots par minute and caractères par minute. No sign up.
pages.heroP: Real French text with the characters that decide accuracy: é, è, ê, à, ç, ù, œ and the space before a colon. Works on an AZERTY keyboard, and the score is reported in mots par minute and caractères par minute.

seo.h2: What makes French different to type
p: Three things. First, accents: é, è, ê, à, ç and ù each have their own key on AZERTY, and œ (as in cœur) is a separate character again. Second, punctuation spacing: French typography puts a space before : ; ! ? and inside guillemets, so a correct sentence has more keystrokes than the English equivalent.

Third, apostrophes. French elides constantly (l'oiseau, qu'il, d'accord), and the apostrophe key on AZERTY sits on the fourth row, reached with the right little finger. That single reach accounts for a large share of errors in French typing tests.

seo.h2: Mots par minute et caractères par minute
p: French tests report mots par minute (MPM) and caractères par minute (CPM). The word count uses five characters per word, the same convention as English, so a French and an English score are comparable - provided both tests count characters the same way.

Caractères/MinMots/MinRepère
15030Débutant, entraînement nécessaire
20040Correct pour le travail de bureau
25050Bon, au-dessus de la moyenne
30060Rapide, secrétariat et saisie
40080Très rapide, 10% supérieurs

seo.h2: AZERTY, and the space-before-colon habit
p: French keyboards are AZERTY: A and Q swap, Z and W swap, M moves next to L, and the accented letters replace the number row. If you use an AZERTY keyboard, this test works directly, because the browser receives the character your system produces.

The detail that catches people is the space before double punctuation. A French sentence writes « Bonjour : voici » with a space before the colon, not « Bonjour: voici ». Typing tests that use real French text include that space, and typists trained on English punctuation lose accuracy on it until they notice.

seo.h2: How to practise, and what jobs ask for
p: One-minute rounds first, then five minutes once accuracy is above 97%. Add a round with quotes once a week, because that is where the guillemets and the double punctuation appear together.

French office and secrétariat postings commonly quote 40-50 mots par minute, and some public-sector concours include a bureautique exercise rather than a formal typing score. Saisie de données roles are quoted in caractères par minute or keystrokes per hour - convert with the WPM to KPH converter.
For benchmarks across languages, see average typing speed; for the English version, English typing test.

faq.q: What is a good French typing speed?
faq.a: 40-50 mots par minute (200-250 caractères par minute) is solid for office work. Secretarial and data-entry roles often ask for 50-60 MPM, with accuracy above 97%.

faq.q: Does this test work on an AZERTY keyboard?
faq.a: Yes. The test compares the characters your operating system produces, so accented letters and ç work directly on an AZERTY layout without configuration.

faq.q: Why does French punctuation slow me down?
faq.a: French typography requires a space before : ; ! ? and uses guillemets, which adds keystrokes. If you learned English punctuation, the extra space is a habit you have to build.

faq.q: How do I type œ and the accents?
faq.a: On AZERTY, accents have their own keys and œ is typed with a dedicated combination. Add the French layout in your OS settings rather than using Alt codes, which do not train the right motion.

faq.q: How many words per minute is 250 caractères?
faq.a: Fifty mots par minute. Characters ÷ 5 = words, the same convention used by English typing tests, so the two scores are comparable.

pages.tldr: Type real French and get mots par minute (MPM) plus caractères par minute. Accents are separate keys on AZERTY, and French punctuation puts a space before : ; ! ? — that spacing is part of the test. 40-50 MPM is a solid office speed.

pages.title: Touch Typing Course — 12 Lessons, 15 Minutes a Day
pages.metaDesc: A 12-lesson touch typing course with a drill and a pass criterion for each lesson. Home row to full sentences in four to six weeks, no account needed.
pages.heroP: Twelve lessons, each with one drill and one pass criterion. You start on the home row and finish typing full sentences without looking, in four to six weeks at 15 minutes a day. No account, no software to install.

seo.h2: Before lesson 1: set up, and accept the dip
p: Sit so your elbows are near 90 degrees, feet flat, screen at eye level. Put the keyboard flat, not tilted. Find the two bumps on F and J with your index fingers, and rest your thumbs on the spacebar.

Expect to get slower for the first week. Typing with ten fingers means abandoning a system that already works, and the new one takes about 300-500 repetitions per key before it stops needing attention. That dip is the cost of the ceiling you are removing, not a sign that it is not working.

seo.h2: Lessons 1-4: the rows
p:
LessonDrillPass criterion
1. Home rowasdf jkl; repeated, hands covered for the last two rounds95% accuracy, no looking down
2. Home row + G, HWords built only from asdfghjkl;95% accuracy at 20 WPM
3. Top rowqwerty uiop added, one minute at a time95% accuracy, 25 WPM
4. Bottom rowzxcvbnm added, then full alphabet words95% accuracy, 30 WPM
Cover your hands for at least one round per lesson. Looking down is the habit that caps most people at 35-40 WPM, and it is far easier to prevent now than to break at 60.

seo.h2: Lessons 5-8: capitals, punctuation, digits, letter pairs
p:
• 5. Capitals. Shift with the hand that is not typing the letter. Drill sentence case until the Shift press stops breaking rhythm.
  • 6. Punctuation. Full stops, commas, apostrophes and question marks in real sentences, not lists of symbols.
  • 7. Digits. Reach the number row with the correct finger. This is the slowest lesson for most adults and the one data-entry work actually needs.
  • 8. Letter pairs. th, he, in, er, an, re, on, at. Practising transitions moves 40-60 WPM faster than practising words, because that is where the hand movement lives.
Pass criteria for this block: 96% accuracy on a two-minute round with capitals and punctuation intact, and 97% on a one-minute numbers round.

seo.h2: Lessons 9-12: words, sentences, control, test
p:
LessonDrillPass criterion
9. WordsTop 200 common words, typed as whole units40 WPM at 97%
10. SentencesThree-minute rounds, normal text45 WPM at 97%
11. Speed control30-second sprints at maximum, then a slow accuracy roundSprint peak 10-15 WPM above your sustainable pace
12. Full testFive-minute net score, unfamiliar keyboard if possibleA number you can reproduce twice
Lesson 12 is not about hitting a target. It is about being able to reproduce a score, because that is what an employer's test will ask of you.

seo.h2: How long this actually takes
p: For an adult starting from two-finger typing: home row secure in one to two weeks, all rows in three to four, and full sentences without looking in four to six. Reaching 60 WPM usually takes two to four months after that, because speed comes from accuracy plus repetition rather than from pushing.
Children need longer on the motor side and shorter on the reading side. The published classroom bands put grade 5 at roughly 25-35 WPM, which matches the same lesson path at a slower pace.

seo.h2: Why this order, and what the evidence says
p: The order is rows first, then modifiers, then transitions. Rows build the map; modifiers build the reach; transitions build speed. Skipping to sentences before the map is automatic produces the hunt-and-peck pattern with extra steps.

One published finding is worth knowing: Feit, Weir and Oulasvirta (CHI 2016, doi.org/10.1145/2858036.2858233) found that consistent finger use and preparing the next keypress predict typing speed more than which specific finger presses which key. That is why the drills here emphasise not looking and rhythmic preparation over rigid finger doctrine.
Lesson 1 assumes you can already find the home row; if you cannot, spend a week on keyboard practice first and come back.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn touch typing?
faq.a: Four to six weeks at 15 minutes a day gets an adult from two-finger typing to full sentences without looking. Reaching 60 WPM typically takes another two to four months of regular practice.

faq.q: Do I have to use the exact fingers?
faq.a: Close to it. Research on typists (Feit et al., CHI 2016) found that consistent finger use and preparing the next keypress predict speed more than which specific finger presses which key - so consistency matters more than doctrine.

faq.q: Why am I slower after starting?
faq.a: You are replacing a working habit with an unfamiliar one. The dip lasts one to two weeks; the ceiling it removes (around 35-40 WPM for two-finger typing) never comes back.

faq.q: Should I cover my hands?
faq.a: For at least one round per lesson. Looking down is the habit that caps speed, and preventing it is much easier than breaking it later.

faq.q: Does this course need an account?
faq.a: No. Lessons run in the browser, results stay on your device, and there is nothing to install. Each lesson links to the test mode it needs.

pages.tldr: Lessons 1-4: home row, then top row, then bottom row, then all letters. Lessons 5-8: capitals, punctuation, digits, common letter pairs. Lessons 9-12: words, sentences, speed control, and a full test. Pass a lesson at 95% accuracy before moving on.

pages.title: Typing Consistency Score — What It Means and How to Raise It
pages.metaDesc: Consistency measures how much your speed varies per second. The exact formula this site uses, how to read the number, and three drills to raise it.
pages.heroP: Two typists can average 60 WPM and be very different: one runs 58-62 the whole minute, the other swings between 40 and 80. Consistency is the figure that separates them, and it predicts your five-minute score better than your peak does.

seo.h2: The exact definition used here
p: Speed is sampled once per second during the round. Let those samples be a series of speeds with mean m. Consistency is one minus the coefficient of variation, expressed as a percentage:
consistency = 100 × (1 − standard deviation ÷ mean)

So a round that holds 60 WPM with a standard deviation of 3 reads 95. A round that averages 60 but swings with a standard deviation of 12 reads 80. It is clamped to 0-100, and a round with fewer than two samples reports 100 rather than an error.
The number appears in the results panel as Consistency (labeled 安定度 / 稳定性 / استحکام in other interface languages) and in the share image.

seo.h2: Why it is worth looking at
p: Average WPM is an average of a curve, and the curve has shape. A typist whose speed collapses in the last ten seconds has a stamina problem; one whose speed spikes at the start and settles has a pacing problem; one whose speed oscillates throughout is reading word by word instead of ahead.

Consistency separates those cases. It also explains a common frustration: two people with the same one-minute score can have completely different five-minute scores, and the one with the higher consistency usually keeps more of it.

seo.h2: Reading the number
p:
ConsistencyWhat it looks likeWhat to do
90-100Nearly flat; the average is the truthNothing - work on speed instead
80-89Mild variation, usually around difficult wordsDrill the words that cause the dips
70-79Visible dips; the average overstates your sustainable paceSlow down 10% and hold it for a full minute
under 70Large swings, often burst-then-recoverAccuracy work first; the swings are usually corrections

seo.h2: Three drills that raise it
p:
1. Metronome typing. Type to a steady rhythm - one word per beat - for 30 seconds. The goal is not speed but flatness; you will feel the urges to sprint and to recover.
  2. Slow-hold rounds. Pick a pace you can hold for the entire round without a single sprint, and finish at exactly that pace. Most typists discover their sustainable pace is 10-15% below their peak.
  3. Dip hunting. After a round, look at the graph and find the lowest second. Type the words around that point again, slowly. Dips concentrate on the same few sequences - usually one hand doing two awkward reaches.

seo.h2: Where consistency is not the right metric
p: On very short rounds (15 seconds) there are too few samples for the figure to mean much. On very hard text, low consistency is expected and correct - the dips are the difficulty, not a technique failure.
For benchmarking, keep using net WPM plus accuracy. Consistency is a diagnostic for how you got the number, not a replacement for it.

faq.q: What is a good typing consistency score?
faq.a: Above 85 is steady, 90+ is nearly flat. Below 70 means your speed swings enough that the average overstates what you can sustain over five minutes.

faq.q: How is consistency calculated?
faq.a: One minus the coefficient of variation of your per-second WPM, as a percentage: 100 × (1 − standard deviation ÷ mean). It is clamped to 0-100.

faq.q: Does consistency matter more than speed?
faq.a: For sustained work, yes. A steady 55 holds up over a ten-minute test; a spiky 60 often drops to 48. For passing a short screening test, speed matters more.

faq.q: Why is my consistency low even when my accuracy is high?
faq.a: Accuracy measures errors, consistency measures rhythm. You can be accurate and still accelerate and stall, usually because you read word by word rather than looking ahead.

faq.q: Which drill helps most?
faq.a: Slow-hold rounds: pick a pace you can maintain for the whole round and finish at exactly that pace. It teaches the difference between peak and sustainable speed.

pages.tldr: Consistency = 100 × (1 − the coefficient of variation of your per-second WPM). 100 means a perfectly flat speed; 80 means your speed varies by about 20% around its average. Above 85 is steady; below 70 means the average is being dragged down by dips.

pages.title: Why Am I Stuck at the Same Typing Speed? Five Causes
pages.metaDesc: If your WPM has not moved in months, the cause depends on where you are stuck. Five plateaus by band - 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 - and the drill for each.
crumbs: Why Am I Stuck at the Same Typing Speed
pages.h1: Why Am I Stuck at the Same Typing Speed?
pages.heroP: A plateau is not one problem. Where you are stuck tells you what is stuck: at 40 it is usually the look-at-keyboard habit, at 60 it is corrections, at 80 it is consistency. Here is the diagnosis by band.

seo.h2: First, check that you are actually stuck
p: Measure the same way three times: same length, same text mode, same time of day. If the three scores sit within 3 WPM, you are consistent and the plateau is real. If they swing by 10, you do not have a plateau - you have noisy measurement, and the fix is a fixed protocol rather than a new drill.

Then check the length. A one-minute score improves faster than a five-minute score, so a plateau on a five-minute test looks like progress on a one-minute one. Decide which number you are tracking and stay with it.

seo.h2: Stuck at 30-40: the habit ceiling
p: Almost always two habits: looking at the keyboard, and backspacing through every slip. Both are cheap to fix and both feel worse before they feel better.

• Covered rounds: hands hidden, 30 seconds, once a day. Expect accuracy to drop 10-20% for a week.
  • No-backspace rounds: finish with mistakes in them. Most people at this level gain 3-5 WPM immediately.

seo.h2: Stuck at 50: the reading bottleneck
p: At 50 WPM your fingers are no longer the limit; your eyes are. You read the word you are about to type, so the hands wait for the eyes on every word. Faster typists read one to three words ahead and let the hands run on a buffer.

Drill: before starting a line, read it silently once, then type it without re-reading. It feels wrong for three rounds and then it stops feeling wrong. Add 15-second bursts to raise your top end, because a 50 average with a 55 peak has no room to grow.

seo.h2: Stuck at 60: the accuracy tax
p: At 60 WPM a 2% error rate costs about 5-6 net WPM over a five-minute test. That is the arithmetic that keeps people at 55-60 for months: they gain speed, lose accuracy, and net out where they started.

Drill: 30-second rounds at 90% of your maximum, with an error budget of one. Stop the round when the budget is blown rather than pushing to the timer. The skill being trained is accuracy at speed, which is different from accuracy at rest.

seo.h2: Stuck at 70-80: variance, not peak
p: Above 70 the ceiling is consistency. Ten rounds might range from 68 to 84; the average is 74 and the peak is irrelevant. Narrowing the spread is what raises the average.

Drill: type ten one-minute rounds and record all ten. Work on the lowest quintile - the rounds where you were tired, distracted or on a hard passage. Slow-hold rounds (pick a pace, hold it exactly) and hard-text rounds do more here than any speed drill.

seo.h2: If none of that applies
p: Then the constraint is probably outside the keyboard: sleep, screen position, keyboard feel, or the fact that you only practise in one-minute bursts and never test endurance. Try one ten-minute round a week - many "plateaus" turn out to be a stamina problem that a short test cannot see.
The band-by-band plans are on the 40, 50, 60 and 70 WPM pages; the diagnostic line is consistency.

faq.q: Why has my typing speed not improved in months?
faq.a: Usually because the practice repeats what you already do well. Plateaus have band-specific causes: habits at 40, reading ahead at 50, error tax at 60, variance at 70+.

faq.q: How often should I practise to break a plateau?
faq.a: Ten to fifteen minutes a day, with one variable changed per week. Longer sessions at the same routine mostly build fatigue.

faq.q: Does a new keyboard help?
faq.a: Slightly, and briefly. A mechanical keyboard can be worth 3-8 WPM for some typists, but it will not break a plateau caused by looking down or reading word by word.

faq.q: Should I switch to Dvorak or Colemak?
faq.a: Not to break a plateau. The switch costs weeks of being slower, and most people return to the same speed on the new layout because the limiting habit moved with them.

faq.q: How long does a plateau usually last?
faq.a: Two to six weeks if you change the drill, months if you keep repeating the same practice. The signal that a drill is working is accuracy rising before speed does.

pages.webAppName: Why Am I Stuck at the Same Typing Speed?

bcItems.name: Why Am I Stuck at the Same Typing Speed

pages.tldr: Stuck at 30-40: you look at the keyboard or backspace too much. At 50: you read one word at a time. At 60: errors, not speed, are the limit. At 70-80: variance, not peak, holds the average down. Each has a different drill.

pages.title: Best Keyboard Layout for Programmers — Symbols First
pages.metaDesc: Code is punctuation with words attached, so the layout question is about brackets. How QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and Programmer Dvorak compare.
pages.heroP: Programmers do not type prose, they type symbols wrapped in words. That changes the layout question: the letters are already solved, and the brackets, braces, quotes and operators are what a layout helps or hurts.

seo.h2: What code actually requires of a layout
p: A rough count of ordinary source code: letters are still the majority of characters, but the shifted symbol row ( ) { } [ ] < > ; : " ' = + - _ / \ | carries a disproportionate share of the awkward reaches, and those reaches are where errors cluster.
So the question is not "which layout is fastest for English" - it is "which layout puts the symbols you type most under the fingers that can reach them without leaving the home row".

seo.h2: The four layouts, compared
p:
LayoutLetter changesSymbol changesCost of switching
QWERTYNoneNone - symbols where every tool, shortcut and tutorial expects themZero
DvorakSubstantial reordering for English comfortNumber row rearranged; brackets movedWeeks of being slower; shortcuts assume QWERTY positions
Colemak17 keys moved; keeps Z X C V in place for shortcutsMostly unchangedWeeks, but lower than Dvorak
Programmer DvorakDvorak lettersNumber row replaced with symbols; digits shiftedHigh - digits need Shift for every number

Programmer Dvorak looks attractive on paper because symbols get the unshifted number row. In practice the digits then require Shift, which is a bad trade for anyone who types numbers - and most code contains them.

seo.h2: The honest verdict
p: For most programmers, stay on QWERTY. The reason is not that it is optimal; it is that every editor shortcut, every bracket-matching habit and every tutorial assumes it, and your bottleneck is thinking, not the 60-70 WPM you already type.

Consider a change only if all three hold: you are past 60 WPM on QWERTY, you type code for several hours a day, and your error report shows the symbol reaches as the main source of mistakes. Even then, expect a month of being slower before any gain.

seo.h2: What helps more than a layout
p:
• Practise the symbols you actually type. Bracket-and-quote drills beat layout changes by a wide margin.
  • Let the editor do the brackets. Auto-pairs, snippets and formatters remove keystrokes; a layout reorders them.
  • Learn five shortcuts properly. Duplicate line, move line, go to definition, rename symbol, format document.
Code typing pools to practise on: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, Go, SQL. The general comparison is on Dvorak vs QWERTY.

faq.q: Is Dvorak better for programming?
faq.a: Not measurably. It reorders letters for English comfort and moves brackets, which breaks shortcut muscle memory. The evidence for a coding gain is anecdotal rather than measured.

faq.q: What about Programmer Dvorak?
faq.a: It puts symbols on the unshifted number row, which sounds ideal until you need a digit - then every number requires Shift. For most codebases that is a bad trade.

faq.q: Should I learn Colemak as a programmer?
faq.a: Only if you are already past 60 WPM, type code for hours a day, and want comfort rather than speed. It keeps Z X C V in place, so shortcuts survive better than with Dvorak.

faq.q: What actually makes programmers type faster?
faq.a: Practising symbols, using snippets and formatters, and learning editor shortcuts. Layout changes come last, if at all.

faq.q: How fast do programmers type?
faq.a: Most sit at 60-90 WPM on prose and 40-55 on real code, because code is symbol-dense. No employer screens for it.

pages.tldr: No layout makes you faster at code than practice does. QWERTY keeps symbols where your muscle memory expects them; Colemak moves some letters for comfort but keeps most symbols; Programmer Dvorak rearranges the number row for symbols. Switch only after 60 WPM on QWERTY.

pages.title: Go Typing Practice — Goroutines, Errors, Interfaces
pages.metaDesc: Type real Go: channels, error wrapping, generics-free structs and methods, test helpers. Trains the punctuation Go uses on nearly every line.
pages.heroP: Go is deliberately plain, and that is what makes it a good typing drill: short declarations, braces on every line, := and error checks appear so often that they become the rhythm of the language.

seo.h2: What makes Go distinctive to type
p: Three things. Braces open on the same line as the statement, so almost every line ends with a reach to the right hand. Short declarations (:=) put the colon and equals in sequence, two keys that are not adjacent. And error checks repeat the same three-line idiom constantly, which makes it the single most valuable sequence to automate in your fingers.
The upside is regularity. Once you can type `if err != nil {` without thinking, a large fraction of Go becomes the same motion with different identifiers.

seo.h2: What is in the pool
p: Thirty-six lines of ordinary Go: a package declaration, grouped imports, a struct with a receiver method, an HTTP server start, JSON decoding with the standard error check, context with timeout, a goroutine range loop, a select, slices.SortFunc with a comparison function, sync.WaitGroup, error wrapping with %w, a type switch, a test helper with t.Fatalf, and a mutex with defer.
They are deliberately short. Go lines are short, and the drill should teach the shape of the language rather than test your endurance with a long expression.

seo.h2: Practising the Go idioms
p: Start with the three highest-frequency sequences: `if err != nil {`, `for _, v := range`, and `defer x.Close()`. Type each twenty times slowly, then in a normal round. Automation of those three is worth more than raw speed.
Then add the punctuation that bites: the colon-equals, the ampersand for addresses, and the backtick for struct tags - which needs the key most typists have never used.

seo.h2: Other languages on this site
p: Same engine, different grammar: Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust, SQL, and Excel formulas. For layout questions, see keyboard layout for programmers.

faq.q: What typing speed do Go developers have?
faq.a: No one measures it formally. Most developers type prose at 60-90 WPM and real Go at 45-55, because braces and short declarations add right-hand reaches.

faq.q: Why is Go slower to type than Python?
faq.a: Go is brace-dense and every block closes with a reach, while Python uses indentation. Go also repeats the error-check idiom, which is fast only once it is automatic.

faq.q: Is this real Go?
faq.a: Yes - 36 lines of ordinary Go covering goroutines, channels, context, error wrapping, generics-era slices helpers, struct tags and tests.

faq.q: What should I drill first?
faq.a: `if err != nil {`, `for _, v := range` and `defer ...Close()`. Those three sequences cover a large share of real Go lines.

faq.q: How long until I see a gain?
faq.a: Two weeks of five-minute daily rounds usually shows 4-7 WPM on Go content, mostly from the brace reach and the := sequence becoming automatic.

pages.tldr: Go code is brace-dense: every function, block and struct literal opens and closes. Expect 45-55 WPM on real Go even if you type prose at 75; the limiting characters are { } and := on the right hand.

pages.title: Wrist Pain From Typing — Setup, Breaks, Red Flags
pages.metaDesc: What in a typing setup usually causes wrist and forearm discomfort, how to change it, and which symptoms need a clinician rather than a new keyboard.
pages.heroP: Most typing-related wrist discomfort comes from position and pace, not from the keyboard itself. This page covers the setup changes that help, the break pattern that matters, and the symptoms that are not a typing problem at all.

seo.h2: What usually causes it
p: Four factors account for most typing-related wrist and forearm discomfort: wrist extension (hands bent upwards because the keyboard sits too high), ulnar deviation (hands angled outwards towards the arrow keys), shoulder elevation (a desk that is too tall, or a laptop on a table), and unbroken duration (two hours without standing up).
None of those are about willpower or typing speed. They are geometry and timing, which is why they respond to setup changes rather than to practice.

seo.h2: Setup, in order of impact
p:
1. Keyboard height. Elbows at roughly 90 degrees, forearms level or slightly downward, wrists straight. If your wrists bend upwards, the keyboard is too high - lower the desk or raise the chair.
  2. Wrist support that supports, not presses. A palm rest should support the heel of the hand between bursts, not compress the wrist while typing. Resting the wrist on a hard desk edge is the single most common cause.
  3. Shoulders down. If your shoulders creep up, the desk is too tall for the chair, or the monitor is too low and you are leaning in.
  4. Keyboard angle. Flat, or slightly negative with the back edge raised. The little feet at the back tilt the keyboard the wrong way for wrist position.

seo.h2: The break pattern that actually helps
p: Thirty to forty-five minutes of typing, then two to three minutes away from the keyboard with the hands doing something else. Micro-breaks beat a single long break, because the load is cumulative and the recovery is what matters.
A useful rule: every time you stop to think, take your hands off the keyboard. Most typists rest their hands on the keys while thinking, which converts thinking time into sustained static load.

seo.h2: Pace and tension
p: Speed work can produce tension without producing pain at the time. If you notice yourself gripping the keyboard, pressing hard on the keys or holding your breath during a timed round, that is a sign to slow down rather than push.
Typing tests reward bursts, but sustained work rewards relaxation. The typists who can type for six hours are not the fastest in a one-minute test; they are the ones who never tense up.

seo.h2: Symptoms that are not a setup problem
p: See a clinician rather than adjusting your desk if you have any of: numbness or tingling in the fingers that persists after you stop typing, pain that wakes you at night, weakness or dropping objects, swelling, or pain that continues at rest for more than a week.
Those patterns are not explained by keyboard geometry, and no ergonomic change or typing drill addresses them. This page is about workstation setup, not about diagnosis or treatment.

seo.h2: What to change first if you only change one thing
p: Move the keyboard down until your wrists are straight, and stop resting them on the desk edge while typing. That single change addresses the most common cause and costs nothing.
If the discomfort continues after two weeks of the setup change plus regular breaks, treat it as a reason to get advice rather than a reason to buy a different keyboard.

faq.q: Can typing cause wrist pain?
faq.a: Sustained typing in an awkward position can produce discomfort in the wrists and forearms. It is usually related to keyboard height, wrist angle and unbroken duration rather than to typing itself.

faq.q: Should I use a wrist rest?
faq.a: For support between bursts, yes; while typing, no. A rest that compresses the wrist during typing can make things worse - the goal is a straight, floating wrist.

faq.q: How often should I take breaks?
faq.a: Every 30-45 minutes, for two to three minutes away from the keyboard. Micro-breaks are more effective than one long break at the end of the day.

faq.q: Does a mechanical keyboard help?
faq.a: It can reduce the force needed per keystroke for some people, but it does not fix wrist angle or duration. Setup comes first.

faq.q: When should I see a doctor?
faq.a: For persistent numbness or tingling, night pain, weakness, swelling, or pain at rest lasting more than a week. Those are not explained by keyboard position.

pages.tldr: Three changes fix most cases: keep wrists straight and floating (not resting on the desk edge), keep elbows near 90 degrees with feet supported, and break every 30-45 minutes. Numbness, tingling or pain that wakes you up needs a clinician, not an ergonomic adjustment.
